What they decided: In 2024 the State Planning Commission, with WRI India as knowledge partner and support from the British High Commission, convened a Heat Action Network of line departments, including disaster management, health, education, agriculture, environment and forests, and water. Together they wrote India’s first state-wide heat strategy, covering people, animals and ecosystems along three pathways: health and well-being, sustained resources and productivity, and cooling. It builds heat into schemes that already exist rather than starting new ones.

What changed: It is a strategy, not yet an evaluated programme. Departments are to take its recommendations to detailed project reports, with progress reviewed every 6–8 months. What it shows is a whole state, not one city, giving heat an owner across departments.

- Heat action plans: led by National governments; paid by Not documented; Departments in the Heat Action Network reporting progress every 6–8 months

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Pregnancy-scheme check-ups that screen for heat risk (proposed)

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Redevelopment tenders for informal settlements that set a limit on heat gain through walls and roofs (proposed)

- Green, cool cities: led by National governments; paid by Public budget; Forest and tree cover rising from 23.8% towards 33% by 2030–31

Source: Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024: Beating the Heat https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf

Source: WRI India: mapping the path to heat resilience in Tamil Nadu https://wri-india.org/perspectives/mapping-path-heat-resilience-tamil-nadu

Source: Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board, G.O. 215, 2023: the tree cover target https://tnpcb.gov.in/PDF/About_Us/Announcementgos/GoNo_215_101123.pdf

### Singapore’s heat rules for outdoor work (Singapore, 2023 onwards)

What happened: In one of the world’s densest, most humid cities, the commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than the outskirts, and builders, shipyard and landscape workers labour outdoors through it. A study of 355 workers found each hot day cost a median S$21 in lost income.

What they decided: In 2023 Singapore launched a national heat stress advisory, developed by the environment ministry and the National Environment Agency with the Ministry of Health and its expert panel on heat stress, based on wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), which counts humidity, sun and wind, with low, moderate and high levels. The Ministry of Manpower made employers check WBGT hourly at outdoor work, give at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy work at 32 °C or above, help new workers acclimatise, and enforced it.

What changed: In March and June 2024 the ministry inspected 250 workplaces and acted against 78, mainly for missing shaded rest breaks and acclimatisation. In September 2024 the rules were revised to follow the advisory’s three levels: at a WBGT of 33 °C or above, at least 15 minutes’ rest an hour is recommended for heavy work, new workers acclimatise over at least 7 days, and construction sites with contracts of S$5 million or more and shipyards are required to keep their own WBGT meters. Their effect on heat illness has not yet been publicly evaluated.

- Heat-safe work: led by National governments; paid by Employers; Outdoor worksites checking WBGT hourly and giving shaded rest breaks; workplaces inspected

- Heat action plans: led by Weather and climate services; paid by Not documented; Heat stress advisory with three WBGT risk levels, shown by location

- Green, cool cities: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Districts modelled for cooling through Cooling Singapore

Source: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment: Heat Stress Advisory, 2023 https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/press-release-heat-stress-advisory/

Source: Ministry of Manpower: enhanced heat stress measures, 2023 https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers

Source: HRD Asia: 78 of 250 worksites non-compliant, 2024 https://www.hcamag.com/asia/specialisation/employment-law/more-than-75-worksites-found-non-compliant-with-singapores-enhanced-heat-stress-measures-report/499570

Source: Ministry of Manpower: revised heat stress framework, 2024 https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2024/0906-revised-framework-to-guide-employers-and-protect-outdoor-workers-against-heat-stress

Source: Ministry of Manpower: heat stress measures for outdoor work https://www.mom.gov.sg/heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work

Source: NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024 https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf

Source: Cooling Singapore https://www.thegpsc.org/sites/gpsc/files/cooling_singapore_-_digital_urban_climate_twin.pdf

### Dhaka acts before the heat peaks (Dhaka, Bangladesh, 2023 onwards)

What happened: Bangladesh’s ‘feels-like’ temperature has risen by about 4.5 °C since 1980, and parts of Dhaka run more than 10 °C hotter than the countryside. In April 2024 a long heatwave closed schools for about 33 million children.

What they decided: In 2023 Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer, a post paid for by the Arsht-Rock foundation rather than the city, to bring heat planning together. The same year the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society’s heatwave early action protocol was approved: when forecasts pass 38 °C, warnings, drinking water, cooling stations and cash grants go out before the peak.

What changed: On 21 April 2024 the protocol was activated for Dhaka, with about CHF 500,000 from the IFRC’s emergency fund to reach some 124,000 people. Its effect on illness and deaths has not been publicly evaluated. What it shows is money and a plan agreed before the heat, released by a forecast.

- Anticipatory action: led by Community and civil society groups; paid by Not documented; Days from a 38 °C forecast to cash, water and warnings reaching people

- Cooling centres and check-ins: led by Community and civil society groups; paid by Not documented; Cooling stations open at three locations during the heatwave

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Philanthropy; A Chief Heat Officer bringing the city’s heat planning together

Source: Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, 2024 https://www.climatecentre.org/13733/red-crescent-activates-early-action-protocol-for-heatwaves-in-dhaka/

Source: Arsht-Rock: Dhaka North’s Chief Heat Officer, 2023 https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/

Source: World Bank, 2025 https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank

Source: NBC News: school closures, 2024 https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485

### Adapt the mechanism, not the city: how five cities organise for heat

From interviews with city officials in October and November 2024 and published material, as described in the report. These are examples of institutional practice, not evaluations of impact, and details may have changed since. Adapt the mechanism to your own powers, budgets and infrastructure; do not copy the city. (MCR2030, Urban Heat Risk Management Resource Package, 2025, https://mcr2030.undrr.org/publication/urban-heat-risk-management-resource-package)

#### Amadora, Portugal (pp. 15–20)

- The problem: Rising heat in a dense city with little room for green space, and older and low-income residents at most risk.

- How they work together: Civil Protection is the single focal point: it coordinates the departments, consolidates their information and runs the heatwave response, with the mayor’s support keeping heat a shared priority.

- Authority and money: About €1 million a year for heat activities within Civil Protection’s budget, which the city itself describes as not enough for comprehensive risk management.

- What reaches people: SMS alerts built with a private partner; the Red Cross, fire service and police help spread warnings; health and social teams visit 3,000–4,000 residents twice a week in summer; prepared cooled shelters.

- Still unresolved: Space for greenery in dense streets, and building codes still to be updated.

- Before adapting it, check: Is there one office that can convene the others and hold a heat budget? Who can do home visits at scale?

#### Incheon, Republic of Korea (pp. 21–27)

- The problem: More heatwave days and tropical nights, with elderly and low-income neighbourhoods most exposed; a sharp rise in heat illness in 2018.

- How they work together: National law treats heatwaves as a disaster, so heat sits inside the city’s disaster structure, led by a Natural Disaster Division, with district headquarters and field units.

- Authority and money: A local heat ordinance (2019) and national grants covering part of project costs; some protection is funded through welfare programmes rather than a heat budget.

- What reaches people: 1,340 heat shelters (2023), shelter locations shared in safety apps, nearly 7,000 volunteer ‘heatwave helpers’, and data analysis to find 52 priority areas for cooling facilities.

- Still unresolved: Competing land uses for urban forests, and long-term funding to scale up.

- Before adapting it, check: Does national law give local authorities a mandate and money for heat? Is there data on where older people live alone?

#### Cape Town, South Africa (pp. 34–40)

- The problem: Heat that falls hardest on low-income neighbourhoods and informal settlements, where most residents have little greenery and no air conditioning, pool or easy way to the beach.

- How they work together: A coordinating department convenes rather than implements, alongside existing structures: a business continuity committee, the disaster risk management centre and a climate forum.

- Authority and money: No dedicated national heat funding; the city relies on general grants, property taxes and tariffs.

- What reaches people: Outreach in the hottest areas, six spray parks in lower-income neighbourhoods, and cooling centres and real-time heat monitoring in planning.

- Still unresolved: Upkeep of green infrastructure, and resources to scale up public communication, including ‘message coupling’, which it plans to bring from its drought response to heat.

- Before adapting it, check: Is there a body that can convene without taking over others’ mandates? Who keeps essential services running in a heatwave?

#### Quito, Ecuador (pp. 28–33)

- The problem: A city centre up to 3 °C warmer than its surroundings, while a drought threatens water and hydropower.

- How they work together: Heat is managed inside the city’s long-term climate action plan, with an environment secretariat in the lead and the risk management secretariat alongside it.

- Authority and money: Funding from national, municipal, corporate and international sources; an ordinance on green and blue infrastructure.

- What reaches people: Nature-based solutions and planning rules, with community and international partners.

- Still unresolved: Heat is a lower national priority, and national weather data is incomplete.

- Before adapting it, check: Does your plan sit inside a wider climate plan with its own budget lines? Are the weather data you rely on maintained?

#### Nairobi, Kenya (pp. 41–45)

- The problem: Rapid development outpacing climate-sensitive planning, and the loss of green space.

- How they work together: Urban heat was made a priority for the first time; work sits with a small climate change department.

- Authority and money: Eight staff for all the department’s activities, no dedicated heat strategy yet, and limited funds.

- What reaches people: Forecasts from the national weather service reach the public through mainstream media; no dedicated heat warning yet.

- Still unresolved: Fragmented, siloed efforts across sectors; no local heat data; low public awareness.

- Before adapting it, check: Starting from little is common. What is the first decision, and the first piece of data, that would let the next step happen?

## Plain-language glossary of extreme heat

91 terms that come up again and again in extreme heat, explained in a sentence or two.

### What heat does to the body

- **Heatstroke**: A medical emergency. The body’s core temperature rises above about 40 °C and its cooling system fails. Without fast cooling it can kill or cause lasting organ damage.

- **Heat exhaustion**: The warning stage before heatstroke: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness and nausea. Rest, water and cooling usually bring recovery.

- **Heat stress**: When the body takes in or makes more heat than it can shed, from hot air, humidity, sun and physical work.

- **Acclimatisation**: The body slowly adjusting to heat over one to two weeks. New and returning workers are most at risk until it has.

- **Excess deaths**: Deaths above the normal number for that place and time of year. Because death certificates rarely say “heat”, this is how the real toll of a heatwave is counted.

- **Older people and heat**: With age, thirst fades and the body sweats less, so it cools more slowly and the heart works harder. Older people in a Kolkata informal settlement were 4.3 times more likely than those in a nearby village to face dangerous heat, because their homes stayed hot at night.

- **Heat in pregnancy**: A pregnant body runs warm and has less room to cool. Each 1 °C rise raises the odds of a preterm birth by about 5%, and a heatwave by about 16%.

- **Babies and young children in heat**: Babies and small children overheat and lose water faster than adults, and depend on someone else to notice. In 2014–2023, each infant in India faced an average of 7.7 heatwave days a year, 47% more than in the 1990s.

- **Heat, kidneys and the heart**: Sweating and dehydration make the heart work harder and can damage the kidneys, especially with repeated exposure. People already living with heart, kidney or lung conditions have less room to cope.

- **Sleep in the heat**: To fall asleep, the body needs to cool. On hot nights sleep comes later and ends sooner, so the next day starts already depleted. A study of 47,628 people’s sleep wristbands in 68 countries found hot nights cut sleep.

- **Heat and the mind**: Heat is linked to more anxiety, distress and suicide, and to worse outcomes for people living with mental illness.

- **When home is hotter than outside**: Thin metal roofs, small windows and crowded rooms can make a home hotter inside than out, worst at night. In Ahmedabad, people in informal settlements faced temperatures up to 7.6 °C higher than people in formal housing.

- **Kitchen heat**: Cooking over a fire in a small, smoky kitchen during a heatwave: a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes.

- **Heat illness first aid**: Heatstroke is an emergency, and cooling buys time: move the person to shade, cool them with water and fanning, call for help, and give small sips of water only if they are awake. Hot skin with confusion can mean heatstroke.

### How heat is measured

- **Wet-bulb temperature**: Heat and humidity combined into one number, read from a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth. It shows whether sweat can still cool you. A wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C is often quoted as the limit of human survival; recent studies suggest the real limit is lower.

- **Dry heat and humid heat**: Dry heat is high temperature with low humidity: sweat still evaporates, but the body soaks up heat fast. It peaks in South Asia’s pre-monsoon months. Humid heat is warm, wet air in which sweat can’t evaporate, so the body can’t cool itself even at lower temperatures. It dominates Southeast Asia and builds through South Asia’s monsoon, and it is rising faster than dry heat. The two need different warnings and different cooling.

- **WBGT (wet-bulb globe temperature)**: The workplace measure of heat. It adds sun and wind to heat and humidity, and is used to set rest breaks and stop work.

- **Heat index**: The “feels-like” temperature in the shade, combining air temperature and humidity. In the Philippines, a heat index of 42 °C or more is officially a danger level.

- **Heatwave**: A spell of unusually hot weather for that place. There is no single global definition: each country sets its own thresholds.

- **Hot nights**: Nights that stay too hot for the body to recover from the day. They are often more dangerous than hot days, and they are rising faster.

- **Urban heat island**: Cities running several degrees hotter than the countryside around them, especially at night, because of concrete, traffic, waste heat and few trees.

- **Mean radiant temperature**: The heat your body takes in from the sun and from hot surfaces around it: roads, walls and roofs. In strong sun it shapes how hot you feel more than air temperature does, which is why shade matters so much.

- **Thermal comfort**: How hot or cold a person feels. It depends on air temperature, humidity, wind, sun, clothing and activity, not on air temperature alone.

- **Climate attribution**: Working out how much climate change has added to an event or its harm. The 2026 Lancet Countdown attributes 71.5% of 2023’s heat deaths to climate change, and 11.3 of 13.5 heatwave days per person in 2025.

- **Undercounted heat deaths**: Heat deaths that are never recorded as heat deaths, because certificates name the immediate cause, such as a heart attack. In India in 2024, 185 heatstroke deaths were confirmed against 48,385 suspected heatstroke cases, up to 28 July.

### Acting before harm

- **Limits to adaptation**: The point beyond which adjusting no longer prevents harm. Places used to heat cope better with days of 30–35 °C, but a study of 2.7 million firms found no adaptation to days above 40 °C. Cutting emissions keeps more places below that limit.

- **Heat action plan**: A city’s or country’s plan for the heat season: who issues warnings, at what temperature, and what hospitals, employers and services do next.

- **Early warning system**: A forecast that reaches people in time, in a form they understand, with clear advice on what to do.

- **Anticipatory action**: Acting on a forecast, before a disaster peaks, by releasing pre-agreed money and help when a trigger is reached.

- **Cooling centre**: A public place, such as a library, school or community hall, kept cool during heatwaves for people with no cool space at home.

- **Community of fate**: People whose wellbeing becomes connected through shared places, work, institutions, services or ecological conditions, such as a market, a school's catchment or a supply chain, even when their exposure, money, rights and say in decisions are unequal. Common Shade uses the phrase as a lens, not a measured finding: see Who shares the heat (beattheheat.asia/shared-heat/).

- **Resilience**: As Common Shade uses it: the ability of people and institutions to see heat coming and reduce the risk, respond when it arrives, recover without falling further behind, and change the arrangements that cause the same harm every year. It rests on a household's own means and on dependable shared services, institutions and public investment.

- **Chief heat officer**: A city official whose job is heat: joining up health, water, power, schools and work so that protection is planned before the hot season. Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first in 2023.

- **Heat alert levels**: Graded warnings, such as caution, danger and extreme danger, set at levels of heat that harm health locally. A good plan ties each level to named actions, so a warning switches protection on.

- **Work–rest cycle**: Building shaded rest into each hour of hot, heavy work. In Singapore, employers must give at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy outdoor work at a wet-bulb globe temperature of 32 °C or more.

- **Ward-level heat plan**: A heat action plan that maps risk neighbourhood by neighbourhood, using felt heat, warm nights and who lives there, so help goes first where risk is highest. Thane, next to Mumbai, built its 2024 plan this way.

- **Heat-resilient city**: A city that moves beyond emergency response each hot season towards lasting change in its buildings, water, transport, work, health services and cooling, with the people most exposed to heat at the centre. This is how India's Heat Resilient Cities Framework (2026) describes it.

- **Heat resilience plan**: A city plan for heat that grows out of a heat action plan. It starts by mapping hotspots and who is most exposed, then sets out interventions for the next one or two years, within a longer-term perspective across city systems. Some Indian cities are setting up urban disaster management authorities to lead them.

- **Core elements of a heat plan**: WHO/Europe’s checklist for a complete heat–health action plan: governance, a warning system, people at risk, communication, a resilient health system, reducing exposure, surveillance, and monitoring and learning.

- **Heat and learning**: Lost schooling when heat closes schools or makes classrooms too hot to learn in. In April 2024, Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children, and 5,288 schools in the Philippines moved to remote learning.

- **Heat check-ins**: A call or a knock for people who live alone or can’t easily leave home. In Chicago’s 1995 heatwave, living alone and not leaving home were among the strongest risks of dying.

- **Heat in closed places**: Prisons, hostels, care homes and crowded shelters, where people can’t leave for shade. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy names prisoners among the groups it is meant to reach, and proposes cool roofs and trees for its jails.

- **Clinics in a heatwave**: Heatwaves bring surges of patients just as staff, power and supplies are under strain. In 2024, Indian hospitals prepared heatstroke rooms, ice baths and cooled beds before the peak.

- **Warning the hospitals first**: A heat warning that reaches clinics a day or two early, so they can add staff, stock fluids and clear beds. After Ahmedabad’s plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an evaluation estimated about 1,190 deaths a year were avoided.

- **Cool classrooms**: A hot classroom is hard to learn in, and when it becomes unsafe, schools close. In 2024, heatwaves disrupted the schooling of 171 million students; South Asia was the most affected region.

### Money and protection

- **Parametric insurance**: Insurance that pays out automatically when a measured trigger, such as a temperature threshold, is crossed. There is no claim form and no damage assessment.

- **Basis risk**: When the trigger and the real loss don’t match: people suffer from the heat, but the threshold isn’t crossed and no payout comes.

- **Risk pool**: A group of countries, cities or insurers that share the cost of disasters, so no single member carries a catastrophe alone.

- **Social protection**: Public support such as pensions, cash transfers and unemployment benefits that keeps households out of poverty when income stops.

- **Shock-responsive social protection**: Public support that can grow or reach more people when a shock such as a heatwave or flood arrives, often by paying early through an existing scheme's list of recipients.

- **Last-mile access gap**: The distance between a scheme on paper and support in hand: people who qualify but do not know about it, lack the documents or cannot complete the steps.

- **Lost work hours**: Work that heat makes unsafe or impossible. The 2026 Lancet Countdown estimates 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, with farm workers losing twice as many hours as any other sector.

- **Informal work**: Work without a formal contract, sick pay or social insurance, often outdoors: street vending, construction, farm and home-based work. An OECD report estimates heat costs informal workers about 2.4% of working hours, against 1.4% for formal workers.

- **Adaptation finance gap**: The difference between what countries say they need to adapt to climate change and the money that arrives. Forty-eight countries put their health adaptation needs at about US$3.3 billion a year; international funding committed in 2024 covered about a third.

- **Heat and credit**: How heat travels from wages to lenders: lost working hours mean missed repayments, and lenders face a cash crunch. About 60% of India’s ₹3.81 trillion microfinance portfolio is in farming and allied work.

### Cooling, land and systems

- **Passive cooling**: Cooling a building without using power: shade, airflow, insulation, orientation and reflective surfaces.

- **Cool roof**: A roof painted or built to reflect sunlight, so less heat reaches the room below.

- **Refrigerant**: The fluid inside air conditioners and fridges that carries heat away. Many common ones are powerful greenhouse gases if they leak.

- **Black carbon**: Soot from diesel, wood, coal and brick kilns. It warms the air, and when it settles on snow and ice it darkens them so they melt faster.

- **Vicious cycle**: A harm that feeds itself: each turn of the loop makes the next one worse. This map shows where those loops could be interrupted.

- **Maladaptation**: A response to heat that makes things worse elsewhere or later, such as air conditioners that cool a room but heat the street.

- **Albedo**: How much sunlight a surface reflects. A white roof has a high albedo and stays cooler; dark asphalt has a low albedo and stores heat.

- **Aquifer**: Underground layers of rock or sand that hold groundwater, the water that wells and pumps draw from.

- **The cooling gap**: The difference between people who can stay cool and those who can’t. Air conditioning may have prevented about 360,000 deaths a year in 2022 and 2023, but only about 3% of households in the poorest countries have it.

- **Cooling demand**: How much cooling people need, and the energy it takes. Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could rise from about 40 million to 300 million by 2040, half of them in Indonesia.

- **Peak power demand**: The highest electricity load of the day or year, which in hot countries comes with heat and air conditioning. In May and June 2023, heat drove demand up in northern Viet Nam as hydropower reservoirs ran low; blackouts cost about US$1.4 billion.

- **Glacier loss**: Mountain ice shrinking faster than snow can replace it. In the Hindu Kush Himalaya, glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s than in the decade before, and could lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100.

- **Peat fires**: Fires that smoulder in drained peatland, the thick, wet soil of tropical swamps. Once dry, peat burns underground for weeks and fills the air with haze. Indonesia’s 2015 forest and peat fires cost an estimated US$16.1 billion.

- **Cold chains in the heat**: Every fridge and cool box from the factory to the patient or the plate. Without reliable power, fridges for food, medicines and vaccines fail; 526 million tonnes of food are lost each year for lack of refrigeration.

- **When phones go quiet**: Phone masts and networks need power and cooling too. In Bangladesh in 2026, mobile signals weakened as blackouts spread; warnings, mobile payments and calls for help all ride on them.

- **Power grids in a heatwave**: Demand peaks as everyone switches on cooling, just as hot lines and transformers struggle. An early World Bank estimate put the cost of northern Viet Nam’s power cuts in May and June 2023 at US$1.4 billion.

- **Water for power, power for water**: Many power plants need water to cool, and water pumps need power to run, so in a heatwave each strains the other. In 2016, India lost 14 TWh of electricity because thermal power plants ran short of water.

- **The diesel fallback**: When the grid fails, homes, shops and hospitals that can afford it switch to diesel generators, which keep the lights on and add to the heat and the smoke. There are 20 to 30 million back-up generator sites in low- and middle-income countries.

- **Roads and rails in the heat**: Steel rails expand and can buckle, so trains slow; roads soften; hot, thin air means planes need longer runways. Journeys, shifts and supplies, including medicines and food, are delayed.

### Nature in the city

- **Evapotranspiration**: Water evaporating from soil and leaves. It draws heat out of the air, so well-watered plants cool their surroundings. Plants short of water stop cooling.

- **Nature-based solutions**: Using living systems such as trees, wetlands, soils and water to tackle problems like heat and flooding while also benefiting people and nature. A park only works as one if it is planned for those benefits and kept alive.

- **Ecosystem services**: The benefits people get from nature: shade and cooling, cleaner air and water, rain soaking into the ground, food and places to rest. The same service is worth most to those with the fewest alternatives, such as cooling for people without air conditioning.

- **Blue-green infrastructure**: A network of water (blue) and plants and soil (green), such as rivers, ponds, wetlands, parks and planted drains, designed to manage rain and heat together.

- **Grey infrastructure**: Engineered, mostly concrete systems such as pipes, drains, embankments and pumps. Many good solutions mix grey and green.

- **Sponge city**: A city designed to soak up, store, clean and slowly release rainwater through parks, wetlands, permeable ground and planted drains, not only pipes. China piloted it in 30 cities from 2014 to 2019; Chennai and Bangkok are building sponge parks.

- **Co-benefits**: The extra gains a measure brings beyond its main aim, such as a park built to hold floodwater that also cools the street and gives children somewhere to play.

- **Ecosystem-based adaptation**: Using nature to help people adapt to climate change, such as mangroves against storm surges or trees for shade. A kind of nature-based solution.

- **Green gentrification**: When a new park or greening raises rents and land prices so much that the poorer residents it was meant to help are pushed out.

- **Environmental justice**: A fair share of environmental benefits and harms, and a fair say in decisions about them. Poorer neighbourhoods are often hotter and less green.

- **Agroforestry**: Growing trees alongside crops or livestock. The trees shade the soil, help it hold moisture and give farmers another source of income.

- **Hot nights and crops**: Crops need cool nights too. At the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, rice yields fell about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature.

- **City trees under heat**: Heat, drought and missing upkeep can kill street trees just when their shade is needed. Across 164 cities, 56% of urban tree and shrub species already face temperatures beyond their natural range, and 76% could by 2050.

- **Shade follows wealth**: Trees and parks cluster in better-off neighbourhoods, which can pay for them and their upkeep, so poorer districts stay hotter. In Jakarta, green space is concentrated in wealthier areas while dense low-income neighbourhoods act as heat islands.

- **When dry soil heats the air**: Moist soil cools the air as its water evaporates. When soil dries, that cooling stops, so the air heats faster and dries the soil further: a loop that water kept in the ground can break.

- **Asia’s last tropical ice**: On Puncak Jaya in Papua, Indonesia, 99% of the glacier area has gone since 1850. About 0.17 km² was left in 2024, and it will very likely disappear around 2030.

- **Heat, drought and salt water**: Heat and drought lower rivers and canals, and the sea pushes inland. In Viet Nam’s Mekong Delta in February 2024, farmers who pumped salty canal water onto their rice lost up to half their crop.

## Organisations working on extreme heat

367 organisations across Asia and the world already working on parts of the web of extreme heat. Inclusion describes relevant published work. It does not imply partnership, affiliation or endorsement.

Each organisation is marked with its main side in a heat alliance. Demand: Holds the need or the duty to protect people: governments and public agencies, employers, and organisations of the workers and communities affected. Supply: Provides what protection needs: technology, services and delivery on the ground, insurance, lending and grants, research and data. Platform: Connects demand and supply: networks, alliances and conveners, and the bodies that set shared rules or standards for a market. Many play more than one part; this is the main one.

Choose a place, an action, a part played or a kind of organisation to narrow the list. A place is where the listed work is, as each listing describes it; it is not where an organisation has its office. The list shows what this site has found so far, so a short list for a place describes this list, not that place.

Every link was opened by an automated check on 17 November 2026. A listing says so where its link did not answer, where the site turned the check away, or where the link opens only a homepage.

### Global networks and organisations

- Global Heat Health Information Network (WHO, WMO and NOAA) (Platform; Network or alliance; Global): A member-driven forum of scientists, practitioners and policymakers. Its resource library gathers guidance on heat warnings, heat action plans and case studies, heat at work and heat in cities. (https://heathealth.info/resource-library/)

- International Labour Organization (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Sets out the evidence and standards for protecting workers from heat stress. (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80)

- UNICEF (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Tracks how heatwaves and other climate hazards disrupt children’s schooling. (https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024)

- Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance (Platform; Network or alliance; Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Philippines, Viet Nam): An alliance of humanitarian, development and research partners with Zurich Insurance Group. In 2024 it expanded from floods to extreme heat, with work in countries including Bangladesh and Nepal. Its 2026 study of heat early warning systems covered eight countries, among them Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, the Philippines and Vietnam. (https://zcralliance.org/resources/?q=heat)

- Heat Resilience Action (HERA), formerly Climate Resilience for All (Platform; Non-profit organisation; India): Works on extreme heat with a focus on women and low-income communities. With SEWA and Swiss Re, it combined insurance payouts and cash for lost income after India’s 2024 heatwaves. (https://heranow.org/resources/as-extreme-heat-threats-grow-can-heat-insurance-offer-protection/)

- UNEP Cool Coalition (Platform; Network or alliance; Global): A global network for clean, efficient cooling and cooler cities. With the COP30 Presidency, it runs Beat the Heat, an initiative supporting cities in the Global South with heat assessments and cooling action. (https://coolcoalition.org)

- Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre (Supply; Red Cross or Red Crescent; Global): Wrote the Heatwave Guide for Cities with more than 25 partners, covering how cities prepare for, respond to and learn from heatwaves. (https://preparecenter.org/resource/heatwave-guide-for-cities)

- Sustainable Energy for All (Platform; Non-profit organisation; Global): Measures who lacks access to cooling through its Chilling Prospects series. (https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023)

- International Energy Agency (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Analyses cooling demand and how efficiency standards can cut it. (https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-cooling)

- Practical Action (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Bangladesh, Nepal): Connects heat risk intelligence, local action, practical technology, institutions and finance, following a Sense → Decide → Act → Sustain logic. In Nepal, Dhangadhi’s heat action plan links temperature, humidity and health data, hotspot mapping and community views to thresholds and set municipal responses. In Bangladesh, heat is being built into early warning and livelihood work. A partner in the Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance. (https://practicalaction.org/news-stories/zurich-climate-resilience-alliance-to-expand-focus-on-destructive-extreme-heat/)

- People’s Courage International (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Across the region): Works on safe migration and labour protection for migrant workers in South and Southeast Asia. Its Migrants Resilience Collaborative supports more than seven million households. (https://www.weforum.org/organizations/peoples-courage-international/)

- World Bank (Supply; UN or multilateral body; Across the region): Its 2026 report A Livable Future finds extreme heat already costs South Asia the equivalent of about 31 million full-time jobs a year, and sets out how cities can protect jobs and growth. (https://www.worldbank.org/en/region/sar/publication/a-livable-future-protecting-jobs-and-growth-from-extreme-heat-in-south-asia-s-cities)

- World Meteorological Organization (Platform; UN or multilateral body; India): With WHO, runs the South Asia Climate–Health Desk with India’s meteorological agencies, turning weather and climate information into health protection. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- C40 Cities (Platform; Network or alliance; India, Singapore): Its Cool Cities Accelerator brings together cities including Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Mumbai and Singapore on early warnings, building standards and tree cover. (https://www.deccanherald.com/india/karnataka/bengaluru/bengaluru-joins-global-coalition-to-beat-extreme-heat-3786724)

- Vital Strategies (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Thailand): Through the Partnership for Healthy Cities, supports Bangkok to pilot heat-health action in high-risk districts: outdoor worker protection, cooling spaces and drinking water. (https://www.nationthailand.com/pr-news/40071201)

- Global Buildings Performance Network (Supply; Network or alliance; India): Works on residential building codes in India and Southeast Asia, where demand for cooling homes is rising fastest. (https://gbpn.org/news-gbpn-sharpens-its-focus-decarbonising-housing-india-and-south-east-asia)

- Start Network (Platform; Network or alliance; Pakistan): Its members run heatwave anticipatory action in Pakistan, releasing funds automatically when forecasts cross agreed triggers. (https://startnetwork.org/news-and-blogs/getting-ahead-deadly-heat)

- Mercy Corps (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Nepal): A Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance partner leading work on extreme heat in Nepal, where the southern plains passed 40 °C on 50 days in 2024. (https://europe.mercycorps.org/sites/default/files/2025-09/too-hot-to-ignore.pdf)

- United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Thailand): Helps governments connect heat resilience with health systems, urban planning and finance. Its work includes a financing strategy for tackling urban heat in Bangkok. (https://www.undp.org/thailand/publications/bangkok-financing-strategy-tackling-urban-heat)

- UN-Habitat (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Develops guidance on urban heat management, helping cities combine planning, building design, green infrastructure and cooling to protect vulnerable residents. (https://unhabitat.org/handbook-on-urban-heat-management-in-the-global-south)

- UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Helps governments strengthen heat risk governance through practical assessment tools, coordinated planning and investment across sectors and levels of government. (https://www.undrr.org/our-work/extreme-heat-resilience)

- Resilient Cities Network (Platform; Network or alliance; Across the region): Works with cities and communities on heat resilience, including indoor heat monitoring and locally designed cooling in Southeast Asian cities. (https://resilientcitiesnetwork.org/heat-stays-in-peoples-homes/)

- ICLEI South Asia (Platform; Network or alliance; India, Bangladesh, Nepal): Supports cities with heat risk assessments, heat action plans, urban greening and preparedness tools in India, Nepal and Bangladesh. (https://southasia.iclei.org/news/extreme-heat-new-knowledge-products-highlight-need-to-build-resilience-adaptation/)

- United Cities and Local Governments Asia-Pacific (UCLG ASPAC) (Platform; Network or alliance; Bangladesh, Philippines): Provides technical assistance for urban heat resilience, including work with Iloilo City in the Philippines and Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh. (https://uclg-aspac.org/turning-the-heat-into-action-how-iloilo-city-and-coxs-bazar-respond-to-urban-heat/)

- Women in Informal Employment: Globalizing and Organizing (WIEGO) (Demand; Worker organisation; Global): Documents how heat affects informal workers’ health and earnings, and develops worker education, policy recommendations and protection guidance with local organisations. (https://www.wiego.org/research-library-publications/working-heat-street-vendors-delhi-india/)

- International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) (Platform; Red Cross or Red Crescent; Global): Mobilises national societies and communities to prepare for heatwaves and reach people at risk, including through its global Heat Action Day campaign. (https://www.ifrc.org/get-involved/campaign-us/heat-action-day)

- Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN) (Platform; Network or alliance; India): Supports locally relevant climate knowledge and partnerships, including heat early warning, urban health resilience and preparedness planning in India. (https://cdkn.org/project/urban-health-and-climate-resilience-in-india)

- United for Efficiency (UNEP-led) (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Across the region): Helps countries strengthen appliance efficiency policies and standards, including work across Southeast Asia on efficient, climate-friendly air conditioning. (https://united4efficiency.org/project/asean/)

- Humanity & Inclusion (HI) (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Across the region): Sets out disability-inclusive approaches to climate action, including accessible early warnings, which people with disabilities often lack. A heat-specific programme in Asia is not confirmed. (https://www.hi-canada.org/sn_uploads/Disability-Inclusive-approaches-to-climate-action_1.pdf)

- Human Rights Watch (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Global): Documents how extreme heat endangers older people and people with disabilities, and how heat and climate plans leave them out. (https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/06/30/extreme-heat-signals-need-inclusive-climate-action)

- World Health Organization (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Indonesia): Supports Indonesian heat-health coordination and publishes occupational heat guidance with WMO. (https://www.who.int/news/item/22-08-2025-who-wmo-issue-new-report-and-guidance-to-protect-workers-from-increasing-heat-stress)

- The Conduit Foundation (Platform; Non-profit organisation; Global): Develops an urban-heat workstream connecting city leaders and finance. (https://www.conduitfoundation.org.uk/programmes-impact)

- International Union of Food, Agricultural, Hotel, Restaurant, Catering, Tobacco and Allied Workers’ Associations (IUF) (Demand; Worker organisation; Global): Calls for negotiated heat protection covering migrant, seasonal and informal workers. (https://www.iuf.org/news/iuf-call-to-action-on-extreme-heat/)

- Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Co-produced the extreme heat and agriculture report. (https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/extreme-heat-is-pushing-agrifood-systems-to-the-brink-worldwide/en)

- ICLEI: Local Governments for Sustainability (Platform; Network or alliance; Global): Supports urban heat governance and heat-relevant planning tools. (https://iclei.org/heat-action-day/)

- UN Environment Programme (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Global): Convenes heat-resilience and sustainable-cooling initiatives. (https://www.unep.org/interactives/beat-the-heat/)

- Freetown City Council (Demand; City or district government; Sierra Leone): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://fcc.gov.sl/freetown-joins-global-effort-to-tackle-deadly-extreme-heat/)

- City of Athens (Demand; City or district government; Greece): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://www.cityofathens.gr)

- International Organization for Standardization (Platform; Standards body; Global): Publishes the WBGT-based occupational heat-stress screening standard. (https://www.iso.org)

- Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), India programme (Supply; Non-profit organisation; India): Works with Indian cities and states on heat action plans. It developed Ahmedabad's 2013 heat action plan, the first in South Asia, with the Indian Institute of Public Health-Gandhinagar, and reviews heat policy in India. (https://nrdcindia.org/pdf/extreme-heat-India-report1.pdf)

### Governments and regional bodies in Asia

- National Disaster Management Authority, India (Demand; Government body; India): Issues national guidance for state and city heat action plans. (https://ndma.gov.in)

- Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with IIPH Gandhinagar and NRDC (Demand; City or district government; India): Launched South Asia’s first heat action plan in 2013: early warnings, public outreach and training for medical staff. (https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/new-evidence-shows-pioneering-heat-action-plan-helps-millions-avoid-killer-heat)

- Dhaka North City Corporation (Demand; City or district government; Bangladesh): Appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer in 2023, focused on cooling the poorest neighbourhoods. (https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/310693/arsht-rock-bangladesh%E2%80%99s-first-chief-heat-officer)

- Nepal Red Cross Society (Supply; Red Cross or Red Crescent; Nepal): Published the Dhangadhi Heat Action Plan in 2025 with the Climate Centre, setting out when and where to act before and during heatwave days in a city that passes 40 °C every year. (https://www.climatecentre.org/publications/16234/dhangadhi-heat-action-plan-2025/)

- Department of Education, Philippines (Demand; Government body; Philippines): Lets school heads suspend in-person classes when the heat index is dangerous, and moved the school year back to a June start to keep classes out of the hottest months. (https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1940232/deped-all-set-for-june-school-opening-in-25)

- Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (Supply; Red Cross or Red Crescent; Bangladesh): Runs an early action protocol for heat, first activated in April 2024 during Dhaka’s longest recorded heatwave. - ICIMOD (Platform; UN or multilateral body; India): Monitors the Himalaya’s snow and ice, and helps brick kilns switch to cleaner technology that cuts the soot darkening the glaciers. (https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/existing-solutions-could-slash-soot-emissions-by-80-by-2030-icimod)

- Asian Development Bank (Supply; UN or multilateral body; Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Cambodia): Supports heat resilience in Asian cities, including technical assistance on heat stress among women and girls in Bangladesh, Cambodia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Tajikistan. Its 2026 report on the heat crisis in Thailand and Southeast Asia calls for mobilising public and private finance, and proposes a heat action plan for Thailand. (https://www.preventionweb.net/publication/beating-heat-investing-pro-poor-solutions-urban-resilience)

- UN ESCAP (Platform; UN or multilateral body; Bangladesh, Philippines): Helps fast-growing cities in South and Southeast Asia plan for extreme urban heat, working with Iloilo City and Cox’s Bazar. - PAGASA, Philippines (Demand; Weather service; Philippines): Issues heat index warnings with danger levels that local governments use to decide when to suspend classes. (https://www.gmanetwork.com/regionaltv/news/115185/pagasa-urges-public-to-brace-for-more-intense-heat/story/)

- Ministry of Manpower, Singapore (Demand; Government body; Singapore): Requires hourly wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) checks on outdoor worksites, shaded rest breaks when heat stress is high, and time for new workers to acclimatise, and enforces the rules. ### Research and evidence

- Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) (Supply; Research body; India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan): Assessed heat risk in all 734 districts of India in 2025, finding 57% of districts, home to three in four Indians, at high or very high risk. Its 2026 heat-health reports for the GHHIN South Asia hub cover India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan, and it helped Thane build its heat action plan. (https://www.ceew.in/publications?field_focus_area_tid=All&field_pub_type_tid=All&field_authors_target_id_selective=All&title=heat)

- Lancet Countdown (Supply; Research body; Place not stated in the listing): Tracks heat deaths, lost working hours and other health impacts of climate change every year. (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1)

- NUS Heat Resilience & Performance Centre (Platform; Research body; Singapore): Hosts the Southeast Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network, bringing governments and partners together on heat and health. (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/newsletters/issue54/dossier/nus-centre-designated-southeast-asia-hub-for-global-heat-health-info-exchange)

- Cornell Global Labor Institute (Supply; Research body; Bangladesh, Viet Nam, Cambodia): With Schroders, mapped heat and flood risk in garment hubs including Dhaka, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Phnom Penh, and found few fashion brands require heat protection in their supplier codes. (https://www.ilr.cornell.edu/global-labor-institute/higher-ground-fashions-climate-breakdown)

- International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) (Supply; Research body; Philippines): Showed from its Philippine farm that warmer nights cut rice yields, and breeds rice that copes better with heat. (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101)

- icddr,b (Supply; Research body; Bangladesh): Works with Bangladesh’s Department of Agricultural Extension and others on HeatShield, which helps farmers cope with extreme heat. (https://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/perspective/who-owns-the-response-to-heat-in-bangladesh-everyone-does/)

- BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health (Supply; Research body; India): Part of a South Asian partnership with CEEW, NRDC, UN ESCAP and the Global Heat Health Information Network assessing heat-health action across countries. (https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-sfc-nrdc-unescap-brac-jpgsph-ghhin-countries-synthesis-press-release.pdf)

- IISER Pune (Supply; Research body; India): Leads the South Asia Scientific Research Consortium on how heat affects different populations, with Rockefeller Foundation support. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) (Supply; Research body; Bangladesh): Has researched the health and economic toll of heat stress on informal workers in urban Bangladesh. (https://www.iied.org/node/83215)

- Heat and Health Research Centre, University of Sydney (Supply; Research body; Bangladesh): Tested low-cost cooling for Bangladeshi garment workers: fans, drinking water and reflective roofs recovered much of the 12–15% output lost to heat. (https://www.sydney.edu.au/news-opinion/news/2025/10/21/garment-factories-are-sweltering--these-simple-fixes-could-keep-.html)

- Salata Institute, Harvard University (Supply; Research body; India): Published Critical Perspectives on Extreme Heat in India in 2026, covering heat action plans, insurance and informal work. (https://salatainstitute.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/April-2026-Critical-Perspectives-on-Extreme-Heat-in-India_web.pdf)

- WRI India (Supply; Research body; India): Works on heat mitigation planning with Indian cities, including greening and cooling pilots in Kochi and Mumbai and the Bengaluru Heat Collective. (https://india.mongabay.com/2025/04/safeguarding-indian-cities-from-heat-in-conversation-with-sudeshna-chatterjee-interview/)

- Good Business Lab (Supply; Research body; India, Bangladesh): Researching heat, health and gender in India’s and Bangladesh’s garment sector, 2025–2027. (https://lirneasia.net/futureworksasia/projects/heat-health-and-gender/)

- Integrated Research and Action for Development (IRADe) (Supply; Research body; India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka): Develops heat hotspot assessments and gender-sensitive heat action plans in India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. (https://irade.org/Rajkot-Heat-Action-Plan.pdf)

- Indian Institute for Human Settlements (IIHS) (Supply; Research body; India): Researches urban heat and tests passive and low-energy cooling shelters that give outdoor workers safe places to rest and recover. (https://iihs.co.in/publication/evaluating-indoor-thermal-resilience-of-passive-and-low-power-cooling-shelters-for-outdoor-workers-in-india/)

- Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP) (Supply; Research body; India): Builds heat intelligence and decision-support tools for Indian cities, including the BHRIGU National Heat Insights Explorer. (https://cstep.in/projects/building-heat-resilience-in-indias-growing-urbanscapes-bhrigu/)

- The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) (Supply; Research body; Place not stated in the listing): Researches thermal comfort, efficient buildings and sustainable cooling, combining passive design with better cooling equipment. (https://www.teriin.org/project/sheetal-alliance-sustainable-habitat-energy-efficiency-and-thermal-comfort-all-cooling)

- Sustainable Futures Collaborative (Supply; Research body; Place not stated in the listing): Studies heat action plans and their implementation gaps, and how policy, finance and social protection can make heat resilience last. (https://www.sustainablefutures.org/blog/beyond-heat-action-plans-inclusive-heat-policy-needs-grounded-research-and-collaborative-action/)

- Karachi Urban Lab (Supply; Research body; Pakistan): Researches how low-income residents and informal workers in Karachi live with heat, including access to shade, cooling, water and reliable infrastructure. (https://www.karachiurbanlab.com/projects/cool-infrastructures-life-with-heat-in-the-off-grid-city.html)

- Singapore Management University, Urban Institute (Supply; Research body; Singapore): Studies urban heat vulnerability and cooling through the Cooling Singapore collaboration, linking neighbourhood conditions to climate-sensitive planning. ### Working on the ground

- Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) (Demand; Worker organisation; India): Protects women informal workers’ income in heatwaves. After the May 2024 heatwaves, more than 46,000 members received insurance payouts. (https://www.swissre.com/our-business/public-sector-solutions/insights/parametric-structure-for-sewa-in-south-east-asia.html)

- Mahila Housing Trust (Supply; Non-profit organisation; India): Cools homes in informal settlements with reflective and modular roofs, and runs heat income insurance for women workers. (https://citizenmatters.in/new-cool-roof-solutions-heat-in-informal-settlements/)

- ADRA India (Supply; Non-profit organisation; India): Ran an anticipatory heatwave response in 2025 with national and district authorities. (https://adraindia.org/anticipatory-heatwave-response-in-2025/)

- HomeNet Thailand (Demand; Worker organisation; Thailand): With WIEGO, surveyed more than 1,000 informal workers in Bangkok on heat: nearly 80% had cut their hours. A trusted link between workers and authorities. (https://www.wiego.org/research-library-publications/climate-change-and-heat-stress-impacts-bangkok-thailand/)

- All India Disaster Mitigation Institute (AIDMI) (Supply; Non-profit organisation; India): An Ahmedabad-based institute that helps Indian states, districts and cities turn heat warnings into local action. It supports local heat action planning, surveyed 121 street vendors, auto drivers and construction and domestic workers in Lucknow on how heat hits their work, offers Afat Vimo disaster microinsurance to low-income families, and runs a regular southasiadisasters.net series on extreme heat. (https://aidmi.org/key-resources-on-extreme-heat-cooling/)

- SEEDS (Supply; Non-profit organisation; India): Combines building-level heat risk mapping, community preparedness and affordable cool roofs for vulnerable urban settlements in India. (https://www.seedsindia.org/portfolio/partnering-to-strengthen-climate-resilience/)

- SELCO Foundation (Supply; Non-profit organisation; Place not stated in the listing): Develops sustainable energy and cooling for underserved communities, including thermally comfortable buildings, cool roofs and decentralised cold storage. (https://selcofoundation.org/built-environments/)

(https://www.chintan-india.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/HEAT-SOLUTIONS-FOR-WEB-final.pdf)

- Hasiru Dala (Demand; Worker organisation; India): Works with waste workers in Bengaluru to document heat-related health and income losses and press for water, shade, safer housing and workplace protection. (https://hasirudala.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/HW-HD-report_final.pdf)

### Insurance and finance

- Atlantic Council Climate Resilience Center (formerly Arsht-Rock) (Platform; Non-profit organisation; Place not stated in the listing): Places Chief Heat Officers in cities, and with SEWA tested the world’s first parametric insurance for extreme heat in 2023. (https://onebillionresilient.org/project/extreme-heat-protection-initiative/)

- Swiss Re (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; Place not stated in the listing): Designed heat insurance for SEWA members with payout triggers set for each of 23 locations’ own climate. (https://www.swissre.com/our-business/public-sector-solutions/insights/parametric-structure-for-sewa-in-south-east-asia.html)

- IBISA (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; India): Launched a parametric heat-index product in Ahmedabad in 2024 that pays women workers when heat cuts their working hours, and Ushma Kavach, which protects dairy farmers against heat-stress losses. - ICICI Lombard (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; India): Carries the risk on heat insurance for women workers in India, including IBISA’s heat-index product. (https://www.icmif.org/news_story/ibisa-launches-a-new-parametric-heat-index-product-in-india-to-protect-women-workers-from-heat-induced-wage-losses/)

- Howden (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; Place not stated in the listing): Insurance broker working on parametric heat insurance and catastrophe bonds that give local governments and relief organisations money to act during heatwaves. (https://www.howdengroup.com/uk-en/news-insights/article-name/parametric-insurance-for-extreme-heat-protecting-people-in-a-warming-world)

- Climate Policy Initiative (Supply; Research body; India): Analyses how heat resilience in India is financed, and where money is missing. (https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/financing-indias-heat-resilience/)

- International Finance Corporation (IFC) (Supply; UN or multilateral body; Place not stated in the listing): Supports private investment in sustainable cooling, including district cooling, cooling-as-a-service and temperature-controlled food supply chains. (https://www.ifc.org/en/what-we-do/programs-projects/sustainable-cooling)

- Basel Agency for Sustainable Energy (BASE) (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; Place not stated in the listing): Develops financing models for sustainable cooling, such as cooling-as-a-service, where customers pay for cooling and providers own and maintain the equipment. Dastur Insurance and Reinsurance Brokers (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; India): Indian broker and partner, with Go Digit and Jan Sahas, in a temperature-triggered heat cover that pays migrant workers automatically. Dastur, and heat protection with Mahila Housing Trust. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/godigit_digitinsurance-heatinsurance-parametricinsurance-activity-7341758644490764288-StEd)

### Banks, regulators and microfinance

- Monetary Authority of Singapore (Platform; Government body; Singapore): Its 2020 environmental risk guidelines expect banks to assess physical climate risk, including through scenario analysis and stress tests. Its Singapore-Asia Taxonomy (2023) covers emission cuts only, so there are no criteria yet for finance that helps people adapt to heat. (https://www.mas.gov.sg/news/media-releases/2023/mas-launches-worlds-first-multi-sector-transition-taxonomy)

- Bank of Thailand (Platform; Government body; Thailand): A 2023 policy statement asks banks to build environmental and climate risk into governance, strategy, risk management and disclosure. It has worked with the World Bank on assessing physical climate risk in Thai banks’ loan books. (https://www.bot.or.th/en/financial-innovation/sustainable-finance/green/FIPCS-internalizing_environmental_and_climate_change.html)

- Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (Financial Services Authority), Indonesia (Platform; Government body; Indonesia): Its climate risk guideline for banks (2024, refined in 2026) includes data on Indonesia’s physical climate hazards. A 2022 rule lets banks restructure loans for borrowers in areas it designates as disaster-hit: after the 2025 Sumatra floods, Rp12.58 trillion for 237,083 borrowers. Heat has not yet been designated. (https://ojk.go.id/en/Publikasi/Roadmap-dan-Pedoman/Perbankan/Pages/The-2026-Banking-Climate-Risk-Management-and-Scenario-Analysis-CRMS-Guideline.aspx)

- Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (Platform; Government body; Philippines): Since 2021, banks must check whether a borrower’s collateral or income is exposed to climate hazards. In areas under a state of calamity, banks can give borrowers up to six months’ grace with no interest on interest or penalties, longer for farm loans. It also eased rules for lenders in drought-hit areas during the 2015–16 El Niño. (https://www.philstar.com/business/2025/10/27/2482726/bsp-expands-calamity-relief-banks-borrowers)

- State Bank of Vietnam (Platform; Government body; Viet Nam): Requires banks to assess environmental risk before lending to projects (since 2023). After Typhoon Yagi in 2024, it let lenders reschedule repayments for affected borrowers across 26 provinces, with final repayment allowed until the end of 2027. (https://vietnamnews.vn/economy/1688781/banks-allowed-to-extend-debt-repayment-for-typhoon-yagi-affected-customers-to-2027.html)

- Bangladesh Bank (Platform; Government body; Bangladesh): Steers credit to farmers after climate shocks through its refinancing schemes. In June 2026 it told banks to prioritise farmers hit by heavy rain. Heat is not yet among the shocks that trigger this support. (https://www.bssnews.net/news/391823)

- Nepal Rastra Bank (Platform; Government body; Nepal): Sets environmental and social risk rules for banks (2018), and since October 2024 a green finance taxonomy that sorts lending into green, amber and red. (https://www.nrb.org.np/)

- Reserve Bank of India (Platform; Government body; India): Its 2018 directions let banks reschedule loans and pause repayments in areas hit by notified calamities, which in India now include heatwaves. A 2024 draft framework would require banks to disclose their climate-related financial risks. (https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=10478)

- Sustainable Banking and Finance Network (Platform; Network or alliance; Across the region): A network of financial regulators and banking associations from emerging markets, supported by IFC. Its policy library holds the climate and environmental risk rules of central banks across South and Southeast Asia. (https://www.sbfnetwork.org/)

- KOMIDA, with Build Change (Indonesia) (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; Indonesia): One of Indonesia’s largest microfinance institutions, piloting small home-improvement loans for climate adaptation with Build Change, aimed at women earning under US$5 a day and paired with digital advice. (https://www.globalinnovation.fund/investments/build-change-2)

- Center for Financial Inclusion (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; Place not stated in the listing): Researches how small loans and parametric insurance can help low-income people get through heatwaves. (https://centerforfinancialinclusion.org/inclusive-finance-and-extreme-heat-how-small-loans-and-parametric-insurance-can-help-vulnerable-populations-manage-through-deadly-heat-waves)

- KOMIDA (Supply; Insurer, lender or finance body; Indonesia): Offers incremental housing adaptation loans with heat retrofit support. (https://mitradhuafa.com)

(https://www.prudentialplc.com/en/newsroom/company-news/2024/prudential-advances-climate-resilience-efforts-in-asia-and-africa-with-us-million-investment-to-address-impacts-of-climate-change-on-health/)

- Rohini Nilekani Philanthropies (Supply; Funder; India): Funds heat work in India, including Prayas Energy and Health Group’s work with street vendors and construction workers, and CEEW’s district heat risk assessment. - Rainmatter Foundation (Supply; Funder; India): Funds climate and environment work in India. Its partners’ heat work includes heatwave workshops that help journalists and health experts report on extreme heat. (https://rainmatter.org/blog/tag/heat/)

- Climate & Health Funders Coalition (Platform; Funder; Across the region): Launched at COP30 with US$300 million in initial funding. Extreme heat is a core priority. Members include CIFF, the Gates Foundation, Philanthropy Asia Alliance, the Rockefeller Foundation and Wellcome. (https://wellcome.org/engagement-and-advocacy/advocacy-and-partnerships/climate-health-funders-coalition)

(https://climateworks.org/press-release/statement-on-the-united-nations-secretary-generals-call-to-action-for-extreme-heat/)

- ClimateWorks Foundation (Supply; Funder; Place not stated in the listing): Its Adaptation & Resilience Fund made extreme heat its first focus, awarding US$9.3 million for parametric insurance, adaptive social protection, heat action plans and early warnings. - The Rockefeller Foundation (Supply; Funder; India): Funds the South Asia Climate–Health Desk with Wellcome and a heat research consortium at IISER Pune, and supported C40’s Cool Cities Accelerator. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- Wellcome (Supply; Funder; India): Funds research on extreme heat and health: £17.5 million to test heat adaptations such as cool roofs, with a trial site in India; £17 million across nine projects on heat in pregnancy and early childhood; and work on heat and mental health. With The Rockefeller Foundation it committed US$11.5 million to the WHO–WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme. (https://wellcome.org/our-priorities/climate-and-health/extreme-heat)

- Laudes Foundation (Supply; Funder; Bangladesh): Funds a three-year project with ICCCAD that builds Bangladeshi garment workers’ capacity on climate change, including heat stress, and on labour rights. (https://icccad.net/programmes/just-transition/capacitating-garment-workers/)

- International Development Research Centre (IDRC) (Supply; Funder; India): Funds applied heat research, including gender-sensitive heat action planning in India and studies of heat’s impact on informal workers. - IKEA Foundation (Supply; Funder; Place not stated in the listing): Supports solar-powered cooling that helps farmers preserve food and reduce waste as extreme heat becomes more common. (https://www.ikeafoundation.org/campaign-26)

### Singapore, Singapore

A city-state with hot nights, dense towers and an early national heat stress advisory.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Singapore launched a national Heat Stress Advisory in July 2023. It rates heat stress as low, moderate or high from the wet-bulb globe temperature, and tells people what to do at each level. Since March 2025 a heatwave is declared when the daily maximum reaches at least 35 °C and the daily mean at least 29 °C for three days in a row; a taskforce of 37 public agencies then opens air-conditioned cooling spaces in community centres. In March 2026 a Heat Resilience Policy Office was set up to coordinate action across agencies, oversee research and draft a heat resilience action plan. Sources: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, 2023 https://mse.gov.sg/latest-news/press-release-heat-stress-advisory; Malay Mail: Singapore’s heatwave response plan, 2025 https://www.malaymail.com/news/singapore/2025/03/20/singapore-rolls-out-cooling-measures-as-heatwave-response-plan-unveiled/170163; Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment: Committee of Supply speech, 2026 https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/speech-by-sms-janil-puthucheary-committee-of-supply-2026/

Each count is measured against this station's own record, so it is not a comparison between cities, and the station may sit at an airport or in open ground, so streets nearby can be hotter. Warm nights at a station can also rise as the city grows around it, which is part of the city's own heat. Humidity is not included, so these figures show temperature alone; in humid cities the heat felt in the body can rise even where temperature changes little. Strong El Niño years, such as 2016 and 2023 to 2024, bring hotter years in much of the region, and warm years near the end of a record tilt a trend upward. Trend: Sen's slope with its 95% range, and a Mann-Kendall test: "a clear rise" where the test is under 5%, "leaning upward, not clear" between 5% and 20%, otherwise "no clear change". Sources: NOAA Global Surface Summary of the Day (GSOD) station gsod:48698099999; Open-Meteo Historical Weather API, ERA5-Land reanalysis (Copernicus Climate Change Service).

- The sleepless-nights loop: Singapore has averaged 76 warm nights a year over four decades; by 2100 they could come on most nights.

- The cooling trap: The commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than the outskirts on calm, clear nights.

- The dying-green loop: Among the cities where the most urban tree species already face temperatures beyond their range.

- The invisible-deaths loop: Workplace monitors found more heat stress than nearby weather stations reported.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; Older people

Already at work: National Environment Agency, Singapore; Ministry of Manpower, Singapore; Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, Singapore; Global Heat Health Information Network, Southeast Asia Hub; Singapore Management University, Urban Institute; National Research Foundation, Singapore; Monetary Authority of Singapore; C40 Cities

### Bangkok, Thailand

A tropical megacity where heat costs lives, livelihoods and a share of the city’s economy.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): For the 2026 hot season Bangkok opened 304 cooling centres in schools, health centres and district offices. The city’s own Urban Heat Management Action Plan for 2026 has 22 indicators and a committee chaired by a deputy governor; its targets include cooling rooms in 80% of schools and public health service centres, at least two cooling points in every district, and home visits to at least 5,000 vulnerable households a year during heat alerts. A 2026 financing strategy with UNDP costs the plan at about THB 146 million to set up and THB 10.8 million a year to run, mostly from existing city budgets, and notes that running costs are not always covered. Sources: Government of Thailand, 2026 https://thailand.go.th/issue-focus-detail/bangkok-launches-304-cooling-centers-to-combat-extreme-heat; World Bank, Shaping a Cooler Bangkok, 2025 https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/thailand/publication/shaping-a-cooler-bangkok-tackling-urban-heat-for-a-more-livable-city; UNDP and Bangkok Metropolitan Administration: Bangkok's financing strategy for tackling urban heat, 2026 https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2026-10/en-undp-bma_financial_strategy_on_urban_heat.pdf

What could be done: This hot season: Heat-safe work; Cool nights and support. Over the next few years: Green without pushing people out; Income protection in heatwaves; Social protection floors; Dedicated heat budgets; Anticipatory action

Inside the city: districts side by side: 50 districts, each with estimated residents, the share aged 65 and over, hospitals mapped in OpenStreetMap, built-up share and park area share, side by side and never ranked. Data: https://beattheheat.asia/data/city-districts/bangkok.json. Limits: Residents are modelled estimates from WorldPop, not counts, and can differ widely from registration figures, partly because many people live in a city without being registered there. The model's spread of people within the city may overstate some districts and understate others, including the dense old centre. Please read each figure as a rough order of size. The age mix is modelled from wider-area statistics, so differences between districts may be smoother or sharper than in reality. Shares are rounded to whole numbers. Hospitals are those OpenStreetMap volunteers have mapped so far, not every hospital that exists. Clinics are left out: far more exist than are mapped, so a count would mostly measure mapping. Park area counts only land mapped as parks in OpenStreetMap, as a share of each district's area. It leaves out farmland, orchards, temple grounds, canal-side trees and private gardens, so it is not a measure of all green space. Built-up ground is the share of land mapped as built-up in ESA WorldCover (2021, 10 m), built from Copernicus Sentinel satellite data. Figures use the district outlines named below, a population grid of about 100 m and a land grid of about 50 m, so small districts carry more error. Today's heat-stress estimate above is for the city as a whole: the weather model's grid is wider than a district, so no district-level daily heat is shown.

Heat today and the next three days: the page shows estimated heat stress (wbgt) now and an estimated daily peak for today and the next three days, calculated in the browser from Open-Meteo. Official warnings: Thai Meteorological Department https://www.tmd.go.th/

- The poverty–heat trap: Nearly 80% of informal workers surveyed cut their hours in the heat; 75% of home-based workers lost a day’s work a month to heat illness.

- The reactive-spending loop: Heat deaths, about 593 a year, cost up to 0.7% of the city’s economy: more than its 2020 public health budget.

- The sleepless-nights loop: One of the tropical cities whose nights stay hot.

- The green-displacement loop: Fieldwork is tracing how green urban renewal affects the city’s lower-income residents.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: Bangkok Metropolitan Administration; HomeNet Thailand; Bank of Thailand; United Nations Development Programme (UNDP); Asian Development Bank

### Manila, Philippines

A dense, humid metropolis where heat closes schools and pushes the heat index into danger.

- The invisible-deaths loop: Death certificates usually record the immediate cause, so heat as the trigger goes unrecorded.

Who heat hits hardest: People in informal settlements; Workers in heat-exposed jobs

### Ahmedabad, India

Where South Asia’s first heat action plan began, and where its results were measured.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first heat action plan in 2013, after a 2010 heatwave caused an estimated 1,344 excess deaths. An estimated 1,190 deaths a year were later avoided. Sources: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

Heat over time, 1991 to 2025: No checked station record found yet for this city. The model reconstruction alone leaves out the built-up city, so no trend is shown.

- The overwhelmed-clinic loop: The plan prepared hospitals and warned the public before heat peaked.

- The poverty–heat trap: Up to three-quarters of India’s workforce depends on heat-exposed work.

- The invisible-deaths loop: As in most countries, heat deaths are hard to count, which makes the case for prevention harder to see.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Inside the city: districts side by side: 12 districts, each with estimated residents, the share aged 65 and over, hospitals mapped in OpenStreetMap, built-up share and park area share, side by side and never ranked. Data: https://beattheheat.asia/data/city-districts/phnompenh.json. Limits: Residents are modelled estimates from WorldPop, not counts, and can differ widely from registration figures, partly because many people live in a city without being registered there. The model's spread of people within the city may overstate some districts and understate others, including the dense old centre. Please read each figure as a rough order of size. The age mix is modelled from wider-area statistics, so differences between districts may be smoother or sharper than in reality. Shares are rounded to whole numbers. Hospitals are those OpenStreetMap volunteers have mapped so far, not every hospital that exists. Clinics are left out: far more exist than are mapped, so a count would mostly measure mapping. Park area counts only land mapped as parks in OpenStreetMap, as a share of each district's area. It leaves out farmland, orchards, temple grounds, canal-side trees and private gardens, so it is not a measure of all green space. Built-up ground is the share of land mapped as built-up in ESA WorldCover (2021, 10 m), built from Copernicus Sentinel satellite data. Figures use the district outlines named below, a population grid of about 100 m and a land grid of about 50 m, so small districts carry more error. Today's heat-stress estimate above is for the city as a whole: the weather model's grid is wider than a district, so no district-level daily heat is shown.

- The cooling trap: UN ESCAP projects that the urban heat island could add 2 °C to 7 °C on top of global warming in Phnom Penh.

Caveat: A single station shows how one site has changed against its own past. Each count is measured against this station's own record, so it is not a comparison between cities, and the station may sit at an airport or in open ground, so streets nearby can be hotter. Warm nights at a station can also rise as the city grows around it, which is part of the city's own heat.
