### What this page could not verify

- Full early IPCC heat audit: Repeated access failures affected original FAR, AR4, SREX, SR1.5 and SROCC pages or PDFs. Official mirrors and summaries supported narrower entries. They did not establish every chapter, first term or confidence statement. The older special reports listed in C were identified through an opened bibliography, but their heat passages were not audited.

- All working groups in every cycle: Direct text was not obtained for every WGI, WGII, WGIII and synthesis contribution. In particular, FAR's original heat content, original AR4 heat passages, AR5 WGIII, and detailed AR6 WGII and Synthesis heat-health text remain unresolved. The table leaves these gaps visible.

- First IPCC use of heatwave, humid heat or wet-bulb: This requires a searchable full corpus and term-by-term checks, including spelling variants. No first-use date is claimed.

- Early heat-health records beyond urban climatology: The 1833 entry rests on an EPA historical account. The original was not read. Earlier military, occupational and medical heat records were not verified in primary texts.

- 2004 heatwave event-attribution milestone: The original landmark European attribution paper could not be confirmed in accessible full text in this review. No date, risk ratio or first claim was entered. The verified 2022 WMO account is not presented as the beginning of attribution science.

- Full mortality series for landmark events: Final totals for Europe 2003, Russia 2010 and the combined 2015 South Asian emergencies were not reconciled across studies and official records. Those totals were omitted. Chicago's 465 figure is the opened CDC report's certified-death count and period, not a definitive final excess-mortality estimate.

- Canadian aftermath of the 2021 northwestern heatwave: The opened source supports US surveillance. A verified history of subsequent Canadian warning, building or health-policy changes was not completed.

- Every country named in the scope: Dedicated plan, programme or first-institution milestones were not verified for Maldives, Myanmar, Thailand, Viet Nam, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines or Timor-Leste. Bhutan appears as a regional report host, rather than through a verified domestic heat-plan milestone. Sri Lanka appears through a regional workshop. These are research gaps, not claims of absence.

- Independent firsts and institutional continuity: The first-plan claim for Ahmedabad, first-in-Asia claim for Dhaka North's heat officer, and early insurance claims were not independently audited across all jurisdictions. Current staffing, budgets and continued operation were not established by the historical launch sources. No first national heat plan across Asia is asserted.

- Plan effectiveness: A primary evaluation of Ahmedabad's mortality effects was not opened and checked. Similar outcome evidence for other listed plans was not verified. Timeline launches are not treated as proven reductions in illness or deaths.

- Heat-specific adaptation finance totals: A consistent global or regional spending series separating heat from cooling, health, cities and wider adaptation was not verified. No estimate of a heat-finance gap is supplied.

- Philanthropic heat-fund outcomes: Announcements and specific support are visible in opened sources, but total disbursement, additionality and reach were not reconciled. A reported COP30 health-funding commitment was not entered because its underlying announcement could not be opened and confirmed.

- Insurance outcomes: The opened project record establishes first-year coverage, not verified claim-level payouts, basis risk, sustained affordability or health effects. Later payout figures were not confirmed in primary records.

- Media and public attention: No comparable, reproducible South and Southeast Asian media series, Google Trends extract or multilingual coverage study was opened and verified. A study of research publications could not be confirmed either. No media-attention peak is dated here.

- UNDRR hazard definitions and all database revisions: The opened loss-statistics account and CRED report establish recording limits and delays. A version-by-version audit of heat classification, event thresholds and retrospective revisions across EM-DAT, DesInventar and national systems was not completed. Certified heat deaths, excess deaths and modelled attributable mortality remain separate measures.

- Complete WMO State of the Climate chronology: The 2026 Asian release was read. The earliest global or regional report to give heat a headline role was not established.

- AR7 beyond the verified review notice: The Cities report review is a process event. Its draft findings were not treated as approved evidence. Other AR7 material through the cut-off was not fully audited. No future report or COP outcome is included as completed.

## El Niño and India's smaller cities: preparing for summer 2027

https://beattheheat.asia/el-nino-and-cities/

A practical guide for municipal teams and community organisations in India's Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. Choose where people already have to be in the hottest hours (a school, a market, a clinic or a waiting space), agree who will keep protection working, and decide what changes when a local warning arrives.

A seasonal El Niño outlook gives cities a reason to review preparations early. The local heat season, water supply and places where people spend the hottest hours decide what a city puts in place. District forecasts and official warnings decide when to step up the response.

The first decision: Where do people already have to be in the hottest hours, which one place will we protect first, and who has the authority to keep it working? One setting, chosen with the people who use it, is enough to start. Getting one change working across several schools or markets may protect more people than starting all four settings at once. The rest of this guide helps a municipal team and a local organisation decide in one meeting, with information they already hold.

### Where people already have to be

The best place to offer heat respite may be the place someone already has to be.

A child at the midday meal, a vendor at a stall, a patient in a clinic queue, a passenger at a bus stand: none of them can walk away without losing something. NIUA's Learning Note 1 describes public spaces becoming safe zones during heatwaves (p. 85). Here are four settings where a town can act before the hot season.

- Schools: Pupils in the midday meal queue, at assembly and in the hottest classrooms.

- Markets and vending streets: Vendors at occupied stalls through peak trading hours.

- Clinics and health-centre queues: Patients and caregivers waiting outside to be seen.

- Public waiting and transit spaces: Passengers at bus stands and people in ration-shop queues.

These are choices, not a checklist. Pick the one where your town can remove the most avoidable exposure before the first hot spell.

### Where the outlook stands

"Summer 2027" in this guide's title is a planning horizon, not a forecast. For March to May 2027, NOAA Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of El Niño at 80%, most likely weak (53%) or moderate (25%); for April to June 2027, ENSO-neutral becomes more likely (61%) than El Niño (38%). A hot season can be dangerous with or without El Niño, so what follows is preparation that pays off in either case.

- Forecast, NOAA Climate Prediction Center, issued 12 November 2026, through January to March 2027, Tropical Pacific Ocean: El Niño Advisory in effect. A strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027 (a greater than 79% chance), before it begins to weaken in early 2027. A forecast for the Pacific Ocean, not for an Indian city. Next issue: 10 December 2026.

- Forecast, World Meteorological Organization, issued 21 October 2026, November 2026 to January 2027, Tropical Pacific Ocean: The seasonal average anomaly is forecast at about +3.8 °C, peaking around December 2026; a positive Indian Ocean Dipole is forecast to decline to +0.3 °C. WMO's latest quarterly El Niño Update, of 3 September 2026, gave a nearly 100% likelihood that El Niño persists through February 2027. Strength in the Pacific does not decide how severe impacts are in any one country.

- Observed, India Meteorological Department, issued 1 October 2026, June to September 2026, India as a whole: Rainfall over India in the 2026 monsoon was 87% of its long period average. A national total. It does not show how much water your city's own supply holds.

IMD releases its seasonal outlook for the hot season between March and May. Until it is out, use your district's warnings, and read the outlook for your own region when it is issued.

### Four protections that keep working

Four protections decide much of the harm in a hot season. For each, the same nine questions show whether an arrangement can keep working. The answers below are prompts for a local agreement, not national rules; confirm each role with the body that holds the mandate.

The question: What has to be working before the hot season, and who keeps it working?

#### Workplace protection without income loss

- Who is exposed: Outdoor and semi-outdoor workers paid by the day or the piece: construction, loading, vending, sanitation, delivery. They lose money if they stop.

- Where they spend the hottest hours: Worksites, labour chowks where day workers wait for hire, markets and delivery routes, from late morning to late afternoon.

- What can be ready before the season: Water and shade at worksites and labour chowks; agreed shifted hours for the heaviest work; rest breaks that do not cut pay; someone on each site who knows the signs of heat illness and who to call.

- What activates more action: The official district heat warning under the state or district heat plan. The seasonal El Niño outlook sets the timetable for preparation, not the day-to-day trigger.

- Who authorises it: The labour department and the district administration, under the heat plan; each employer or contractor on its own site. In April 2026 the Government issued a nationwide heatwave advisory to safeguard workers, as reported by All India Radio; whether it binds an employer depends on the directions each state issues.

- Who operates it: Employers and contractors on their sites; the municipal body at labour chowks and public worksites.

- Who pays the recurring costs: The employer for its own workforce. For own-account and informal workers there is no employer to pay: options include a municipal or state budget line and welfare or insurance schemes that replace lost earnings, which need an agreed payer before the season.

- How workers and communities shape it: Unions, workers' associations and vendors' committees agree the hours, breaks and water points with employers and the municipality, and report when they fail.

- How to check it is usable: Is there water at the site at 2 p.m.? Did anyone lose a day's pay for resting? Count breaks actually taken and complaints received, not posters put up.

#### Heat-safe homes, including homes used for paid work

- Who is exposed: Households under tin or asbestos roofs in informal settlements; women who do paid work at home (stitching, food processing, piece-rate work); older people and people who are ill.

- Where they spend the hottest hours: Inside the home, often a single room or a top floor that stays hot into the night; for a home-based worker, the home is also the workplace.

- What can be ready before the season: Roof coatings or shading, ventilation and water storage; a list, made with residents, of households that cannot cool their homes; agreed check-in visits for people living alone.

- What activates more action: The district warning starts check-in visits and longer water-supply hours in the settlement.

- Who authorises it: The municipal body or housing department for work on roofs and settlement services, with the consent of owners and tenants.

- Who operates it: Community organisations and municipal staff; local fabricators and painters.

- Who pays the recurring costs: A coating or shade is a one-off cost; repainting, repairs and water supply recur. Agree who pays them, or the protection fades after one season.

- How workers and communities shape it: Residents choose which measures suit their homes; women who work at home say which hours and rooms they need to keep working.

- How to check it is usable: Indoor temperatures in a sample of homes before and after; whether coatings still reflect after a season; whether home-based workers kept their working hours.

- Evidence: Mahila Housing Trust's 2024 study in an Ahmedabad informal settlement attributes almost 75% of women's heat-related productivity losses to unpaid labour, including care for others made ill by heat. NIUA notes that informal settlements face higher exposure to heat, flooding and water scarcity.

#### Continuity of care, including childcare and maternal services

- Who is exposed: Pregnant women and newborns, young children, older people and anyone who depends on regular care; and the carers, usually women, who lose earnings when care moves home.

- Where they spend the hottest hours: Clinic queues and waiting areas, labour rooms, anganwadi and childcare centres, and homes.

- What can be ready before the season: Shaded, ventilated waiting space and drinking water at clinics; heat checks during antenatal visits; referral routes agreed for warning signs; a plan for childcare when schools or centres change hours.

- What activates more action: The district warning brings extended or shifted clinic hours, queues moved indoors and calls to people at highest risk.

- Who authorises it: The district health department, under the state health department's guidance; the department that runs anganwadi and childcare centres.

- Who operates it: Clinic staff, community health workers and anganwadi workers.

- Who pays the recurring costs: Health department budgets for clinic measures; staff time, water and cooling recur and need a line in the annual budget.

- How workers and communities shape it: Women and carers say which hours and places they can actually reach; community health workers report gaps.

- How to check it is usable: Waiting times in the heat; whether pregnant women received heat checks; appointments missed on hot days; families left without childcare.

- Evidence: NCDC's advisory for summer 2026 asked state health departments to report heatstroke cases and deaths daily from 1 March 2026 and to consider public cooling and drinking water facilities. NCDC's guidance on heat and pregnancy notes higher risks for pregnant women and the fetus, and lists checks such as temperature, blood pressure, hydration and fetal heart rate, with timely referral.

#### School-based protection and appropriately governed respite

- Who is exposed: Pupils, especially at assembly and in the midday meal queue; teachers and cooks; parents waiting at the gate.

- Where they spend the hottest hours: Classrooms under tin roofs, open assembly grounds, the midday meal queue and school transport.

- What can be ready before the season: Shade and drinking water at assembly and meal points; timetable options agreed in advance; first aid and a named person for heat illness. If a school is also to offer respite to the public, decide it explicitly beforehand.

- What activates more action: The district warning, through an instruction from the education authority, shifts the timetable or moves activities indoors.

- Who authorises it: The education authority and school management committee. A school does not automatically become a public shelter: respite for the public needs written permission from the education authority, agreed with the district administration.

- Who operates it: The head teacher and staff during school hours; for public respite outside school hours, a named operator who is not the teaching staff by default.

- Who pays the recurring costs: The education budget for school measures; respite operations (staffing, cleaning, water, toilets) need their own budget line.

- How workers and communities shape it: Parents and pupils, through the school management committee, and neighbours if the school will open to them.

- How to check it is usable: Water available at lunchtime; pupils taken ill; whether a timetable change reached families in time. For respite: whether it opened when needed, who used it, and whether children stayed safe.

- Respite for the public: Before a school offers respite to the public, settle: permission and liability; safeguarding, with children and adults from outside kept apart; drinking water and toilets for the extra numbers; staff or volunteers on duty and their hours; access for people with disabilities; and what happens if the site floods or loses power. NDMA's guidelines for cooling centres cover site selection in high-risk areas, retrofitting, and operations and maintenance.

- Evidence: The Ministry of Education has issued guidelines on precautions schools take against heat waves (as published on Vikaspedia).

### What a seasonal signal can and cannot tell a city

Can: Give a reason to start ordinary protection early. In India's records for 1961-2013, most years with above-normal heatwave activity (April to June) followed El Niño events: an India-wide pattern, not a city forecast.

Cannot: Give your city's chance of a heatwave, a water shortage or a flood. An ENSO probability describes the Pacific, never a municipality.

Long-term warming raises the baseline; the local heat island and failing infrastructure (a pump, a feeder, a drain) decide much of the harm, and those are within a city's reach.

### Adapt this to your city

Cities differ in when heat arrives, how humid it is, where water comes from, which public spaces people rely on and which authority manages them. Find the rows that describe your city; most cities fit more than one. They are illustrative situations, not categories, and a city's size says nothing on its own about its climate risk or its powers.

- If outdoor markets, transport stands, school yards or worksites stay busy through the hottest hours: Where can shade, drinking water and rest be provided without asking people to give up earnings or lose their place in a queue? Information you may already hold: Market registers and association lists, last summer's municipal orders on working hours, the ward office's count of afternoon stalls.

- If homes or public buildings stay hot at night, or humidity limits relief: Which existing accessible spaces can offer meaningful respite, at what hours, and who can operate them? Check any technical cooling advice against NDMA's guidance on cooling centres. Information you may already hold: Clinic attendance in past hot spells, community organisations' knowledge of crowded homes, the list of public buildings open in the evening.

- If summer water supply is intermittent, or depends on electricity and tankers: Which priority sites have usable storage or another supply? Who can authorise a refill, pay for it and confirm it arrived? Information you may already hold: The water department's supply schedule, last summer's tanker orders, ward complaints about dry taps, the reservoir or groundwater figures for your own source.

- If short, intense rain can flood routes or public sites during an otherwise dry period: Which sites or access routes may fail, which alternative location is usable, and who decides when to switch? Information you may already hold: Last monsoon's waterlogging complaints, the drain-cleaning schedule, the district disaster plan, residents' knowledge of which lanes flood.

None of these rows needs a new vulnerability assessment before the first meeting. Start with what the municipal body, the clinic and the local organisation already know, and write down what is missing.

### Six linked risks

- Extreme heat (India-wide pattern). Evidence and its limit: Most above-normal Indian heatwave years (1961-2013) followed El Niño events. An ENSO probability does not give your city's chance of a heatwave. How it becomes harm: Hours outdoors without shade: a long queue, an unshaded stall, a worksite with no rest. What to check locally: Last summer's municipal orders, clinic attendance in hot spells, the IMD district warnings issued for your district.

- Water scarcity (Observed, national). Evidence and its limit: India's 2026 monsoon was 87% of normal. A national total does not establish water in your system. How it becomes harm: A supply cut, a pump without power or a late tanker leaves a water point dry at peak hours. What to check locally: Your utility's supply schedule and the reservoir or groundwater information for your own source.

- Intense rainfall (Central India, 1950-2015). Evidence and its limit: Widespread extreme rain events over central India tripled as total rain declined. A regional trend, not an El Niño prediction for India. How it becomes harm: Very heavy rain within hours, often with wind, tearing covers and closing routes. What to check locally: Which sites lost access in past downpours; how covers are fixed.

- Urban flooding (Depends on the city). Evidence and its limit: Rain becomes flooding through drains, terrain, land use and building over water paths; isolated fixes leave the system exposed (NIUA). How it becomes harm: A blocked drain, a low-lying site or a single access lane under water. What to check locally: Waterlogging complaints and the drain-cleaning schedule around each priority site.

- Public health (A pathway, not a probability). Evidence and its limit: A long outdoor wait or interrupted water raises the risk of heat illness. NCDC's advisory for summer 2026 asked states for public cooling and drinking water facilities. How it becomes harm: Unshaded clinic queues, delayed treatment, no water at the wait. What to check locally: Where heat illness reports clustered last summer; which clinics have outdoor queues.

- Livelihoods (A pathway, not a probability). Evidence and its limit: Lost trading hours, fewer customers, spoiled goods. Informal settlements face disproportionately higher exposure to heat, flooding and water scarcity (NIUA). How it becomes harm: Leaving a stall to cool down means losing sales or a place in the queue. What to check locally: Vendors' and workers' own account of which hours they lose, through their association or a local organisation.

- Scenario: Heat with the taps off. An afternoon of heat, the ward's supply cut for a repair, the market water point running low by noon. What helps: storage sized to a hot day's demand, a refill arranged with enough lead time for the tanker to arrive, and someone who calls when it runs low.

- Scenario: A downpour in a dry year. A below-normal monsoon, then one night of very heavy rain before the season turns. Covers tear, a lane floods, and a cover that blocks a drain turns one hazard into two. What helps: covers fixed against wind, drains cleared around each site, and an agreed alternative site.

### Your warning route

This guide sets no warning thresholds of its own. Find who issues your warning and who acts on it:

1. IMD district warnings: The official warning for your district, issued by the India Meteorological Department. (India Meteorological Department: https://mausam.imd.gov.in/responsive/districtWiseWarningGIS.php)

2. Your regional or state meteorological centre: IMD works through Regional Meteorological Centres, assisted by Meteorological Centres at the state level that disseminate advisories and warnings for their region. (India Meteorological Department: https://mausam.imd.gov.in/event/evolution.php)

3. Your state or district disaster authority: The state and district heat action plans say which department acts at each alert level. Find yours in the India heat action plan archive. (https://beattheheat.asia/resources/heat-action-plans/india/)

4. The municipal officer or service operator named locally: The person who extends water hours, moves a queue indoors or moves a school assembly into the shade. If no one is named for your chosen service, name them before the season.

For health departments, NCDC's advisory for summer 2026 asked states to start daily heat illness reporting from 1 March 2026 and to set local early warning thresholds.

### By lead time: months, weeks, days, during, afterwards

- Months ahead: Select the service and sites, confirm permissions, budgets and recurring costs, procure what has to be bought, and sign service agreements with whoever will operate and repair. Work backwards from when heat usually arrives in your city and how long procurement takes. The seasonal El Niño outlook is a reason to start early; it is not the trigger. Who decides: The body that manages each site (municipal body, education authority or school management, market committee, health department or transport authority), the operator and the local organisation.

- Weeks ahead: Check that each measure works: water flows, shade is up, keys are with the right person, staff know their hours. Read the national seasonal and extended-range outlooks for your region, and confirm who receives the official warning. Who decides: Each site's operator, with the local organisation checking from the user's side.

- Days ahead: an official local warning: The core protection is already working. Agree in advance who receives the warning and what is added under the applicable plan: an operator extends water hours, brings a refill forward, moves a clinic queue indoors or shifts a school timetable. Who decides: IMD issues district warnings; departments act under the state and district heat plans.

- During an event: Keep each service running at the hours people rely on it: refill water, staff the site, keep cooling and care open during power cuts. Check on people who cannot come to a site. Who decides: Each site's operator and the named repair officer, with the local organisation reporting what users see.

- Afterwards: Review who could not get water, shade, cooling or care, which measures failed and how fast they were fixed, and what it cost. After heavy rain, check covers and drains before reopening. Change next season's arrangements using what happened. Who decides: The municipal body with operators and the local organisation; workers and residents say what did not work.

Before opening a site, check how people will get drinking water during a power cut. If the supply depends on a pump, agree who can release stored water or order a refill, how long it will take, and where people can go in the meantime. If a site floods, the agreed alternative site takes over. Clinical care follows official guidance such as NCDC's.

### Worked example: a school at lunchtime (illustrative)

Children queue for the midday meal in an open courtyard, in full sun. Along one side, a veranda is in shade at the time the meal is served. Could the school move the serving point to the veranda, keeping the route step-free and leaving kitchen staff room to serve the children quickly?

Nothing had to be built to see this. Watching one ordinary part of the school day, at the hour it happens, changed the proposal: from new shade over the whole courtyard to moving where the meal is served.

- Choose the right exposure: The meal queue is one exposure. Where a classroom is the main problem, there are alternatives: move the hottest lessons to a cooler room that is free at that time, shade the sun-facing windows, or treat a suitable roof. Match the choice to the building, the hours the room is used and the permissions available.

- Give people a real design decision: Children can point out where they stand in the sun. Meal staff know where they can serve safely and quickly. Teachers know which rooms are occupied during the hottest lessons. The headteacher and the School Management Committee can help choose a change that works in this school. The education authority or building owner approves changes to the building and maintains them. Who that is varies by town, so confirm it before the plan is agreed.

- Use the school calendar: Ask which schools are open, on which dates and at what hours during the hot weeks. Count reach only for the days children are present. Opening a school as neighbourhood respite during the holidays is a separate decision, needing permission, staff, drinking water, a step-free entrance and safeguarding.

- What changes on a heat-warning day: Something within the school's own authority: hold the morning assembly in the shaded area instead of the open yard, and check that the drinking-water point works before pupils arrive. Changes to school hours or closures follow the education department and the state or district heat action plan. A shorter school day also moves care to families and can cost a parent paid work, so changes are easier to carry when agreed with families early.

- Check the result: For the meal queue, time how long pupils wait in direct sun during comparable lunch periods, before and after the change. For a roof or a classroom change, compare temperatures in occupied rooms at similar times of day and in comparable weather; NIUA's Table 2 pairs roofs treated with lower indoor temperatures (Learning Note 2, p. 54). Claims about attendance, learning or illness need evidence of their own.

The question for the education team: Which schools share this problem, are open during the relevant weeks, and could have the change in place before the first hot spell?

### Markets, clinics and waiting spaces

- Markets and vending streets. The decision: Vendors mark which occupied stalls lose shade during peak trading hours. Agree who can authorise shade and who can order a water refill. Who runs it: The market committee or municipal body authorises; a named officer orders refills; the vendors' association reports problems. What to check: Are vendors shaded while they trade? Is drinking water there when they need it?

- Clinics and health-centre queues. The decision: Move waiting into accessible shade or a cooler area, and change how patients are called so they keep their place in the queue. Patients, caregivers and clinic staff decide it together. Who runs it: The clinic in-charge, often under the health department rather than the municipality. What to check: How much of the wait is still spent in direct sun? Can someone using a wheelchair or a walking aid use the same arrangement? Patients and disability groups walk the route from the gate and say whether the shaded line is reachable with a wheelchair or a walking stick; their answer can move the queue indoors or change where the seating goes.

- Public waiting and transit spaces. The decision: At a bus stand, put shade and seating where passengers can see and reach the arriving bus. At a ration shop, protect the queue while people keep their place. Who runs it: Whoever controls the site: for a bus stand, often the transport authority or the depot; for a ration shop, the shop's licence holder with the supplies department. Confirm it locally. What to check: Is the actual waiting line shaded at peak hours? Can people use the shelter without missing their bus or their turn?

### Worked example: a market at 2 p.m. (illustrative design)

A vegetable seller would lose sales if she walked to a distant cooling room. So protection goes to her stall, in the hours she trades.

Vendors, through their association or a local organisation walk the market at 2 p.m. and mark which occupied stalls lose shade in the afternoon. Their map can move the shade: from the entrance, where it looks visible, to the aisle where sellers actually sit after lunch.

- Authorises the site: Whoever manages the market: a municipal body, a market committee or another authority. Gives permission for shade and a water point.

- Pays for installation: May be the municipal budget, a state scheme or a district allocation; agreed before procurement starts.

- Covers summer operations: Water, cleaning and small repairs through the season; may be a different body from the one that paid to install.

- Authorises a repair or emergency refill: One named person who can order a tanker or fix a torn cover the same day.

On a warning day: Water hours extend and the refill comes forward, timed to the storage on site and the tanker's delivery time; the association checks the water point at noon and mid-afternoon.

A badly sited cover can trap heat, pour rain onto the walkway or block a wheelchair or handcart. The check: stand under it at 2 p.m., pour a bucket on it, walk the aisle with a handcart.

### Reach: how much protection people got

Start with one setting and show how much of it can be protected this season. A change working across many schools or markets is what reaches a city: NIUA's Learning Note 2 describes city-scale resilience planning as a coordinated approach across a city's systems, moving beyond isolated projects (section 2.6, p. 40), and Learning Note 1 points to entry points within municipal functions.

- Service coverage: Functioning sites out of eligible sites, always with the eligible count stated: say 6 of 40 schools open during the hot weeks (an illustrative figure).

- People reached: Regular users counted once, and repeated visits counted separately: a pupil present on 30 school days is one pupil and 30 school-day visits. Footfall is not protection.

- Protection delivered: What was available at the hour that matters, and to whom. Claim no avoided deaths or illness without health data and a fair comparison.

- Schools. Coverage: Participating schools with the change working, out of eligible schools open during the hot weeks. People and visits: Pupils reached, each counted once, and school-day visits (pupils times days present), reported apart. Count only days children are present.

- Markets and vending streets. Coverage: Markets, or occupied stalls, shaded and watered at peak trading hours, out of those trading through the hottest hours. People and visits: Regular vendors counted once; shopper footfall reported apart, as visits.

- Clinics and health-centre queues. Coverage: Clinics with shaded or indoor waiting, out of clinics where patients queue outside. People and visits: Patient visits are visits: one person may come several times. Count caregivers who wait too.

- Public waiting and transit spaces. Coverage: Stops or queues shaded where people actually wait, out of those with peak-hour queues. People and visits: Boardings and ration collections are trips, not people; report them as visits.

Pair each output with an observable result (after NIUA's Table 2, Learning Note 2, p. 54):

- Shade installed -> Occupied vendor stalls shaded at 2 p.m.

- Water point installed -> Drinking water available during peak trading hours

- Cooling space opened -> People using it at peak hours, with staff on duty

- Meal served from the shaded veranda -> Minutes pupils wait in direct sun at lunch, on comparable days

- Classroom roof treated -> Lower temperature in occupied rooms at similar times and in comparable weather

- Clinic waiting moved into shade -> Share of the wait still spent in direct sun

- Bus-stand shelter installed -> Waiting line shaded at the peak hour, with the arriving bus in view

Give users a simple way to report a failure (a number on the post, the association's contact) and ask the operator to record when it was fixed. The log shows whether protection held, not only whether it was built.

Exposure is uneven: NIUA's Learning Note 1 notes that informal settlements face disproportionately higher exposure to heat, flooding and water scarcity, and that smaller cities often work with constrained resources (pp. 33, 35). Count who the service reaches in those places.

### Worksheet: One setting, protected before the heat

One sheet for each setting, filled in together at one meeting with what you already know. In part 3, tick each item on the day and fix anything left unticked.

Settings to choose from: Schools, Markets and vending streets, Clinics and health-centre queues, Public waiting and transit spaces, or another of your own.

1. Choose the setting: Which setting, the site, who is exposed and at what hours, the change you propose, and what you already know.

2. Agree who runs it: Who authorises it, who runs it day to day, who pays to install and to run it, who can order a same-day repair or refill, and the date it is ready by, with the reason.

3. Three pause points: Ticks before opening, when an official warning is issued, and during and after: shade, water, power cuts, access and failures fixed.

4. Check and agree: One observable result before and after, what the local organisation changed, who agreed, and when you check again.

A filled-in example (illustrative): Setting: Schools; Site: A ward primary school: the midday meal queue; Who is exposed, and when: Pupils queuing in the open courtyard, 12:30 to 1:15, on school days; Proposed change: Serve from the shaded veranda; keep the ramp clear; meal staff agree the layout; Authorises it: Headteacher with the School Management Committee; the building owner for any fixture; Runs it: Meal staff; a teacher checks the drinking-water point each morning; Ready by: Before the first hot week of term; One result to check: Minutes pupils wait in direct sun at lunch, on comparable days, before and after.

Printable A4 sheet: https://beattheheat.asia/print/el-nino-worksheet/

Hints and the example are illustrative; write your own answers. Bring this sheet to the next check.

### Preparedness that has happened in India

A published plan shows a planning decision, an installed facility shows installation, and measured benefit needs outcome evidence; each example says which it is, and cites its own source.

- Jodhpur, Rajasthan (Hot, dry; Installed, reported by a partner in the plan; the decision: Where to put protection): In April 2024 the city corporation and its partners opened a net-zero cooling station in a heat-vulnerable ward of Jodhpur North, chosen through the vulnerability assessment in the city's heat action plan. The 2023 plan also sets out passing heat warnings by SMS and WhatsApp. (NRDC: https://www.nrdc.org/bio/vijay-limaye/jodhpur-india-unveils-its-first-net-zero-cooling-station) (Jodhpur Nagar Nigam North with Mahila Housing Trust and NRDC: https://www.mahilahousingtrust.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/MHT-Jodhpur-Heat-Action-Plan-2023small.pdf)

- Kerala (Humid, coastal; An allocation, reported in the news; the decision: Who can pay at short notice): In March 2026 the state decided to give each district collector ₹1 crore for summer measures, and asked officials to set up drinking water kiosks where people gather: markets, junctions and bus stands. The government order itself was not found online. (Business Standard (PTI): https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/kerala-allocates-1-crore-each-to-districts-for-summer-mitigation-126031001041_1.html)

- Uttar Pradesh (Northern plains; A state method, with district thresholds reported; the decision: What triggers a step-up): The state disaster management authority set yellow, orange and red alert temperatures for each of its 75 districts, from percentiles of each district's own temperature record, so an alert reflects local conditions. Its 2024 heat plan sets out the method, first drafted for Agra. (Down To Earth: https://www.downtoearth.org.in/governance/step-towards-prompt-action-uttar-pradesh-sets-district-specific-thresholds-to-send-out-custom-heatwave-alerts) (Uttar Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority: https://pure.manchester.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/352692064/Heat_Wave_Action_Plan-2024.pdf)

- Ahmedabad (A large city, with outcome evidence): A 2018 evaluation estimated about 1,190 deaths a year avoided after Ahmedabad's heat action plan was fully implemented (95% confidence interval 162 to 2,218): an association, not proof of cause. The scale differs; the practice a smaller city can adapt is a named plan in which a warning sets agreed actions moving across departments. (Journal of Environmental and Public Health (Hess et al.): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6236972/)

The method travels; the warnings do not. Outside India, use your own country's weather service and disaster authority.

## El Niño and heat in Asia

https://beattheheat.asia/el-nino/

How a change in the Pacific affects rainfall, heat and the choices available to people.

How El Niño in the Pacific can shift heat and rainfall across South and Southeast Asia, what the current outlook establishes and what it cannot, and which preparations deserve attention locally.

### In two minutes

- El Niño is a warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific, coupled with a shift in winds and rainfall. It is one phase of ENSO, which swings every three to seven years on average.

- It can tilt the odds towards drier or hotter conditions in parts of Asia. It does not decide whether a heatwave, drought or flood happens in any one place.

- The current bulletin expects El Niño to persist into early 2027 and then weaken. For March to May 2027, NOAA Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of El Niño at 80%, most likely weak (53%) or moderate (25%); for April to June 2027, ENSO-neutral becomes more likely (61%) than El Niño (38%).

- Effects differ by region and season. India, Bangladesh, Nepal, mainland Southeast Asia, Indonesia and the Philippines each have their own pattern and their own national service.

- The useful response is early, ordinary preparation, tied to the official local warning when it comes.

### An ordinary decision (illustrative)

A municipal team hears on the news that El Niño may last into the coming hot season. Nobody has issued a heat warning for the town, and none will come for months. The team has to decide now what to repair, staff and budget before the first warning arrives.

What the outlook gives: A seasonal outlook tells the team that the odds in the Pacific favour El Niño for the next few months, and how confident forecasters are. It is a reason to start ordinary preparation early.

What the team still needs: It cannot tell the team which week will be hottest, which ward will suffer, or whether the water supply will hold. For that the team needs its national weather service's seasonal outlook for its region, its own records of past summers, and, closer to the time, the official local warning.

### What El Niño is

### A pattern of ocean and air together

ENSO, short for El Niño-Southern Oscillation, is a natural pattern in the tropical Pacific that involves both the ocean and the atmosphere. It has three states: El Niño, La Niña and neutral, when conditions are near their long-term average. Its phases swing back and forth every three to seven years on average.

### The usual pattern

In most years the trade winds blow from east to west across the tropical Pacific. They push warm surface water towards the western Pacific, near Indonesia and the Philippines, where a deep pool of warm water builds up. In the east, off South America, colder water rises from below to replace it, a process called upwelling. Warm water in the west heats the air above it, which rises, forms clouds and brings rain; drier air sinks over the cooler east. This loop of rising and sinking air is called the Walker circulation.

### What changes in El Niño

In El Niño the trade winds weaken. Warm surface water spreads farther east, and the central and eastern Pacific become warmer than average. Upwelling in the east weakens and the boundary between warm surface water and cold deep water, the thermocline, deepens there. The area of rising air and heavy rain shifts towards the central or eastern Pacific, while sinking air, and dryness, increase over Indonesia.

Ocean and atmosphere reinforce each other: warmer water weakens the winds, and weaker winds let the water warm further. La Niña is roughly the reverse: cooler water strengthens the trade winds and increases upwelling, reinforcing the cooling.

### Anomalies and indices

An anomaly is a departure from a stated reference average. NOAA measures ENSO from sea surface temperature departures in the Niño-3.4 region of the east-central equatorial Pacific (5°N to 5°S, 120°W to 170°W), against a 1991 to 2020 base period. A Pacific sea surface temperature anomaly of +2.5 °C is not a forecast that air temperatures anywhere in Asia will rise by 2.5 °C.

NOAA now verifies its outlooks with the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI): a three-month running mean of Niño-3.4 anomalies with the average tropical anomaly subtracted, so that warming of the whole tropics does not count as El Niño. El Niño is declared at +0.5 °C or more. The latest RONI values are estimates that can change for up to two months. Other agencies, and many news reports, use the older Oceanic Niño Index or the plain Niño 3.4 anomaly, which can differ; always check which index a figure uses.

Schematic (illustrative): Neutral: Trade winds blow east to west. Warm water pools in the western Pacific, where air rises and rain falls. Cold water upwells in the east, where drier air sinks. El Niño: Trade winds weaken. Warm water spreads east and the thermocline deepens there; upwelling weakens. Rising air and heavy rain shift to the central and eastern Pacific, and sinking, drier air settles over Indonesia. La Niña: Trade winds strengthen. Warm water is pushed farther west and deeper; upwelling in the east increases. Rising air and rain strengthen over the western Pacific and Indonesia.

### How a change in the Pacific reaches Asia

### Connections over distance

When the area of rising air over the Pacific shifts, the large circulation that links it to the rest of the tropics shifts too. Scientists call these long-distance links teleconnections. In everyday terms, a change in where the Pacific rains can change where air sinks and skies stay clear thousands of kilometres away, including over parts of Asia.

### From rain and cloud to heat

Rainfall and temperature move together in much of the region: Southeast Asia's regional centre describes opposite rainfall, and consequently temperature, conditions in La Niña years to those in El Niño years. Where rain is scarcer than usual, the same season can also run hotter.

### Season, place and other drivers

The same El Niño can matter a great deal in one season and little in another. Over Southeast Asia, its drying effect is typically stronger over the southern and eastern parts of the region from June to October, and over most of the Maritime Continent from September to November. India's Ministry of Earth Sciences notes that the Indian Ocean Dipole, the Madden-Julian Oscillation and regional ocean-atmosphere interactions also shape the monsoon. No two El Niño events produce identical impacts, and outcomes depend on the pattern of Pacific warming, the timing and other climate drivers.

### Peak and effects at different times

An event's peak in the Pacific and its effects in a region need not coincide. This year's El Niño is forecast to peak around the end of 2026, while India's heatwave season runs mainly from April to June. Effects arrive through each region's own seasonal cycle, so there is no single delay that applies everywhere.

### South and Southeast Asia, region by region

- India and the South Asian monsoon. Historical pattern: El Niño has historically been associated with weaker summer monsoon rainfall over parts of India, but it is not the only influence: the Indian Ocean Dipole and the Madden-Julian Oscillation matter too. In India's records for 1961 to 2013, most years with above-normal heatwave activity in April to June followed El Niño events. This season: India's Ministry of Earth Sciences reported in August 2026 that INCOIS assessed El Niño as likely to persist from June 2026 to February 2027, with probabilities of 70 to 90 per cent. IMD's ENSO and IOD bulletin for October 2026 indicates a high likelihood of strong-to-very strong El Niño conditions persisting through January to March 2027, with neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions. IMD releases its seasonal outlooks for the hot season between March and May. Cannot be inferred: An India-wide pattern does not give the outlook for one district or city, and the monsoon relationship does not carry over to all of South Asia. Service: India Meteorological Department (https://mausam.imd.gov.in/). Question: Which wards and services had the most heat-related problems in the last hot season, and are their repairs funded before March?

- Bangladesh and Nepal. Historical pattern: These neighbours do not simply follow India's pattern. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology data, as reported, show eight of nine El Niño years with reduced monsoon rainfall, and one with above-average rain. For Bangladesh, this page found no national statement of a typical El Niño relationship; its weather department's monsoon outlook for July to September 2026 expected near-normal rainfall overall, with above-normal temperature across the country. This season: No current outlook for the 2027 hot season from either service was verified here. Cannot be inferred: A pattern for one country, or one season, does not transfer to its neighbour or to a single district. Service: Bangladesh Meteorological Department (https://www.bmd.gov.bd/); Nepal Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (https://www.dhm.gov.np/). Question: Who receives the national service's heat and rainfall bulletins in our area, and who passes them on to the people most exposed?

- Mainland Southeast Asia. Historical pattern: El Niño typically brings drier-than-average conditions to Southeast Asia, with the effect usually stronger over the southern and eastern parts of the region from June to October, and more pronounced in moderate or strong events. This season: ASMC's seasonal forecast of 5 November 2026 predicts below-normal rainfall over southeastern mainland Southeast Asia for November 2026 to January 2027, and above-normal temperature over the ASEAN region. Towards the end of the year the northern ASEAN region enters its dry season, with a possible rise in hotspots and haze. Cannot be inferred: A regional tercile forecast does not give any one province's rainfall, and the northern and southern parts of the mainland have different seasons. Service: ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (https://asmc.asean.org/asmc-seasonal-outlook/). Question: If the dry season runs hotter, which water points, schools and worksites lose water or shade first, and who can fix them?

- Indonesia and the maritime region. Historical pattern: El Niño typically brings drier-than-average rainfall to most of the Maritime Continent from September to November, raising the risk of forest fires and smoke haze. In El Niño, sinking air over Indonesia brings higher pressure and dryness. This season: NOAA's November discussion, and its weekly update of 23 November, note suppressed rainfall persisting over Indonesia. ASMC's forecast predicts below-normal rainfall over parts of the southeastern and northeastern Maritime Continent through January 2027; hotspots with local smoke plumes may still occur where rain stays below normal. Cannot be inferred: Rainfall varies sharply between islands; a regional forecast does not show one island's water supply or fire risk. Service: BMKG, Indonesia (https://www.bmkg.go.id/); Meteorological Service Singapore (https://www.weather.gov.sg/climate-el-la/). Question: Where do smoke and heat arrive together, and do clinics and schools there have a plan for both?

- The Philippines. Historical pattern: PAGASA advises that El Niño increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall, which may bring dry spells and droughts in some areas, while above-normal rainfall may still occur over the western part of the country during the southwest monsoon (Habagat). This season: PAGASA's current monthly outlook was not verified here; check PAGASA's latest El Niño advisory and climate outlook. Cannot be inferred: Rainfall differs between Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao, and between the archipelago's eastern and western sides. Service: PAGASA (https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/). Question: Which barangays relied on water deliveries in past dry spells, and is that arrangement funded for the coming months?

### How it can travel through daily life

- Drier conditions -> pressure on water supply -> less reliable water and cooling. Whether this happens depends on how a town's water is stored and pumped, whether supply depends on electricity or tankers, and who has storage at home.

- Hotter days -> more demand for cooling -> possible pressure on electricity. It depends on how much spare capacity the grid has, how much cooling is electric, and whether outages fall on the hottest hours.

- Work disrupted by heat -> less income -> less money for protection. It depends on whether workers can take breaks without losing pay, whether wage support exists, and whether employers adjust hours.

- Schools or care services close -> care moves into homes -> more unpaid care, and lost earnings for whoever provides it. It depends on whether closures come with alternatives, and who is expected to stay home.

- Dry vegetation and fires lit by people -> more fire and smoke haze -> heat and smoke together. Most relevant where land is cleared by burning and where El Niño brings drier months, as in parts of the Maritime Continent.

Where the pathways meet: These pathways tend to meet in the same places. A pump that needs power, a clinic that needs water, a worker who cannot afford a break and a school that closes early can all fall on one household in the same week. Which of them matters depends on the local season and on how a town's services are arranged, which is why the outlook alone cannot say.

The same dry, hot season lands differently. A street vendor who cannot leave a stall, a construction worker paid by the day, an older person living alone under a tin roof, a person with a disability who cannot reach a cooling space, and a mother who stays home when the school shuts all face the heat with fewer choices than a salaried office worker with a fan and a refrigerator.

Illustrative: Picture a household in a dense ward: the father does day-labour, the mother sells vegetables, the grandmother has diabetes. If water is cut in the afternoon and the school closes for heat, someone loses a day's earnings to collect water and look after the children, and the grandmother waits longer in the clinic queue. None of this is a forecast; it shows where preparation helps.

### The current outlook

El Niño watch (bulletin: NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, issued 12 November 2026; next scheduled 10 December 2026)
- Official status: El Niño Advisory. NOAA's alert status when El Niño conditions are observed and expected to continue.
- What changed: No substantive change since NOAA's discussion of 12 November 2026: no newer monthly discussion has been issued (the next is due 10 December 2026). NOAA's weekly update of 23 November, the Bureau of Meteorology's weekly values to 22 November and ASMC's status page are consistent with it. WMO's update of 20 November 2026 is a project update on preparedness, not a new forecast.
- Observed: El Niño strengthened compared with the previous month: sea surface temperature anomalies exceeded 4.0 °C and extended farther west across the eastern equatorial Pacific. The weekly Niño-3.4 index reached +2.5 °C, and rainfall stayed suppressed over Indonesia. NOAA's monthly review of conditions in the tropical Pacific. The +2.5 °C Niño-3.4 figure is the latest weekly value it reports, not the three-month RONI used to classify events.
- Forecast (January to March 2027): A strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027 (a greater than 79% chance), before it begins to weaken in early 2027.
- For March to May 2027, NOAA Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of El Niño at 80%, most likely weak (53%) or moderate (25%); for April to June 2027, ENSO-neutral becomes more likely (61%) than El Niño (38%).
- ENSO phase probabilities (NOAA Climate Prediction Center, issued November 2026; Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), Niño-3.4 region, 1991–2020 base, ±0.5 °C thresholds): January to March 2027: El Niño 100%, neutral 0%, La Niña 0%; February to April 2027: El Niño 98%, neutral 2%, La Niña 0%; March to May 2027: El Niño 80%, neutral 20%, La Niña 0%; April to June 2027: El Niño 38%, neutral 61%, La Niña 1%.
- Strength, March to May 2027: weak 53%, moderate 25%, strong 2%, very strong 0% (these share out the 80% chance of El Niño; they are not added to it).
- NOAA Climate Prediction Center calls an event historic if its three-month RONI reaches +2.5 °C or more, and gave that about a 60% chance for October to December 2026 and for November 2026 to January 2027.
- Observed, NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO: Recent Evolution, Current Status and Predictions (weekly update), issued 23 November 2026, covers recent weeks to 23 November 2026, Tropical Pacific (Weekly Niño indices and RONI (weekly values are not three-month indices)): A weekly monitoring summary between monthly discussions, not a new outlook. - Observed and forecast, Australian Bureau of Meteorology, Climate driver update: ENSO and the Indian Ocean, issued November 2026, covers week ending 22 November 2026; outlook to March to May 2027 (southern autumn), Tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean (Weekly relative Niño3.4 (not RONI); weekly Indian Ocean Dipole index): Weekly relative Niño3.4 of +2.67 °C for the week ending 22 November 2026, below the event's peak so far of +2.88 °C. Most models expect warming to peak in December or January and to stay above El Niño thresholds into the southern autumn of 2027 (March to May 2027). The Bureau notes that a strong Niño3.4 signal does not necessarily mean strong impacts. https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/enso/
- Observed and forecast, ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, Regional Climate: El Niño / La Niña (status with October 2026 values), issued November 2026, covers October 2026, and August to October 2026; outlook to April 2027, Niño3.4 region, read for Southeast Asia (Relative Niño3.4; RONI (three-month); events classified at ±0.65 °C): Relative Niño3.4 of 2.3 °C for October 2026 and 2.0 °C for August to October 2026. The index is predicted to peak during November to December 2026; strong El Niño conditions are predicted to persist until February to March 2027, with El Niño continuing until at least March to April 2027; most models (more than 70%) predict El Niño will still be present in April 2027. https://asmc.asean.org/asmc-el-nino/
- Observed and forecast, India Meteorological Department, ENSO and IOD Bulletin, October 2026, issued October 2026, covers September 2026; outlook through January to March 2027, Tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean, read for India (Niño 3.4 SST anomaly, ±0.5 °C (Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecast System, September 2026 start); Dipole Mode Index, ±0.4 °C): A high likelihood of strong-to-very strong El Niño conditions persisting through January to March 2027. Neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions prevail and are most likely to continue; IMD notes some international centres expect the positive phase to continue in the near term. This was IMD's latest bulletin online on 26 November 2026. https://mausam.imd.gov.in/ClimateInformation/imdweb/CLIMATE_FCST/Bulletin/ENSO_IOD_Update_Bulletin.pdf
- Forecast, World Meteorological Organization, Global Seasonal Climate Update for November 2026 to January 2027, issued 21 October 2026, covers November 2026 to January 2027, Niño 3.4 region and the Indian Ocean (Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly, multi-model ensemble mean (not RONI)): The seasonal average anomaly is forecast at about +3.8 °C, peaking around December 2026; a positive Indian Ocean Dipole is forecast to decline to +0.3 °C. https://wmo.int/resources/publication-series/global-seasonal-climate-updates/gscu-ndj2026
- Forecast, World Meteorological Organization, El Niño/La Niña Update (WMO's latest quarterly update; no newer one was found by 26 November 2026), issued 3 September 2026, covers through February 2027, Tropical Pacific (Consensus of WMO Global Producing Centres): An exceptionally high likelihood, nearly 100%, that El Niño persists through February 2027. https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027
- Forecast, ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, Seasonal forecast for November 2026 to January 2027, issued 5 November 2026, covers November 2026 to January 2027, ASEAN region (Multi-model rainfall and temperature terciles): Below-normal rainfall over parts of the southeastern and northeastern Maritime Continent and southeastern mainland Southeast Asia, and above-normal temperature over the ASEAN region. National services hold the national-scale outlook. https://asmc.asean.org/asmc-seasonal-outlook/
- The Indian Ocean: Agencies read the Indian Ocean Dipole differently, because each uses its own index and threshold. The Bureau of Meteorology reports a weekly index of +0.53 °C for the week ending 22 November 2026 and expects the positive event to weaken and return to neutral in early southern summer; ASMC expects positive conditions to return to neutral in January 2027; IMD's October bulletin reports neutral conditions on its ±0.4 °C threshold. Read each with its own date; they are not averaged.
- Our reading (Common Shade's interpretation): The odds favour El Niño persisting into the start of the hot season in much of South and Southeast Asia, then easing. That is a reason to get ordinary heat protection working early, in the places where people already spend the hottest hours. It is not a forecast of a heatwave anywhere.
- Uncertain locally: A Pacific probability is not any town's chance of a heatwave, a water shortage or a flood. NOAA's strength odds describe the Pacific index, not the strength of local impacts. Local outcomes depend on the season, geography, other drivers such as the Indian Ocean Dipole, long-term warming and local conditions; national seasonal outlooks and official local warnings carry that detail.
- Earlier bulletins, kept as history: Meteorological Service Singapore, El Niño/La Niña status, issued 16 October 2026 (The relative Niño3.4 index was 2.1 °C for September and 1.7 °C for July to September, and was predicted to peak during October to December 2026.).

- Phase: The chance that ENSO is in El Niño, neutral or La Niña in a given three-month season. Example: NOAA (November 2026): For March to May 2027, NOAA Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of El Niño at 80%, most likely weak (53%) or moderate (25%); for April to June 2027, ENSO-neutral becomes more likely (61%) than El Niño (38%).

- Strength: The chance that the Pacific index falls in a strength band. A stronger Pacific event does not necessarily mean stronger local impacts. Example: NOAA (November 2026), March to May 2027: weak 53%, moderate 25%, strong 2%, very strong 0% (these share out the 80% chance of El Niño; they are not added to it).

- Seasonal climate: The chance of above- or below-normal rainfall or temperature in a region over a season, from a regional or national service. Example: ASMC (5 November 2026): above-normal temperature over the ASEAN region, November 2026 to January 2027.

- Local warning: An official warning of heat, rain or storms for a district over the coming days. This is what sets local action moving. Example: Issued by the national weather service for your district, as the event approaches.

Forecasts made in the northern spring are less reliable than at other times of year. Forecasters call this the spring predictability barrier, though it is more a dip in accuracy than a wall. It matters here because the odds for April to June 2027 rest partly on that season: NOAA Climate Prediction Center's chance of El Niño falls from 80% for March to May 2027 to 38% for April to June 2027, when neutral becomes more likely.

El Niño sits on top of long-term warming rather than replacing it. Scientists have low confidence in predicting exactly how a warmer world will change ENSO itself. Attributing any single heatwave or flood solely to El Niño needs a study of that event.

Bulletins can seem to disagree because they measure different things. NOAA's strength odds use RONI over three-month seasons; WMO's seasonal update forecasts the plain Niño 3.4 anomaly from many models; a weekly value is not a three-month index. Thresholds differ too: NOAA and IMD use ±0.5 °C for El Niño and La Niña, ASMC classifies events at ±0.65 °C and calls those above 1.5 °C strong, and IMD reads the Indian Ocean Dipole on a ±0.4 °C threshold. Read each with its own date, index and period, and never average them.

### From outlook to preparation

- Months ahead: Review the places people are most exposed; repair existing water points and shade; agree who is responsible for what; prepare staffing and recurrent budgets; agree how an official local warning will set actions moving. Who might lead: Municipal body with the departments that run water, health and markets; employers; community organisations. Confirm locally: Who holds the budget and the authority to act, locally.

- Weeks ahead: Read the national and regional seasonal outlooks; check supplies and that services are ready; confirm arrangements reach the people most affected, in their languages and formats. Who might lead: Service operators; health departments; community organisations. Confirm locally: That messages reach people who cannot read, cannot hear or have no phone.

- Days ahead: Follow the official local warning and the agreed procedures for each sector: longer water hours, rest breaks at work, queues moved under cover. Who might lead: Whoever the local plan names. Confirm locally: The warning source and who receives it.

- During and after: Monitor who could not get water, shade or care; log failures and how fast they were fixed; revise the arrangements using what happened. Who might lead: Operators, with community organisations reporting what users see. Confirm locally: Who records failures, and who changes the plan.

Throughout: workers' ability to take breaks, household access to water and cooling, communication people can understand, and continuity of care for those who depend on it.

- Municipality: Pick one public service to protect first, and the sites where people wait or work in the heat. Name who authorises, pays for, runs and repairs each measure; they can be different bodies. Agree what an official local warning changes: water hours, opening times, staff on duty. Check that warnings reach people who cannot read, hear or get online.

- Employer: Plan rest breaks, shade and water at work before the hot season, without loss of pay. Move the heaviest work away from the hottest hours when a warning is issued. Know the signs of heat illness, and who to call. Check national rules on heat at work.

- Community organisation: Map who is most exposed: people living alone, outdoor workers, people with disabilities, households without water storage. Agree with the municipality how you will report failures and pass on warnings. Keep a list of cool, accessible places and their opening hours. Plan for care when schools or clinics change hours.

- Funder: Fund recurrent costs, such as water, staff and repairs, not only installation. Release money on agreed triggers, so it arrives before the heat, not after. Ask how reach will be counted: sites working out of sites needed, and who was left out. Support national services' outlooks reaching local decision-makers.

### Questions

- Does El Niño mean every place will have a heatwave? No. El Niño raises or lowers the likelihood of hotter, drier, wetter or cooler conditions in different regions. It does not predict that a particular heatwave will happen anywhere.

- Does a strong El Niño mean severe local impact? Not necessarily. NOAA states that the strength of El Niño does not necessarily correspond with the strength of its influence or expected impact. Even a very strong event makes typical impacts more likely, not certain.

- Does El Niño guarantee drought or a failed monsoon? No. In India, El Niño has historically been associated with weaker monsoon rain over parts of the country, but other drivers also shape the monsoon. In Nepal, one of nine El Niño years in its national records brought above-average rain.

- Can floods happen during an El Niño? Yes. An ENSO forecast shifts the odds; it does not rule out heavy rain. In the Philippines, PAGASA notes that above-normal rainfall may still occur over the western part of the country during the southwest monsoon in an El Niño year.

- Does an ENSO-neutral period remove heat risk? No. Heat depends on the local climate, the season, long-term warming and other drivers such as the Indian Ocean Dipole. NOAA's odds favour neutral conditions by April to June 2027, which is much of India's heatwave season.

- What does "super El Niño" mean? It is not an official category. NOAA's strength table uses bands in 0.5 °C steps of the RONI index, the highest being 2.0 °C or more (very strong). NOAA Climate Prediction Center calls an event historic if its three-month RONI reaches +2.5 °C or more, and gave that about a 60% chance for October to December 2026 and for November 2026 to January 2027. A forecast chance of a historic event is not an observed record. Use the issuing agency's own terms, with their index and period.

- What local information is worth checking next? Your national weather service's seasonal outlook for your region, its heat and rainfall warnings for your district, and your own records of what failed in the last hot season. Regional centres such as ASMC add the regional picture.

## Heat inside factories
https://beattheheat.asia/factory-heat/
Understand the sources. Protect the people. Improve the conditions.
Why two people in the same factory can face very different heat, what each source of heat does to the body, and which measures address it: an interactive floor plan, an intervention library with its evidence and limits, a finder, four worked examples, a measurement guide and a worksheet for workers and managers to fill in together. Garment manufacturing is the main example.

### Why can two people in the same factory experience very different heat?
Because heat is not one number. It depends on where a person stands, what the work asks of their body, what is near them, what they wear, how long they stay and whether they can step away to recover. A thermometer on the wall, or the weather forecast for the city, describes none of that on its own.
An illustrative walk, not a measurement:
- A sewing line, mid-morning: An operator sits at a machine under the second-floor roof. The work is light for the body but steady, and the line target leaves little room to stand up. Motors and lamps add a little heat; the roof above is warming as the sun climbs. By early afternoon the same seat may be much hotter than it was at nine.
- A pressing station, early afternoon: A presser stands at a steam iron and vacuum table. Heat comes from the iron and the steam, moisture hangs in the air, and the arms work constantly. The presser feels hot before the sewing floor does, and sweat evaporates less well in the damp air.
- The packing and dispatch bay: A packer lifts and carries cartons near the loading door. The air may be cooler than at the presses, but the work is heavier, so the body makes more heat of its own; sun on the loading apron and the trucks waiting there add more.
- The rest space: If there is a cool, shaded place close by, water within reach, a toilet nearby and permission to use them without losing pay, the body can recover. If the rest space is a hot corridor, far away, or effectively off limits during a rush order, the heat of the morning carries into the afternoon.
Exposure changes by task, by location, by time of day and by how long it lasts. Protection works when it reaches each of those, and when people can actually use it.

### Understand the heat
Occupational guidance separates heat stress, the total heat load on a worker from the work, the clothing and the surroundings, from heat strain, the body's response to that load. Seven things set the load.
- Air temperature: What an ordinary thermometer reads. It matters, but it is one of seven parts. Two places with the same air temperature can feel and act very differently on the body.
- Radiant heat: Heat that reaches the skin across a gap, without touching: from a sun-heated roof or wall, from sunlight through a window or skylight, and from hot equipment such as irons, boilers, ovens, furnaces and steam pipes. A worker can face strong radiant heat in air that does not feel very hot.
- Humidity and evaporation: The body cools mainly by sweat evaporating from the skin. Damp air slows evaporation, so in humid places sweating does less to cool. Steam, wet processes and evaporative coolers all add moisture.
- Air movement: Moving air carries heat away from the skin and helps sweat evaporate, as long as the air is cooler than the skin. Very hot air moved across the body can add heat instead.
- Heat made by work: Muscles make heat. Lifting, carrying, pushing carts and fast repetitive work make more than sitting at a machine. The same room is a different exposure for a packer and for a seated operator.
- Clothing and protective equipment: Clothing that blocks air and sweat, aprons, gloves and protective suits keep heat in. Some protection is essential for the task; its weight, fit and fabric still change the heat load.
- Duration and recovery: Heat builds over time. Long spells without a break, overtime, and nights too hot to sleep all reduce the body's chance to recover before the next exposure.
- Touching hot surfaces is a separate hazard: Conduction is heat passing by direct contact. At work it matters most as a contact burn from an iron plate, a steam pipe, a mould or a hot product. That is a burn hazard, controlled by guards, insulation, handles and gloves. It is different from whole-body heat stress, which builds from all seven parts above even when nothing hot is touched.
Four words:
- Environmental heat stress: The heat load the surroundings and the work place on a person. It can be estimated by measurement.
- Physiological heat strain: The body's response: rising core temperature, faster heart rate, sweat loss. Two people under the same heat stress can show different strain.
- Thermal discomfort: Feeling too hot. It matters for wellbeing and attention, but feeling cooler is not proof of being protected, and feeling fine is not proof of being safe.
- Heat-related illness: Harm to health, from heat rash and cramps through heat exhaustion to heat stroke, which is a medical emergency.
Why a shaded indoor workplace can still be hot. A roof keeps the sun off people but can itself become a large radiant heater, and machines, lamps, steam and bodies add heat inside. Without enough air exchange the heat stays.
Why the outdoor weather reading may poorly describe a workstation. The city's weather station measures air in open shade away from buildings. A workstation under a hot roof, beside a press or near a loading door has its own conditions. In assessments of Cambodian apparel factories in the hottest months, about half were above the programme's indoor threshold while hotter than the air outside at the same time.
Why a measure that feels better still needs checking. A fan, a cooling vest or a misting system can feel pleasant at once. Whether it lowers the heat load enough, for the people most exposed, through the whole shift, is a separate question that only measurement and worker feedback answer. Changes also need checking so that they do not add a new risk, such as moving hot air or blocking exhaust ventilation.
Where this page gives a number, it names its source and the conditions it applies to. A figure from a laboratory, another climate or another kind of work does not transfer to your factory without checking.

### Explore a factory (an illustrative garment factory, not a thermal survey)
#### Receiving and material handling
- Heat sources: Sun on the loading apron and through open doors; Hot air from outside when doors stand open; Truck engines and exhaust nearby
- Work: Moderate to heavy: lifting rolls of fabric and cartons, pushing trolleys. Work comes in bursts when deliveries arrive, often at the hottest time.
- Who works here: Loaders and material handlers, often men, often on contract or daily terms; drivers waiting with vehicles.
- Ask: When do deliveries arrive, and can any be moved to cooler hours? How heavy are the loads, and are there trolleys or lifts that work? Where do drivers and loaders wait?
- Measure: Air temperature and humidity at the dock at peak delivery times; Globe temperature in sun and in any shade; Weights and distances carried
- Measures to consider: Shaded loading bays and waiting areas; Mechanical handling aids: trolleys, conveyors, lifts; Reschedule hot processes and heavy tasks; Relief operators and extra staffing in hot periods
- Depends on: Shade and doors depend on who owns the building; rescheduling depends on suppliers and buyers.
#### Cutting and sewing
- Heat sources: Radiant heat from the roof and walls; Many people working close together; Machine motors and lighting; Sun through windows and skylights
- Work: Light for the body, but long and steady: hours at a machine against a line target.
- Who works here: Machine operators, most of them women in garment factories, with helpers and line supervisors; cutters, more often men, at cutting tables.
- Ask: Which lines are hottest, and at what time of day? Can people leave the line to drink, use the toilet or rest without losing pay or being scolded? Where does air move, and where does it stagnate?
- Measure: Air temperature, humidity and air speed at seated head height on several lines; Globe temperature under the roof versus near the floor; Readings across the shift, not only at noon
- Measures to consider: Reflective (cool) roof surfaces; Roof and wall insulation; Ceiling and large-diameter fans; Workstation fans; Replace hot lighting and switch off idle equipment; Paid recovery breaks; Cool, safe drinking water close to every line; Unrestricted, clean, safe toilets
- Depends on: Roof work needs the building owner; break rules need production planning and, often, the buyer's delivery schedule.
#### Pressing and finishing
- Heat sources: Steam irons and vacuum tables; Steam leaks and uninsulated steam lines; Moisture in the air; Fusing and heat-press machines
- Work: Moderate: standing, repetitive arm work, often fast near the end of an order.
- Who works here: Pressers and finishers; in many factories pressing is done mostly by men, with women in thread-cutting, checking and folding nearby.
- Ask: Where does steam escape, and who reports leaks? Are steam lines and boilers insulated? Is pressing next to sewing lines, so its heat spreads?
- Measure: Humidity and globe temperature at the pressing tables; Surface temperature of steam lines and irons (for contact risk); Air speed at the presser's position
- Measures to consider: Repair steam leaks and maintain the steam system; Insulate hot pipes, boilers and vessels; Local extraction of heat and moisture at the source; Separate, enclose or relocate hot processes; Zoned or workstation cooling; Task rotation, where it truly reduces exposure
- Depends on: Steam repair and insulation need maintenance budget and an owner; extraction needs replacement air and commissioning.
#### Packing and dispatch
