- Heat sources: Heavy physical work; Sun at the loading door; Little air movement among stacked cartons
- Work: Moderate to heavy: lifting, carrying and stacking cartons, sometimes at speed before a shipment.
- Who works here: Packers and loaders, often men, plus women in folding and tagging; workers on short contracts during peak orders.
- Ask: What happens to breaks in the final days before shipment? Do new or returning workers get time to adjust to the heat? Are there carts, conveyors or lifts?
- Measure: Air and globe temperature at packing tables and the loading door; Workload: weights, lifts per hour, distances; Hours worked in the days before shipment
- Measures to consider: Mechanical handling aids: trolleys, conveyors, lifts; Deliver materials to the point of use; Relief operators and extra staffing in hot periods; Acclimatisation for new and returning workers; Limits on excessive overtime; Shaded loading bays and waiting areas
- Depends on: Peak workload depends on the order calendar, which buyers set as much as the factory.
#### Roof-exposed upper floors
- Heat sources: Sun-heated roof radiating downward; Hot air rising from lower floors; Few openings for air to escape
- Work: Depends on the task on that floor; the heat is added to whatever the work already makes.
- Who works here: Whoever is placed there: often sewing lines or finishing, sometimes storage with occasional work.
- Ask: Is the top floor hotter than lower floors, and from what time? What is the roof made of, and who owns it? Is there space to vent hot air at the top?
- Measure: Globe and air temperature just below the roof and at work height, through the afternoon; Compare with a lower floor at the same time
- Measures to consider: Reflective (cool) roof surfaces; Roof and wall insulation; Shaded or ventilated roof layers; Stack ventilation: let hot air out at the top; Reschedule hot processes and heavy tasks
- Depends on: Building owner's permission; roof strength for any added layer or panels.
#### Process equipment and utility rooms
- Heat sources: Boilers and steam generators; Compressors and generators; Hot exhaust and pipes
- Work: Short visits for operation and maintenance, sometimes long repair jobs in a hot room.
- Who works here: Boiler operators, maintenance technicians and electricians, often working alone.
- Ask: Who goes in, how often, for how long? Is anyone working alone in heat? Is waste heat vented outside or into the building?
- Measure: Air and globe temperature during a typical maintenance job; Surface temperatures of pipes and casings
- Measures to consider: Insulate hot pipes, boilers and vessels; Recover or safely remove waste heat; Remote operation and cooled control booths; Buddy arrangements; Trained first responders and a tested emergency procedure
- Depends on: Engineering advice; the plant room may serve the whole site, so changes need planning.
#### Water, toilets, canteen and rest
- Heat sources: Rest areas under hot roofs or in corridors; Canteens with cooking heat; Long distances from the line
- Work: This is where recovery happens, or does not.
- Who works here: Everyone, but especially those whose breaks are shortest: operators on targets, pregnant and breastfeeding workers, older workers.
- Ask: How long does it take to walk from the farthest line to water and a toilet? Is the rest space cool, seated and usable in the time allowed? Is drinking water safe, cool and refilled?
- Measure: Air and globe temperature in the rest space; Walking time from lines to water and toilets; Whether water points run dry, and when
- Measures to consider: Cool, safe drinking water close to every line; Unrestricted, clean, safe toilets; Cooled rest rooms; Lactation breaks and facilities; Paid recovery breaks
- Depends on: Space, plumbing and a budget for cleaning and refilling, every day of the hot season.

### Health and equity
Heat harms through pathways that are well described, through associations seen in surveys, and through outcomes measured in studies. This page keeps them apart.
- Mechanisms: How heat acts on the body, as occupational guidance describes it: core temperature rises when heat gain exceeds loss; sweating removes water and salt; the heart works harder to send blood to the skin; fatigue builds and attention slips; severe strain becomes heat exhaustion and, at worst, heat stroke.
- Associations: What surveys and economic studies observe alongside heat, without proving cause on their own. In a survey of women at three garment factories in Phnom Penh, the share reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months, by their own reports. A research note cites an estimated average 1.5% fall in productivity for moderate manufacturing work for each 1 °C above 25 °C WBGT.
- Measured outcomes: What was measured on people under defined conditions. In a laboratory simulation of garment work, core temperature, heart rate and sweat loss were measured for each cooling option. That shows physiological strain under those conditions; it does not measure illness, injury or long-term health in a factory.
- Fatigue and attention: Heat strain and dehydration make people tired and slower to react. Where needles, blades, presses and moving machinery are close at hand, that is a route from heat to injury. In a survey at Sri Lankan apparel firms, workers linked headaches, dehydration and poorer concentration to needle injuries, by their own accounts; no checked study on this page measures that route directly.
- Dehydration: Sweat losses build over a shift. Water helps only if it is close, safe, cool and people have time and permission to drink, and to use a toilet afterwards.
- Recovery: The body recovers in cool rest, and overnight. Hot homes and short nights carry strain into the next shift.
#### Women's work, women's bodies, and the arrangements around them
Women make up most of the garment workforce in many producing countries. Some differences in heat risk come from the body; many more come from how work is arranged. Keeping the two apart matters, because the answer to an arrangement is to change the arrangement.
In the laboratory simulation, the cooling options lowered core temperature in men more often than in women: women's core temperature fell only with air conditioning. The tasks differed by design (men ironed, women sewed) and the participants were healthy volunteers, so the result points to a question for real factories, not a settled difference.
- What the body brings: Body size, fitness, acclimatisation, age and health all shape heat tolerance, and individuals differ widely. Occupational guidance notes that women tend to sweat less than men of the same fitness, size and acclimatisation, and that differences in heat tolerance narrow once those are taken into account. Physiology is one part; the arrangements below are often the larger one.
- Tasks and authority: Women are often concentrated in seated, target-paced sewing and finishing work, and less often in supervisory roles that decide when lines pause, who rests and where fans go. Ask who holds those decisions.
- Targets, piece rates and attendance bonuses: Where pay depends on pieces completed or on a perfect attendance record, a break or a sick day costs money. In a study at two garment factories in Dhaka, quota pressures restricted workers' use of drinking water. Protection that ignores this may exist on paper and go unused.
- Water and toilets: People drink less when toilets are far, dirty, unsafe or require permission. Water and toilets belong in the same plan, measured in walking minutes and in whether people actually use them.
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Occupational health guidance links a pregnant worker's core temperature rising above 38 °C to risks for the fetus, and suggests doing tasks earlier in the day or in cooler places, with work-rest cycles. Evidence in humans of harm to the developing baby is not conclusive, so this guidance is precautionary. Pregnant and breastfeeding workers need reliable access to drinking water. The response is an individual assessment with the worker and her health provider, adjusted tasks, timing or location, and protected earnings, not exclusion from work by default.
- Lactation: Where the ILO Maternity Protection Convention (No. 183) is ratified, it gives a right to daily breaks or reduced hours to breastfeed, counted as working time and paid. A clean, private, cool place to express milk and store it is part of that.
- Menstruation and menopause: Workers raise these concerns in heat, from access to private, clean facilities to hot flushes. This page has not yet found checked occupational studies on heat and menstruation or menopause in factory work, so it makes no health claim; facilities and confidential support are still matters of dignity and access.
- Protective equipment that fits: Equipment sized for an average man may fit women badly, trap more heat or be left off. This page found no checked study measuring this in garment or textile work; it belongs in the worksheet as a question to ask.
- Commuting, hot homes, sleep and unpaid care: Long commutes, hot homes and unpaid care leave some workers, often women, with less time to rest, rehydrate and recover outside working hours.
- Confidential reporting, representation and freedom from retaliation: Workers know where heat collects and airflow is weak. They can tell you only if reporting is safe: confidential, answered, and free of punishment. Representation needs to include women, contract and temporary workers, and those in the hottest jobs.
Risk also varies within any group: by age, disability, pregnancy, health conditions and medicines, how long someone has worked in heat, and how secure their job is. A temporary worker may not report symptoms for fear of losing work. Plans that count only the average worker miss the people most at risk.
Protection keeps people in work. Moving a pregnant worker to a cooler task with the same pay, adding a relief operator so a line can pause, or shifting a heavy job to the cooler morning are accommodations. Sending people home without pay, or quietly not hiring them, is not protection.

### Intervention library
Evidence types: Authoritative occupational guidance; Field report from operating factories; Controlled experimental study; Modelling or engineering analysis; Manufacturer claim; Proposal requiring validation.
#### A. Process and heat-source reduction
Make less heat, or keep it where it is made.
- Repair steam leaks and maintain the steam system [steam-repair]. Addresses: Heat and moisture escaping from steam lines, valves, traps and irons. How: Every leak adds heat and humidity to the room and wastes fuel. Fixing leaks and faulty traps removes both at the source. Where: Pressing and finishing in garment factories; laundries, food processing, dyeing and wet processing. Works if: A named person checks for leaks on a schedule; Workers can report a leak and see it fixed. Take care: Steam systems are pressurised: repairs need trained staff and isolation of the line. Upfront: Low: parts and labour. Running: Routine inspection and maintenance time. Owners: Maintenance or utilities lead; production reports leaks. Measure: Humidity and globe temperature at pressing tables before and after; count of open leak reports and days to fix. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Insulate hot pipes, boilers and vessels [insulate-hot]. Addresses: Radiant and convective heat from bare hot surfaces; contact burns. How: Insulation keeps heat inside the pipe or vessel, so less reaches the room and the people in it, and less fuel is wasted. Where: Steam lines to pressing; boilers and exhaust-gas boilers; dyeing and wet-processing vessels; ovens and dryers in food processing. Works if: Insulation is fitted completely, including valves and flanges; Damaged cladding is replaced. Take care: Wet or damaged insulation loses its effect and can hide corrosion; Choose materials suitable for the temperature and for fire safety. Upfront: Low to moderate, depending on pipe length and access. Running: Inspection; repair of cladding after maintenance work. Owners: Maintenance or utilities lead, with an energy or engineering adviser. Measure: Surface temperatures of pipes; globe and air temperature at nearby workstations; fuel use. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance; Field report from operating factories.
- Replace hot lighting and switch off idle equipment [led-lighting]. Addresses: Heat given off by old lamps and by machines left running. How: Older lamps turn much of their power into heat; efficient lighting gives the same light with less. Switching off idle machines and heaters removes their heat too. Where: Any production floor with many lamps or machines; sewing floors are a common case. Works if: Light levels stay adequate for the task; Idle switching does not slow production restarts. Take care: Turning lights off to cope with heat creates a low-light hazard; replace hot lamps instead. Upfront: Low to moderate; often paid back in electricity. Running: Little. Owners: Facilities or energy lead. Measure: Light levels at work surfaces; air and globe temperature at head height; electricity use. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Separate, enclose or relocate hot processes [separate-hot]. Addresses: Heat from pressing, fusing, boilers or ovens spreading to people who do not work at them. How: Placing hot processes in their own area, behind partitions or enclosures, or away from sewing lines keeps their heat and moisture from reaching everyone else. Where: Pressing and fusing near sewing lines; boilers and generators inside production buildings; ovens in food processing; furnaces in metalworking. Works if: The separated area has its own extraction or ventilation; Workflow still works after the move. Take care: Enclosing a hot process concentrates heat for whoever works inside it: they need extra protection; Partitions can block air paths and exits. Upfront: Moderate to high, depending on layout changes. Running: Little, once done. Owners: Plant manager with engineering advice. Measure: Temperatures at neighbouring lines and inside the separated area, before and after. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Remote operation and cooled control booths [enclose-hot]. Addresses: Workers whose job is to watch or control a very hot process from close by. How: A cooled booth, or controls placed away from the heat, lets people do the job without standing in the hottest air or radiant field. Where: Foundries, furnaces, kilns, large boilers and some plastics and glass processes; rarely needed in garment assembly. Works if: Booths have their own cooling and fresh air; Tasks that can only be done beside the process are kept short and planned. Take care: Booths need maintenance; a failed booth cooler can become a hot box. Upfront: High. Running: Energy and maintenance for booth cooling. Owners: Plant engineering. Measure: Booth temperature and how long operators spend outside it. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Recover or safely remove waste heat [waste-heat]. Addresses: Hot exhaust and process heat released into the building. How: Ducting exhaust outside, or recovering its heat to make steam or hot water, stops it warming the workspace. Where: Generators, boilers, compressors and dryers in any factory. Works if: Engineering design for safe ducting and pressure. Take care: Recovery equipment that is itself uninsulated adds heat back into the room. Upfront: Moderate to high. Running: Maintenance. Owners: Utilities or energy lead. Measure: Temperatures near plant rooms and exhaust points; energy use. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
#### B. Building envelope and solar heat
Stop the sun's heat getting in through roofs, walls and glass.
- Reflective (cool) roof surfaces [roof-cool]. Addresses: Sun heating the roof, which then radiates heat down onto workers. How: A light, solar-reflective surface absorbs less sunlight, so the roof stays cooler and radiates less heat into the floor below. Where: Single-storey sheds and top floors with metal or concrete roofs, in sunny climates. Works if: The roof is sound and accessible; The surface is kept clean; dirt reduces reflectance. Take care: Less benefit where a well-insulated roof already blocks the heat, or under frequent cloud; Needs the building owner's permission. Upfront: Moderate: coating or reflective sheeting. Running: Cleaning; recoating every few years. Owners: Building owner and factory facilities team. Measure: Globe temperature below the roof and at work height on comparable sunny afternoons, before and after. Evidence: Controlled experimental study (The trial tested a modified rooftop that lowered the room to 37.5 °C from 40 °C in a climate chamber; it did not test a particular coating.); Field report from operating factories (A roof heat shield was one of several measures; its separate effect was not reported.); Modelling or engineering analysis (A simulation of one Dhaka garment factory; a white cool roof was one of four retrofits tested.).
- Roof and wall insulation [roof-insul]. Addresses: Heat passing through the roof and walls into the workspace. How: Insulation slows heat flow, so less of the sun's heat reaches the room and the ceiling surface stays cooler. Where: Metal-roofed sheds and uninsulated concrete roofs. Works if: Fitted without gaps and kept dry; Fire-safe materials. Take care: In a building full of internal heat, insulation can also slow heat escaping at night: pair it with ventilation. Upfront: Moderate to high. Running: Little; check for water damage. Owners: Building owner. Measure: Ceiling surface and globe temperature at work height, afternoons before and after. Evidence: Field report from operating factories; Modelling or engineering analysis (An insulated white cool roof was one of four retrofits simulated for a Dhaka garment factory.).
- Shaded or ventilated roof layers [roof-ventilated]. Addresses: The sun striking the roof directly. How: A second layer above the roof, such as raised sheeting or solar panels, takes the sun's heat; air moving between the layers carries it away before it reaches the roof below. Where: Flat or low-pitched roofs with structural capacity for an extra layer. Works if: A clear air gap that is open at the edges; Structural check of the roof. Take care: Adds load to the roof; Panels need cleaning and maintenance access. Upfront: Moderate to high; solar panels may offset cost through electricity. Running: Cleaning and maintenance. Owners: Building owner and energy lead. Measure: As for cool roofs. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (Rooftop solar panels with new insulation; management-reported, combined effect.); Modelling or engineering analysis (Rooftop shading was one of four retrofits simulated for a Dhaka garment factory.).
- External shading, solar films and skylight control [facade-shade]. Addresses: Sunlight entering through windows, glazed walls and skylights, heating the people it falls on. How: Shading outside the glass stops the heat before it enters; blinds, reflective films and covers on skylights reduce what gets through. Where: Production floors with large windows or roof lights. Works if: Daylight remains adequate; Shading does not block windows used for ventilation. Take care: Internal blinds keep out glare but trap some heat inside the glass. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Little. Owners: Facilities team; building owner for external works. Measure: Globe temperature at sunlit workstations at the time the sun falls on them. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Shaded loading bays and waiting areas [shade-dock]. Addresses: Sun on loading aprons, where people lift and wait. How: A canopy or shade structure over the loading area cuts direct and reflected sun where heavy work happens. Where: Receiving and dispatch in any factory. Works if: Shade covers where people actually work at peak hours. Take care: Wind and vehicle clearance for structures. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Maintenance of the structure. Owners: Facilities team; building owner. Measure: Globe temperature at the dock in sun and in the new shade. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Trees and vegetation around the site [site-shade]. Addresses: Sun heating walls, yards and paths between buildings. How: Trees shade walls and open ground and cool the air around them by evaporating water. Where: Sites with open land around buildings. Works if: Water and care for several years until trees establish. Take care: Takes years to work; not a fix for this summer; Roots and drainage near foundations. Upfront: Low. Running: Watering and care. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Shade at walls and paths; wall surface temperatures. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page measures trees around factories. Common Shade's city pages cover urban greening evidence.).
- Orientation, height and layout for new or rebuilt factories [orientation]. Addresses: Heat designed into a building from the start. How: Facing the long walls away from the low sun, high ceilings that let hot air rise above work height, openings for cross-ventilation, and keeping hot processes on the downwind side all reduce heat for decades. Where: New factories and major renovations. Works if: Decided at the design stage, with the climate and process in mind. Take care: High ceilings help only if hot air can leave at the top. Upfront: Low if planned from the start; high as a retrofit. Running: None. Owners: Owner, architect and engineers. Measure: Compare the new building with the old one at the same time of year. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (High ceilings were one of several measures; their separate effect was not reported.).
- Night ventilation and thermal storage [night-vent]. Addresses: Heat stored in the building during the day. How: Flushing the building with cooler night air, where nights are cool enough, cools the structure so it absorbs heat the next day. Where: Climates with a large drop between day and night temperature; buildings empty or lightly used at night. Works if: Nights are meaningfully cooler than days; Openings can be left open securely. Take care: Does little in humid climates with warm nights; Outdoor air pollution, insects and security. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Someone to open and close. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Morning indoor temperatures with and without night flushing. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page tests night ventilation in factories.).
#### C. Radiant-heat control
Block or move away from hot surfaces people can see.
- Reflective shields and screens [radiant-shield]. Addresses: Radiant heat from hot equipment such as presses, ovens, boilers and furnaces. How: A reflective or heat-absorbing screen between the hot surface and the worker blocks the line of sight, so the radiant heat does not reach the skin. Where: Pressing, fusing, dryers, ovens, kilns, furnaces, moulding machines. Works if: The shield blocks the line of sight from the hot surface to where the worker stands; It is kept clean and in place. Take care: Can block air movement, visibility or safe access; A shield that gets hot itself radiates heat; reflective or insulated faces work better. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Cleaning and replacement. Owners: Maintenance or engineering lead. Measure: Globe temperature at the worker's position before and after. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Distance and repositioning workstations [reposition]. Addresses: Workstations placed close to hot equipment, windows or under hot roof areas. How: Radiant heat falls off with distance and line of sight. Moving people back, or turning the workstation, can reduce exposure with no new equipment. Where: Any floor where layout has grown up around machines. Works if: Workflow and safe access survive the move. Take care: Moving one line can put another in the heat. Upfront: Low. Running: None. Owners: Production manager. Measure: Globe temperature at old and new positions. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Task-specific reflective protection [reflective-ppe]. Addresses: Intense radiant heat at tasks that cannot be shielded, such as pouring molten metal. How: Reflective aprons, sleeves or face shields reflect radiant heat away from the body during the task. Where: Foundries, furnaces and glass; not garment assembly. Works if: Used only for the specific task, for short periods. Take care: Reflective clothing also traps body heat: it adds strain if worn for long or for heavy work. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Replacement. Owners: Safety lead. Measure: Duration of use; wearers' heat symptoms. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page appraises reflective protective clothing; follow the safety rules that apply to the process.).
#### D. Ventilation and air movement
Exchange hot air for cooler air, extract heat and moisture at source, and move air over people.
- Natural cross-ventilation [cross-vent]. Addresses: Hot, stale air trapped in the workspace. How: Openings on opposite sides let wind carry heat and moisture out, as long as the outdoor air is cooler than the indoor air. Where: Narrow buildings with openable windows or louvres on two sides. Works if: Openings on both sides, kept unobstructed; Outdoor air is cooler and reasonably clean. Take care: Brings in dust, outdoor pollution and noise; Can disrupt local exhaust on machinery. Upfront: Low. Running: Keeping openings clear. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Air speed and temperature at lines near and far from openings. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Stack ventilation: let hot air out at the top [stack-vent]. Addresses: Hot air collecting under the roof. How: Hot air rises. Openings high in the roof or walls let it escape, drawing cooler air in lower down. Where: Tall sheds and top floors with roof access. Works if: High outlets and low inlets; Rain protection. Take care: Little effect where outside air is as hot as inside. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Little. Owners: Building owner and facilities team. Measure: Temperature just under the roof and at work height. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page measures stack ventilation in factories.).
- Mechanical supply and exhaust ventilation [exhaust-supply]. Addresses: Heat and moisture building up faster than natural ventilation removes them. How: Fans push or pull air through the building, replacing hot air with outdoor air. Exhaust fans need matching openings or supply fans so that replacement air can enter. Where: Large production floors, especially in humid climates; common in garment factories. Works if: Enough replacement air enters, from a cooler, cleaner place; Fans are maintained and balanced. Take care: Only cools if outdoor air is cooler than indoor air; Exhaust without replacement air starves local extraction and doors slam. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Electricity and maintenance. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Air speed and temperature across the floor; airflow through exhaust fans. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Local extraction of heat and moisture at the source [local-exhaust]. Addresses: Steam and hot air rising from presses, irons, dryers and ovens. How: A hood or extraction point at the hot process removes heat and moisture before they spread into the room. Where: Pressing and fusing in garment factories; laundries; food processing; dyeing and wet processing. Works if: Hoods are close enough to capture the plume; Replacement air enters elsewhere. Take care: General fans can blow the plume away from the hood: position them together; Extraction for heat is different from extraction for fumes or dust; check what each system is for. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Electricity, filter and duct maintenance. Owners: Facilities or engineering lead. Measure: Humidity and temperature at the pressing position before and after; capture visible in steam plumes. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Workstation fans [workstation-fans]. Addresses: Still air at the workstation. How: Air moving over the skin speeds sweat evaporation and carries heat away, when the air is cooler than the skin. Where: Sewing lines, packing tables, any seated or standing station. Works if: Air temperature is below skin temperature and humidity allows sweat to evaporate; Every person who needs one has one, and it has power at the hottest hour. Take care: In very hot air, fans can add heat instead of removing it; the threshold depends on humidity; Can blow away local exhaust plumes, fabric lint or dust; Power cuts stop them when they are most needed. Upfront: Low. Running: Electricity; cleaning and replacement. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Air speed and temperature at head height; workers' reports; check fans run during power cuts. Evidence: Controlled experimental study (A fan alone lowered men's heart rate in the simulation; a fan with drinking water lowered men's core temperature. Women's core temperature did not fall with fans.); Modelling or engineering analysis (The modelling covers population groups, not factory tasks.); Authoritative occupational guidance; Field report from operating factories.
- Ceiling and large-diameter fans [ceiling-fans]. Addresses: Still air across a whole floor. How: Large, slow fans move a lot of air over a wide area with relatively little power. Where: High-ceilinged sheds and large floors. Works if: Enough ceiling height for safe mounting; Air is cooler than skin. Take care: Same air-temperature limits as other fans; Can stir up dust and lint. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Electricity and maintenance. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Air speed across the floor. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Remove obstructions to airflow [remove-obstruction]. Addresses: Air blocked by stacked materials, partitions and closed openings. How: Clearing stored cartons from windows, opening blocked vents and rearranging partitions lets existing ventilation work. Where: Any floor, especially near packing and storage. Works if: A walk-through to find blocked paths. Take care: Storage needs another home. Upfront: Very low. Running: Housekeeping. Owners: Production and facilities. Measure: Air speed before and after at the affected positions. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Maintenance, balancing and commissioning of ventilation [commissioning]. Addresses: Ventilation that was installed but does not deliver. How: Testing airflow when systems are installed and regularly afterwards, cleaning fans and filters, and adjusting dampers keeps systems doing what they were designed to do. Where: Any mechanically ventilated or cooled building. Works if: A schedule, a budget and a named owner. Take care: Systems degrade unseen: without checks, a fan can run while moving little air. Upfront: Low. Running: Technician time. Owners: Facilities or maintenance lead. Measure: Measured airflow against design; maintenance log. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
#### E. Active cooling and humidity management
Remove heat with machines, and manage moisture with it.
- Direct evaporative cooling (water curtains, cooling pads) [evap-cooling]. Addresses: Hot, dry or moderately humid air across a large floor. How: Fans pull outside air through water-soaked pads; the water evaporates and cools the air before it reaches people. It adds moisture as it cools. Where: Large garment floors in hot climates; common in Southeast and South Asia, Central America and North Africa. Works if: Outdoor humidity is low or moderate; Strong exhaust removes the moist air; Pads and water are kept clean. Take care: Cools less as humidity rises, and adds humidity that slows sweating; Humid air can affect fabric and product quality in monsoon conditions; Uneven airflow: people near the pads may be cold, those far away still hot; Uses water; stagnant water needs treatment against bacteria. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Water, electricity, pad replacement and cleaning. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Air temperature and humidity near and far from the pads, across seasons; a heat stress index, not air temperature alone. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Indirect and two-stage evaporative cooling [indirect-evap]. Addresses: The moisture that direct evaporative cooling adds. How: Water evaporates on one side of a heat exchanger, cooling the supply air on the other side without adding moisture to it. Where: Hot climates where direct evaporative cooling makes the air too humid. Works if: Engineering design for the climate. Take care: Costs more than direct systems; Still loses effect in very humid weather. Upfront: Moderate to high. Running: Water, electricity, maintenance. Owners: Facilities and engineering. Measure: Supply air temperature and humidity; heat stress index at work positions. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page tests indirect evaporative cooling in factories.).
- Whole-space air conditioning [air-con]. Addresses: Heat and humidity across the whole workspace. How: Refrigeration removes heat and moisture from the air, which works in any climate. Where: Electronics assembly and other climate-controlled processes; some garment floors. Works if: Reliable power; The building is reasonably sealed and insulated; Maintained systems. Take care: High energy use and cost; heat is rejected outdoors; Power cuts stop it. Upfront: High. Running: High: electricity and maintenance. Owners: Owner and facilities team. Measure: Temperature and humidity across the floor; energy use; what happens in a power cut. Evidence: Controlled experimental study; Field report from operating factories (Refrigerant air-cooling combined with evaporative units and exhaust fans.).
- Zoned or workstation cooling [spot-cooling]. Addresses: A few very hot positions in an otherwise tolerable floor. How: Cooled air delivered to specific workstations, or air conditioning for one zone, cools the most exposed people without cooling the whole building. Where: Pressing stations; operator positions at hot machines. Works if: Cooled air reaches the person, not the ceiling. Take care: Spot coolers that reject heat into the same room add heat overall. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Electricity and maintenance. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Temperature at the cooled position and around it. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Dehumidification with heat removal [dehumid]. Addresses: Humid air that stops sweat evaporating. How: Removing moisture helps sweat evaporate. A dehumidifier on its own, however, releases heat into the room; it helps only as part of a system that also removes heat, such as air conditioning or ventilation that carries it out. Where: Humid climates and wet processes. Works if: Heat from the dehumidifier is rejected outdoors. Take care: A standalone dehumidifier in a closed room makes it hotter. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Electricity. Owners: Facilities and engineering. Measure: Humidity and air temperature together; a heat stress index. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance (Guidance lists dehumidification among ways to reduce humidity. The warning about standalone units follows from where their heat goes, not from a measured study.).
- Cooled rest rooms [cool-rest]. Addresses: Breaks taken in the same heat as work. How: A cooled, seated rest space close to work lets the body shed heat during breaks. Where: Every factory. Works if: Close to the lines; Big enough for everyone on break; Usable in the time allowed. Take care: A cool room far away goes unused in a short break. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Electricity, cleaning. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Rest-room temperature; walking time from lines; how many people use it. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance; Field report from operating factories (A cooling station beside the work lowered heat strain in a pilot field trial, but workers found it interrupted work: placement and break time matter.).
#### F. Workload and workstation design
Reduce the heat bodies make by reducing effort.
- Mechanical handling aids: trolleys, conveyors, lifts [handling-aids]. Addresses: Heat made by lifting and carrying. How: Less effort means less heat made by the body. Where: Receiving, cutting, packing and dispatch; metalworking and food processing. Works if: Aids are suitable for the loads and floors; They are maintained and actually used. Take care: Mechanisation adds its own hazards: moving parts, crushing, noise; Can reduce staffing, which affects jobs. Upfront: Low to high. Running: Maintenance. Owners: Operations manager. Measure: Weights and distances carried; workers' exertion reports. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Deliver materials to the point of use [point-of-use]. Addresses: Walking and carrying to fetch bundles and materials. How: Bringing work to people reduces unnecessary movement and effort. Where: Sewing lines, packing. Works if: Workflow redesign with line supervisors. Take care: Do not let it become a reason never to leave the line. Upfront: Low. Running: None. Owners: Industrial engineering. Measure: Steps and carries per hour. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page measures this for heat; it rests on the principle that less effort makes less body heat.).
- Relief operators and extra staffing in hot periods [relief]. Addresses: Lines that cannot pause without stopping production. How: A relief operator covers each station in turn, so everyone gets a real break without the line stopping or targets slipping. Where: Sewing lines; pressing; packing before shipment. Works if: Relief staff are trained for the stations they cover. Take care: Costs money; needs budget in the order price. Upfront: None. Running: Wages. Owners: Production manager. Measure: Breaks actually taken per person, per shift. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page evaluates relief staffing for heat.).
- Reduce pace or workload when heat is high [pace]. Addresses: Targets set for cooler conditions. How: Lowering hourly targets in hot conditions reduces effort and makes time to drink and rest. Where: Any target-paced work. Works if: Pay is protected when targets are lowered. Take care: Without pay protection, workers lose money and may refuse it. Upfront: None. Running: Lower output in hot periods. Owners: Management, with worker representatives. Measure: Targets in hot versus cool periods; pay; breaks taken. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (Adjusted breaks are listed among measures that can be put in place quickly.).
#### G. Work organisation and earnings
Change time, pace and pay so that people can recover without losing income.
- Paid recovery breaks [paid-breaks]. Addresses: Strain building without recovery. How: Breaks in a cool place, with water, let the body shed heat. Paying for them means people take them. Where: Every factory. Works if: Breaks are paid and scheduled; Cool rest and water are close by. Take care: Breaks in a hot corridor do little. Upfront: None. Running: Paid time. Owners: Management. Measure: Breaks taken; where they are taken; pay records. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Work-rest arrangements based on assessment [work-rest]. Addresses: Fixed schedules that ignore conditions. How: Using a heat stress measure and the intensity of the work to set how much rest each hour needs, as some national rules and guidance do. Where: Hot processes and heavy tasks especially. Works if: Qualified assessment and a measure suited to the place. Take care: Thresholds from one country or programme do not transfer without checking. Upfront: Low: a meter and training. Running: Measurement time. Owners: Safety lead, with qualified advice. Measure: Index readings and rest taken. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Protection from piece-rate and attendance penalties [no-penalty]. Addresses: Pay systems that punish breaks, slowing down or sick days in heat. How: Paying a guaranteed rate in hot periods, or keeping attendance bonuses when heat causes absence, removes the reason to work through symptoms. Where: Piece-rate and target-paid work; attendance-bonus systems. Works if: Written rules, communicated and kept. Take care: Informal pressure from supervisors can undo a written rule. Upfront: None. Running: Cost of guaranteed pay. Owners: Management, buyers through order pricing. Measure: Pay in hot versus cool months; attendance bonus losses; symptom reports. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (Proposed by the research note; not evaluated.); Field report from operating factories (Quota pressure restricted drinking water in two Dhaka garment factories.).
- Limits on excessive overtime [overtime-limits]. Addresses: Long hours in heat with little recovery. How: Shorter days reduce total exposure and leave time for sleep and recovery. Where: Peak order periods. Works if: Order schedules allow it. Take care: Lost overtime pay matters to workers. Upfront: None. Running: Lost output or extra staff. Owners: Management and buyers. Measure: Hours worked; symptoms; sleep reports. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page evaluates overtime limits for heat.).
- Reschedule hot processes and heavy tasks [reschedule]. Addresses: The heaviest or hottest work falling in the hottest hours. How: Moving heavy loading, boiler maintenance or pressing peaks to cooler hours reduces exposure. Where: Receiving, dispatch, maintenance, pressing. Works if: Suppliers and buyers can adjust deliveries. Take care: Earlier or later hours affect transport, care and sleep. Upfront: None. Running: Coordination. Owners: Operations manager. Measure: Heat at the time tasks are done; workers' feedback. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance; Authoritative occupational guidance (Guidance on pregnant workers suggests completing tasks earlier in the day.).
- Shift changes developed with workers [shift-change]. Addresses: Shifts that place long work in the hottest part of the day. How: Starting earlier, splitting shifts or adding a cooler shift can move work out of peak heat. Where: Whole-factory decisions. Works if: Agreed with workers, including transport and safety. Take care: Redistributes exposure rather than reducing it if hot periods still fall on someone; Night travel safety, especially for women; childcare. Upfront: Low. Running: Transport, supervision. Owners: Management and worker representatives. Measure: Exposure by shift; who works which shift; transport and care effects. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page evaluates shift changes for factory heat.).
- Acclimatisation for new and returning workers [acclimatise]. Addresses: People who are not yet used to the heat. How: Building up time in heat over days lets the body adapt; people new to heat, or returning after leave or illness, are at higher risk. Where: Every factory, especially with high turnover or seasonal hiring. Works if: Supervisors know who is new and plan their workload. Take care: Production pressure on new hires. Upfront: None. Running: Lower output from new staff for the first days. Owners: Supervisors and HR. Measure: Symptom reports among new workers. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Escalation, interruption and restart procedures [stop-work]. Addresses: No agreed point at which work slows or stops. How: Agreed triggers, based on measurement and symptoms, for extra breaks, slowed work, moving people or stopping, and a clear way to restart. Where: Every factory. Works if: Written, known and practised. Take care: Stopping without pay protection will not be used. Upfront: Low. Running: Drills and review. Owners: Management and safety committee. Measure: Trigger readings; actions taken; time to act. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (A right to stop work without penalty or loss of income is proposed, not evaluated.).
- Task rotation, where it truly reduces exposure [rotation]. Addresses: The same people in the hottest jobs all shift. How: Rotating people between hot and cooler tasks can cut each person's time in the heat. Where: Pressing and other hot stations. Works if: The cooler task is genuinely cooler and lighter; People are trained for both. Take care: Rotation spreads exposure; it does not reduce the total; Rotation onto unfamiliar tasks can raise injury risk. Upfront: Low. Running: Training. Owners: Production manager. Measure: Time each person spends in hot tasks. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance (Guidance lists job rotation; it spreads exposure rather than reducing the total, and no checked study here evaluates it in factories.).
#### H. Water, sanitation and rest
Make recovery possible: water, toilets and cool rest, close by and usable.
- Cool, safe drinking water close to every line [water-access]. Addresses: Sweat losses not replaced. How: Water close by, cool and safe, with time and permission to drink, replaces fluid lost to sweat. Where: Every factory. Works if: Water points within a short walk of every station; Refilled and cleaned; safe to drink; Toilets nearby, so people do not drink less to avoid them. Take care: One schedule does not fit everyone: needs vary with work, heat and the person; Long, heavy sweating also loses salt; follow health guidance on electrolytes. Upfront: Low. Running: Supply, cooling, cleaning, testing. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Walking time to water; water points running dry; workers' reports. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance; Controlled experimental study (In the simulation, a fan with drinking water reduced sweat-loss fluid deficit for both men and women.); Field report from operating factories.
- Unrestricted, clean, safe toilets [toilet-access]. Addresses: People drinking less to avoid toilets that are far, dirty, unsafe or need permission. How: Toilets close by, clean, private and safe, used without asking, make drinking possible. Where: Every factory. Works if: Enough toilets for the workforce, separate and safe for women; Cleaned through the day. Take care: Supervisor permission rules quietly cut drinking. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Cleaning, supplies. Owners: Facilities team; management for permission rules. Measure: Walking time; cleaning; whether permission is needed. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked study on this page links toilet access to drinking in factories; the site's actions page carries one funder-commissioned summary.).
- Seating and cooling during breaks [cool-seats]. Addresses: Breaks spent standing in heat. How: Shaded, seated, cooled rest lets heart rate fall and the body shed heat. Where: Every factory. Works if: Enough seats for everyone on break. Take care: none noted. Upfront: Low. Running: Little. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Seats per worker on break; rest-space temperature. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
#### I. Personal cooling and clothing
Cool the person directly, where the space cannot be cooled enough.
- Breathable workwear [workwear]. Addresses: Uniforms that trap heat. How: Light, loose, breathable fabrics let sweat evaporate. Where: Any uniformed workplace. Works if: Fabric choice tested with wearers. Take care: It still meets any safety requirement of the task. Upfront: Low. Running: Replacement. Owners: Management. Measure: Wearers' reports. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance (Clothing is one part of the heat load.).
- Optimise necessary protective equipment and its fit [ppe-optimise]. Addresses: Protective equipment that adds heat. How: Choosing lighter, breathable protection where it gives the same protection, sizing it to fit, and limiting time in heavy protection reduce the heat it adds. Where: Chemical handling in dyeing; foundries; food processing; cleanrooms. Works if: Protection is not reduced below what the hazard needs. Take care: Never remove needed protection to cope with heat; change the heat or the time instead. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Replacement. Owners: Safety lead. Measure: Time in protection; wearers' symptoms. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance (Guidance on how protective clothing holds heat; no checked study here measures fit for women in factory heat.).
- Cooling garments: phase-change, ice, air- or liquid-cooled [cooling-garments]. Addresses: Heat that cannot be removed from the space, especially under protective clothing. How: Packs or circulating fluid in a vest or wrap draw heat from the body. Where: Foundries, hot maintenance jobs, work in heavy protective clothing. Works if: Packs are recharged or replaced on schedule; Compatible with the task and equipment. Take care: Limited duration; weight; hygiene of shared garments; Air- or liquid-cooled garments need tethers or power that may snag machinery. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Recharging, cleaning, replacement. Owners: Safety lead. Measure: Duration of benefit; wearers' heat symptoms; whether people keep using it. Evidence: Controlled experimental study (A meta-analysis of trials among workers or acclimatised adults; certainty low to very low.); Field report from operating factories (A pilot field trial with 12 workers in an indoor sawmill, not a garment factory.).
- Skin wetting and misting [misting]. Addresses: Sweat that cannot keep up. How: Water on the skin evaporates and cools, if the air is dry enough. Where: Only where water near fabric, electricity and machinery is safe. Works if: Low humidity. Take care: Wet fabric spoils product; Electrical hazards near machinery; Little effect in humid air. Upfront: Low. Running: Water and hygiene. Owners: Facilities and safety. Measure: Humidity effects; product quality. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked study on this page tests misting in factories; review literature supports skin wetting in some settings.).
#### J. Women's participation and accommodation
Make sure protection reaches women, with their say in how.
- Worker-led heat assessments [worker-led]. Addresses: Assessments done without the people who know the floor. How: Workers, including women and contract workers, walk the floor with management, mark hot spots and propose fixes. Where: Every factory. Works if: Representatives chosen by workers; Time paid; findings answered. Take care: Token participation erodes trust. Upfront: Low. Running: Paid time. Owners: Safety committee. Measure: Issues raised and fixed; workers' trust in the process. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Individual pregnancy and lactation accommodation [pregnancy-accom]. Addresses: Pregnant and breastfeeding workers facing the same heat as everyone else. How: An individual assessment with the worker and her health provider, leading to adjusted tasks, timing, location, breaks and water, with earnings protected. Where: Every factory. Works if: Confidential, voluntary disclosure; Pay and job protected. Take care: Exclusion from work is not accommodation. Upfront: Low. Running: Cost of adjusted work. Owners: HR, occupational health, supervisor. Measure: Accommodations requested and given; pay kept. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Lactation breaks and facilities [lactation]. Addresses: No time or place to breastfeed or express milk. How: Paid breaks and a clean, private, cool room with a way to store milk. Where: Every factory employing women. Works if: Close to work; usable in break time. Take care: none noted. Upfront: Low to moderate. Running: Cleaning. Owners: Management and HR. Measure: Use of the facility; breaks taken. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance.
- Accessible menstrual hygiene facilities [menstrual]. Addresses: No private, clean place and supplies. How: Clean, private toilets with water, disposal and supplies. Where: Every factory employing women. Works if: Cleaned through the day. Take care: none noted. Upfront: Low. Running: Supplies and cleaning. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: Facilities available and used. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked study on this page links menstrual facilities to heat outcomes; it is presented as access and dignity.).
- Representation of every employment category [representation]. Addresses: Contract, temporary and agency workers left out of committees and plans. How: Including all categories gives a voice to those in the hottest and least secure jobs. Where: Every factory. Works if: Seats for each category; meetings in paid time. Take care: none noted. Upfront: None. Running: Paid time. Owners: Management and unions. Measure: Who sits on the committee. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
#### K. Management, health services and emergency response
Make protection someone's job, and make the response to illness fast.
- A written heat programme with accountable owners [heat-programme]. Addresses: Protection that depends on goodwill. How: A written plan names the measures, who owns each, the budget, the triggers and the review dates. Where: Every factory. Works if: Budget for maintenance and running costs, not only installation. Take care: A plan on paper with no budget. Upfront: Low. Running: Review time. Owners: Senior management. Measure: Plan reviewed; budget spent; actions done. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance; Field report from operating factories.
- Joint worker-management oversight [committee]. Addresses: Decisions made without workers. How: A joint committee reviews measurements, complaints and incidents, and tracks fixes. Where: Every factory. Works if: Meets regularly, including before the hot season. Take care: none noted. Upfront: None. Running: Paid time. Owners: Management and worker representatives. Measure: Meetings held; issues closed. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Supervisor training [supervisor-training]. Addresses: Supervisors who push through symptoms. How: Training on recognising heat illness, on the rules for breaks and water, and on responding without blame. Where: Every factory. Works if: Supervisors are judged on safety as well as output. Take care: none noted. Upfront: Low. Running: Refreshers each season. Owners: HR and safety. Measure: Symptom reports handled; worker feedback. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (Training for workers, not supervisors; it measured knowledge and practice scores, not exposure or illness.).
- Non-punitive, confidential symptom reporting [no-retaliation]. Addresses: Workers hiding symptoms for fear of losing pay or jobs. How: A safe, confidential channel and a written promise of no penalty make reporting possible. Where: Every factory. Works if: Reports are answered and visible changes follow. Take care: none noted. Upfront: None. Running: Handling time. Owners: Management and safety committee. Measure: Reports received and answered. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Buddy arrangements [buddy]. Addresses: People working alone in heat, and symptoms people miss in themselves. How: Two people agree to check on each other for signs of heat illness during hot shifts, and know what to do and whom to call when one of them shows symptoms. It adds to, and never replaces, heat controls, rest arrangements and a tested emergency procedure. Where: Utility rooms, maintenance, night shifts, new and returning workers. Works if: Paid time for both people to learn the signs, the response and the escalation route, and for the checks themselves; Pairs that both people accept, in a language both understand, with arrangements for workers with hearing, speech or literacy needs; A named supervisor or responder who answers every call, and a rule that raising the alarm never costs pay or work; Privacy: a buddy notices symptoms, not medical details, and nothing is recorded about a person's health without consent. Take care: Checking on others is work: if it falls repeatedly on the same people, often women, without time or pay, it becomes unpaid caring work; A buddy cannot cool a workplace or stop production; responsibility stays with supervisors and the employer; Pairs break down when shifts, overtime or staffing change; review them each hot season; Not a substitute for trained first responders or medical care. Upfront: Training time for both people and their supervisor, during paid hours; local costing needed. Running: Paid time for checks and refresher training before each hot season; supervision of the arrangement. Owners: The employer, through supervisors, with the safety committee or worker representatives agreeing how pairs are formed. Measure: Lone working in heat; calls raised and how fast someone responded; whether checking time is paid. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (Recommended practice in national occupational guidance; no evaluation of buddy systems in factories was found in the sources checked for this page.).
- Trained first responders and a tested emergency procedure [first-response]. Addresses: Slow response to heat stroke. How: Trained people on every shift, a known procedure for rapid cooling and transfer to care, and a clear way to call for help in languages people use. Where: Every factory. Works if: Drilled before the hot season; Transport to care arranged. Take care: A first-aid procedure follows local medical guidance and the occupational rules that apply where you work; this page does not set one. Upfront: Low. Running: Training and drills. Owners: Safety lead. Measure: Drill time to cooling and transfer. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (This page has not checked a first-aid protocol; follow local medical guidance and the occupational guidance that applies where you work.).
- Incident and near-miss review [incident-review]. Addresses: Heat illness that is never recorded. How: Recording fainting, illness and near-misses, and reviewing them with the committee, shows where protection fails. Where: Every factory. Works if: No blame for reporting. Take care: none noted. Upfront: None. Running: Review time. Owners: Safety committee. Measure: Incidents recorded and reviewed. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked study on this page evaluates incident review for factory heat.).
- Confidential occupational health support [confidential-health]. Addresses: Health conditions and medicines that raise heat risk. How: Confidential advice for workers with conditions, pregnancy or medicines that change heat risk, without disclosure to supervisors. Where: Every factory. Works if: Access to a health provider. Take care: none noted. Upfront: Low. Running: Health service cost. Owners: Occupational health. Measure: Consultations; accommodations. Evidence: Authoritative occupational guidance (Health guidance in India includes a heat-risk checklist for pregnancy.).
- Continuity plans for power or water failure [continuity]. Addresses: Fans, coolers and water that stop when the grid or supply fails. How: Backup power for critical ventilation and water, stored water, and agreed actions when cooling fails. Where: Wherever power or water supply is unreliable. Works if: Tested before the hot season. Take care: Generators add heat and fumes; locate them well. Upfront: Moderate. Running: Fuel, tests. Owners: Facilities team. Measure: What runs during an outage. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (No checked source on this page evaluates continuity plans for factory heat.).
- Measure heat where people work, and log it [measure-wbgt]. Addresses: Decisions made from a wall thermometer or a forecast. How: Regular readings at representative workstations, across the shift, with a heat stress index where the work calls for one, visible to workers and managers. Where: Every factory. Works if: Instruments placed where people work, maintained and calibrated. Take care: A single reading at noon misses changes over the shift. Upfront: Low. Running: Reading and logging time. Owners: Safety lead. Measure: This is the measure. Evidence: Field report from operating factories; Authoritative occupational guidance.
#### L. Buyer, supply-chain and financing arrangements
Institutional measures: who pays, who schedules, and who checks.
- Purchasing practices that allow safe production schedules [fair-purchasing]. Addresses: Order deadlines and prices that leave no room for breaks or slower work in heat. How: Lead times and prices that account for hot-season productivity, and flexibility when heat disrupts production. Where: Buyer-supplier relationships in export industries. Works if: Written into purchasing terms. Take care: Institutional: effects are rarely evaluated. Upfront: None. Running: Cost borne in pricing. Owners: Buyers and suppliers. Measure: Lead times; overtime in hot months. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (Proposed; not evaluated.).
- Climate events as force majeure in contracts [force-majeure]. Addresses: Penalties for late delivery caused by extreme heat or floods. How: Contracts that excuse delays caused by extreme climate events remove the pressure to work through dangerous conditions. Where: Buyer-supplier contracts; labour agreements. Works if: Agreed definitions of the triggering events. Take care: Proposal; no evaluation found. Upfront: None. Running: None. Owners: Buyers, suppliers, unions. Measure: Contracts with the clause; penalties waived. Evidence: Field report from operating factories (A recommendation in the research note.).
- Shared financing for upgrades, and money for running costs [shared-finance]. Addresses: Upgrades that need capital the factory lacks, and systems that stop when running money runs out. How: Buyers, lenders and programmes co-finance roofs, cooling and insulation, and agree who pays to run and maintain them. Where: Export factories; sustainable finance programmes. Works if: Running costs funded, not only installation. Take care: Institutional: effects are rarely evaluated. Upfront: Shared. Running: Shared. Owners: Buyers, lenders, factory. Measure: Funds committed and spent; systems still running a year later. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.
- Supplier support and verification that includes heat [verify-supply]. Addresses: Audits and agreements that leave indoor heat out. How: Including indoor heat, measurement, water, toilets and breaks in supplier codes, audits and safety agreements, with worker participation in checking. Where: Export supply chains. Works if: Measured, not just ticked; Workers take part in verification. Take care: An audit on a cool day finds little. Upfront: Low. Running: Audit cost. Owners: Buyers and programmes. Measure: Heat included in audits; findings fixed. Evidence: Field report from operating factories.

### Finder: what you observe, and where to look
Tick what you see. The finder returns the families of measures that address those conditions, with the reason, and what to find out next. It does not score your factory or declare work safe: only measurement, worker feedback and qualified assessment can do that.
- Hot roof or direct sunlight: Radiant heat from the roof or sun adds to every task beneath it. Families: Building envelope and solar heat; Radiant-heat control; Ventilation and air movement. Investigate next: Measure globe temperature just below the roof and at work height through an afternoon, and compare with a lower floor.
- Nearby hot machinery: Hot surfaces radiate heat and can burn on contact. Families: Process and heat-source reduction; Radiant-heat control. Investigate next: List the hot surfaces each worker can see from their position, and measure globe temperature there.
- Steam or moisture: Moisture slows sweat evaporation and steam adds heat. Families: Process and heat-source reduction; Ventilation and air movement; Active cooling and humidity management. Investigate next: Walk the steam system for leaks; measure humidity at the pressing tables.
- Heavy physical work: The body's own heat rises with effort. Families: Workload and workstation design; Work organisation and earnings. Investigate next: Record weights, distances and pace for the heaviest tasks, and when they happen.
- Poor air movement: Still air stops heat and sweat leaving the skin. Families: Ventilation and air movement. Investigate next: Measure air speed at workstations; check that air entering is cooler than air inside.
- Protective clothing: Clothing and equipment trap heat. Families: Personal cooling and clothing; Radiant-heat control. Investigate next: List what is worn for each task and whether all of it is needed for the hazard.
- Breaks that are difficult to take: Protection that cannot be used does not protect. Families: Work organisation and earnings; Water, sanitation and rest; Women's participation and accommodation; Buyer, supply-chain and financing arrangements. Investigate next: Ask workers privately how often they take breaks, drink and use the toilet on a busy day, and what it costs them.
- Unreliable electricity or water: Fans, coolers and water stop when supply fails. Families: Management, health services and emergency response; Building envelope and solar heat. Investigate next: Record what stops during an outage, and for how long, in the hot season.

### Worked examples (illustrative)
#### A sewing floor under a sun-heated roof
- Observed problem: Operators on the top floor say the afternoon is unbearable; some lines switch off lights to cope. A wall thermometer reads the same on every floor.
- Missing information: Globe temperature and air speed at seated head height, across the afternoon, on the top and lower floors; whether breaks, water and toilets are actually used; who owns the roof.
- Candidate measures: Reflective (cool) roof surfaces; Roof and wall insulation; Replace hot lighting and switch off idle equipment; Ceiling and large-diameter fans; Workstation fans; Cool, safe drinking water close to every line; Cooled rest rooms
- Organisational arrangements: Can operators take breaks without losing piece-rate or target pay, or being scolded? If not, relief operators, paid breaks and protection from attendance penalties come first, because cooling the roof does not help someone who cannot leave the line to drink. Agree with the building owner who pays for roof work; agree with the buyer whether lead times allow slower afternoons while works are under way.
- Verification: Repeat the same afternoon readings at the same stations after each change; ask operators on several lines; count breaks taken and water points running dry; keep checking through the season.
#### A pressing section with heat and moisture
- Observed problem: Pressers are soaked by midday; steam drifts onto the nearby finishing tables. Nobody remembers when the steam lines were last checked.
- Missing information: Where steam escapes; surface temperatures of lines and boilers; humidity at the tables; whether extraction exists and works.
- Candidate measures: Repair steam leaks and maintain the steam system; Insulate hot pipes, boilers and vessels; Local extraction of heat and moisture at the source; Separate, enclose or relocate hot processes; Zoned or workstation cooling; Cool, safe drinking water close to every line
- Organisational arrangements: Name a maintenance owner with a budget; give pressers a quick way to report leaks; rotate only if the other task is genuinely cooler.
- Verification: Surface temperatures before and after insulation; humidity and globe temperature at the tables; leak reports and days to fix; pressers' feedback.
#### A packing and dispatch area with heavy handling
- Observed problem: Before shipment, packers lift and stack cartons for long hours near an open loading door in the afternoon sun; new temporary workers join for the rush.
- Missing information: Weights and pace; heat at the door; hours worked in the final days; whether new workers get time to adjust.
- Candidate measures: Mechanical handling aids: trolleys, conveyors, lifts; Shaded loading bays and waiting areas; Reschedule hot processes and heavy tasks; Acclimatisation for new and returning workers; Relief operators and extra staffing in hot periods; Limits on excessive overtime
- Organisational arrangements: Plan the shipment calendar with the buyer so the last days are not the hottest and longest; give new workers lighter loads for the first days.
- Verification: Workload and heat at the time of the work; symptom reports among new workers; hours in the final week.
#### A hot-process area where protective equipment is required
- Observed problem: Workers at a furnace or oven wear heavy protective clothing; the radiant heat is intense and the task cannot simply be moved.
- Missing information: Radiant heat at each position; how long each task takes; what protection the hazard actually requires.
- Candidate measures: Reflective shields and screens; Remote operation and cooled control booths; Insulate hot pipes, boilers and vessels; Zoned or workstation cooling; Optimise necessary protective equipment and its fit; Cooling garments: phase-change, ice, air- or liquid-cooled; Work-rest arrangements based on assessment; Buddy arrangements
- Organisational arrangements: Qualified assessment of work-rest needs; buddy checks; a cooled rest point next to the area; trained first responders on every shift.
- Verification: Globe temperature at positions before and after shielding; time in the hot zone; wearers' symptoms; drills.

### Measure effectiveness
Measurement tells you whether a change reached the people it was meant for. Each instrument answers a different question.
- Air temperature: The ordinary thermometer reading. Simple and useful for trends; it misses humidity, radiant heat and air movement.
- Humidity: How much moisture is in the air. High humidity slows sweat evaporation; evaporative cooling and steam raise it.
- Air speed: How fast air moves past the worker. Shows whether ventilation and fans actually reach people.
- Globe temperature: A thermometer inside a black globe, which responds to radiant heat. The difference from air temperature shows how much radiant heat there is.
- Wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT): A heat stress index that combines a natural wet-bulb reading (humidity and air movement), the globe temperature (radiant heat) and, outdoors, the air temperature. Guidance and some national rules use it, adjusted for how hard the work is.
- Measure at representative workstations, at the height where people work, not on a wall or by a door.
- Measure across the shift and the season, not only at noon on one day.
- Record the task and how hard it works the body; the same reading is a different risk for a packer and an operator.
- Ask workers. Their reports find hot spots instruments miss, and tell you whether protection can be used.
- Repeat the same measurements, at the same places and comparable times, after each change.
- Make readings visible to workers and managers alike.
Four levels of evidence that a measure worked:
- Installation completed: The fan, roof coating or water point exists. This says nothing yet about exposure.
- Measured exposure changed: Readings at workstations differ, under comparable weather and work.
- Workers could use the protection: People reached the water, took the breaks, sat in the cool room, without losing pay.
- Health outcomes improved: Fewer symptoms, illnesses or injuries. This needs records over time and a fair comparison; claim it only with that evidence.
Thresholds and design standards come from qualified assessment and the rules that apply where the factory is. A legal threshold from one country does not transfer to another without explaining its jurisdiction and whether it applies.
- European Union: The Workplaces Directive requires the temperature in rooms containing workstations to be adequate for human beings; most legislation sets no specific maximum, and national law adds detail.
- United States: OSHA and NIOSH publish guidance and recommended exposure limits that depend on work intensity. NIOSH's criteria are recommendations, not law.
- Viet Nam: Ministry of Health WBGT limits fall as work gets heavier and as the share of time exposed rises.
- Bangladesh: The Labour Act requires adequate ventilation and comfortable temperatures, and the Labour Rules a thermometer in every workroom, without numerical thresholds.
- Cambodia: Prakas 147 governs workplace thermal environments and may be revised to add WBGT thresholds. The 32 °C dry-bulb figure Better Factories Cambodia uses is a programme threshold, not law.

### Other manufacturing
Garment assembly is the worked example. Other manufacturing shares the same seven parts of heat, in different proportions. Each line below names what to check first; none is a finding.
- Textile spinning and weaving: Different from garment assembly: large machine halls running continuously, where the air's humidity may be controlled for the yarn. Check how process humidity interacts with workers' heat.
- Dyeing and wet processing: Hot water, steam, open vessels and wet floors, plus chemicals that may require protective equipment. Check moisture, radiant heat from vessels, and the heat added by protection.
- Food processing: Ovens, fryers, boilers and steam beside cold rooms; wet floors; hygiene clothing. Check moves between hot and cold areas, steam, and what hygiene clothing adds.
- Electronics assembly: Often climate-controlled for the product, so the main heat risk may lie in warehouses, loading and utility areas, or in protective gowning. Check areas outside the controlled rooms.
- Metalworking and foundries: Intense radiant heat from furnaces and molten metal, heavy protective clothing and contact-burn hazards. Check radiant heat at each position and time in heavy protection.
- Plastics, ceramics and glass: Moulding machines, kilns and furnaces radiate heat; hot products are handled. Check radiant heat, contact burns and ventilation around machines.
Heat begins before the factory gate: Explore cotton farming, harvesting and transport, and the working arrangements that shape protection upstream. https://beattheheat.asia/cotton-and-heat/

### Evidence gaps
The wider evidence has the same shape. A 2026 scoping review of 90 intervention studies found 68% were in laboratories and 73% in developed countries, with only four testing engineering controls. A 2026 mapping review of field research on workers' heat in low- and middle-income countries found only 9% of reports included any intervention, and 39% included no women.
- No checked independent before-and-after evaluation of a heat intervention in an operating garment factory was found for this page; garment field evidence is from reports by management, programme staff and researchers. The nearest field trial found is a pilot with 12 workers in an indoor sawmill in Thailand.
- The one controlled garment study was a laboratory simulation with healthy volunteers; how its results transfer to factory floors, other climates and other tasks needs testing.
- No checked occupational study was found on heat and menstruation or menopause in factory work, or on protective-equipment fit for women in heat.
- No checked study was found linking toilet access to drinking and heat illness in garment factories, beyond summaries.
- Many intervention records rest on guidance or principle; their effect sizes in factories in South and Southeast Asia are not established here.
- No manufacturer claims are used; products are described by type only.
- Injury pathways from heat in garment work were not found measured in a checked study; the one link found is workers' own accounts in a Sri Lankan survey.

Worksheet to print: https://beattheheat.asia/factory-heat/worksheet/


## Heat in markets and street vending
https://beattheheat.asia/market-heat/
Where heat comes from in an open market, who it reaches between dawn and dusk, and what helps vendors and porters drink, rest and keep earning, with the evidence for each measure and its limits.

### Why the same market hits six people differently between dawn and dusk
An open market holds many working days at once. A wholesale buyer, a porter, a woman selling vegetables alone, a fish seller, a vendor with a child at the stall and a shopper waiting for a bus all share the same street, and meet its heat at different hours, in different places, with different room to stop.
An illustrative market day:
- 06:00 Wholesale buying and loading: The day starts before sunrise with heavy lifting. Porters carry loads paid by the trip, and fish and produce sellers buy ice to keep stock fresh for the day ahead.
- 11:30 The exposed produce row: The sun is overhead. Heat comes from above and bounces up from paving, and shop air conditioners blow hot air into the aisle. A vendor alone has nobody to mind the stall.
- 14:00 The locked or distant toilet block: The toilet is far, paid, locked or unsafe, so some vendors drink less to avoid leaving their goods. The body gets less water in the hottest hours.
- 17:30 The empty aisle and unsold stock: Footfall drops, produce has wilted, and the day's loan repayment or cart rent is still due tomorrow morning.
The same heat lands differently because of where people stand, what they carry, whether they can leave the stall, and what an hour off costs them.

### Understand market heat
A vendor's or porter's heat load is not one number. It builds from the air, the sun, surfaces and machines around them, the work their body does, how long they go without recovering, and how much water they can drink.
- Air temperature: The shade temperature a forecast gives. It is the starting point, and in a market often not the main part of the load.
- Overhead sun and radiant bounce: Direct sun, and heat given back by paving, concrete and metal, can add more to the body than the air does. Light-coloured or reflective paving can make this worse for people standing on it unless there is shade overhead.
- Air-conditioner exhaust and vehicle heat: Shops that cool their rooms push the heat into the street, and engines idling at the kerb add more.
- Humidity and still, narrow aisles: Sweat cools the body only when it can evaporate. Humid air and aisles closed off by stalls and awnings slow it down.
- Heavy lifting and carrying: Porters and loaders make much of their own heat through effort, often at the hottest pace when trucks arrive.
- Long hours without recovery: Many vendors trade from dawn to dusk, standing or squatting, with nowhere cool to sit and no one to take over.
- Drinking less on purpose: Where toilets are far, paid, locked or unsafe, some vendors drink less to avoid needing them. The body then has less water to sweat with in the hottest hours.
This page gives no safe temperature or safe working time. Heat stress depends on all seven factors together; measurement, vendors' own reports and local health advice are the guides.

### Explore a market (an illustrative street market, not a survey)
#### Exposed produce and fish stall row
- Heat sources: Overhead sun on stalls and sellers; Heat bouncing up from paving and concrete; Hot air from neighbouring shop air conditioners; Still air in narrow aisles
- Around 13:30: The sun is nearly overhead and nets or umbrellas give the least cover; stock wilts and spoils fastest.
- At the edges of the day: Low sun reaches under canopies from the side; the row is busiest with buyers, so stepping away costs the most sales.
- Who works or waits here: Vegetable, fruit, flower and fish sellers, many of them women trading alone, some with children.
