- Ask: Which stalls sit in full sun, and at what hours? Who can mind your stall if you need water or a toilet? What spoils first, and when in the day?
- Measure: Globe or mean radiant temperature under stalls around 13:00; Share of stock thrown away at closing; How often sellers leave the stall to drink
- Measures to consider: Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection; Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns; Shared produce cooling, fair-price ice and heat-triggered cash for vendors; Trees for long-term shade at the market's edges
- Depends on: Who holds the pitch, what the street authority allows overhead, and whether shade keeps aisles and fire access clear.
#### Loading bay and porter and cart queue
- Heat sources: Heavy lifting and carrying; Sun on open loading ground; Vehicle exhaust and engine heat
- Around 13:30: There are fewer loads but no shade; porters waiting for a turn stand in the open.
- At the edges of the day: At 06:00 and in the evening the heaviest loads move fast; a porter who stops to drink may lose a paid turn.
- Who works or waits here: Porters and loaders paid by the load, cart pullers, drivers' helpers; mostly men, many of them migrants.
- Ask: Do you lose your place in the queue if you rest? Where is the nearest water and shade from the queue? How many loads make a day's pay?
- Measure: Loads per hour at different times of day; Breaks taken without losing a turn; Reported heat symptoms over a hot week
- Measures to consider: Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns; A shaded place to sit and recover; Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row
- Depends on: Whether porters' associations or the market committee control the queue, and how loads are paid.
#### Public toilet and menstrual-hygiene block
- Heat sources: A hot, airless block; Distance from stalls in the sun
- Around 13:30: The cost of a walk to a far or paid toilet is highest, and so is the pull to drink less.
- At the edges of the day: At 06:00 and after 18:00 the block may still be locked, though trading has begun or not yet ended.
- Who works or waits here: Every vendor and porter; women vendors, people who menstruate, pregnant women, older and disabled vendors and transgender vendors most affected by fees, distance, lighting and safety.
- Ask: Is the toilet open, free, clean and safe for the whole trading day? Is there water, soap, a lock and a bin for menstrual waste? Do you drink less so you need it less?
- Measure: Days and hours open during trading; Water, soap and lighting working on a spot check; How much vendors drink on a hot day
- Measures to consider: Free, clean, women-safe market toilets with water and menstrual hygiene; Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns
- Depends on: Who owns and pays for cleaning, and whether opening hours match trading hours.
#### Drinking-water and ice refill point
- Heat sources: Sun on taps and containers that warms the water; Queues in the open
- Around 13:30: Demand peaks; a dry or warm tap is felt most now.
- At the edges of the day: At 06:00 ice is bought for the day's stock; its price sets how much sellers can keep cool.
- Who works or waits here: Vendors, porters, shoppers and passers-by; fish and produce sellers buying ice.
- Ask: Is free, safe drinking water within a short walk of every row? Who refills and cleans it, and is that paid? Has the price of ice changed this season?
- Measure: Minutes walk from the furthest stall; Days the point was dry; Ice cost as a share of a day's sales
- Measures to consider: Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row; Shared produce cooling, fair-price ice and heat-triggered cash for vendors
- Depends on: Water supply, a named person paid to keep it clean and working, and a way to report when it fails.
#### Bus, auto-rickshaw and delivery waiting edge
- Heat sources: Exposed kerb with no shelter; Vehicle exhaust and engine heat; Hot paving and road
- Around 13:30: Few people wait, but those who do have no shade.
- At the edges of the day: Shoppers, children and vendors heading home crowd the kerb in low sun.
- Who works or waits here: Shoppers with children, older people, vendors arriving and leaving, delivery riders.
- Ask: Where do people wait, and for how long? Is there shade or a seat? Who comes on foot from far away?
- Measure: People waiting at peak hours; Shade over the waiting area through the day
- Measures to consider: Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection; Trees for long-term shade at the market's edges; Two-way market heat boards and trusted vendor messengers
- Depends on: The road authority and transport operators, as well as the market.
#### Nearby storage room, rest bench and crèche room
- Heat sources: A tin roof over a small room; Little air movement; Power cuts that stop fans
- Around 13:30: A cool room could serve as rest and child care, if it is open and someone minds the stalls.
- At the edges of the day: It is a store for goods and carts.
- Who works or waits here: Vendors storing goods overnight, parents with young children, older vendors needing to sit.
- Ask: Is there anywhere cool to sit for ten minutes? Where are children during school closures? Who holds the key?
- Measure: Room temperature in the afternoon; Use by vendors and children on hot days
- Measures to consider: A shaded place to sit and recover; A cool, supervised corner for children near the market
- Depends on: Who owns the room, whether it can be cooled cheaply, and paid staff if children are cared for.

### Health and equity
Heat harms the body the same way everywhere. Who it harms most in a market depends on how the market is run, who holds space in it, and who looks after whom.
- Physiology and microclimate: Heat load, dehydration, strain on the heart and kidneys, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and the sun, surfaces and air that drive them.
- Market governance, space and care: Toilets, stall security, queue rules, licences, eviction risk, debt, childcare and who sits on market committees: the arrangements that decide whether people can drink, rest and stop.
- Toilets as heat-health infrastructure: Where toilets are poor or missing, people drink less, and that can strain the urinary tract and kidneys as well as add to heat strain.
- Stall security and queue economics: Leaving a stall can cost goods or sales; stepping out of a porter queue can cost a paid load. A break has a price before anyone says no.
- Spoilage and the heat credit squeeze: Fewer customers and spoiled stock fall on the same day as a loan repayment or cart rent, so heat can turn a bad day into debt.
- Menstruation, pregnancy and breastfeeding in open public space: Privacy, clean water, a place to change, sit or feed a baby, and a way to rest without losing a pitch decide whether these are manageable in heat.
- Childcare and school closures: When heat closes schools, children may come to hot stalls, or a parent, often a mother, loses a day's trade.
- Licences, tenure and eviction during upgrades: Street improvements, shade projects and greening can push informal, migrant, women and transgender vendors off their pitches when their space is not protected first.
- Vendors left out of warnings and services: Deaf and disabled vendors, migrants, people who do not read the local language and people without smartphones are easily missed by alerts, signs and services.
- Who sits on market committees: Women vendors are often absent from the market boards and municipal meetings where shade, toilets and water are decided.
Protection without eviction or lost turns. Beautification that clears informal stalls, shade that blocks fire lanes or footfall, or a cooling centre that leaves a vendor to abandon goods or a porter to lose a paid load is not protection.

### Intervention library
Evidence types: Occupational guidance, written for workplaces; Study of the harm, not of this measure; Measured temperature, not health or earnings; Field report from markets; Proposal requiring validation.
#### A. Shade, microclimate and storm-proof canopies
Cut direct sun and radiant bounce where people trade, load and wait.
- Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection [rec-vendor-shade]. Addresses: Direct sun and radiant heat over stalls and aisles, shade that arrives late or tears in pre-monsoon winds, and eviction during street upgrades. How: Anchored, wind-rated shade over rows of stalls or single carts, put up before the hot season, with written protection so that vendors keep their pitches after the work. Where: Open street rows, weekly markets and vending zones with no tree cover or building overhang. Works if: Up before the heat begins, not in the middle of it; Anchored for pre-monsoon gusts, with headroom for air to move and clear fire access; Designed with licensed and unlicensed vendors, who keep their places. Take care: Reflective coatings on paving without shade overhead can add radiant heat to people standing on them; Late, unanchored nets can tear or collapse in strong winds; Designs that clear hawkers to make room protect no one who traded there. Upfront: From a cart umbrella to engineered canopies over a row; local costing needed. Running: Checks before each season, storm-anchor inspection and fabric replacement every few seasons. Who runs it: City and local governments, vendor associations and community groups. Equity and access: Cuts radiant heat for the people standing longest in the sun, if no one loses a pitch to make room. Evidence: Measured temperature, not health or earnings; Field report from markets. Shade lowers measured temperatures; no evaluation of market shade on vendors' health or earnings was found in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Mean radiant temperature under stalls around 13:00; canopies still standing after pre-monsoon storms; vendors on the same pitches a year later.
- Trees for long-term shade at the market's edges [rec-street-trees]. Addresses: Shade that lasts for decades over waiting areas, rest points and the market's edges. How: Trees planted where they have water and room to grow, alongside shade people can use this season while the trees grow. Where: Market edges, bus stops and rest points with space for roots and canopy. Works if: Water and growing space secured before planting; Someone paid to care for the trees; Planting planned so that it does not push vendors or residents out. Take care: A young tree gives little shade for years; Greening that raises rents or clears stalls displaces the people it was meant to cool. Upfront: Saplings, pits, guards and watering; local costing needed. Running: Watering and care for several years. Who runs it: City and local governments, with vendor associations and residents. Equity and access: Long-term shade for everyone at the edge, if greening does not displace them. Evidence: Measured temperature, not health or earnings. Measured cooling under tree clusters comes from one small trial, not a working market. Measure before and after: Shade cover over waiting and rest areas through the day; tree survival after three years.
#### B. Water, sanitation and menstrual hygiene
Free drinking water and clean, safe toilets treated as heat infrastructure.
- Free, clean, women-safe market toilets with water and menstrual hygiene [rec-market-toilets]. Addresses: Vendors, especially women, drinking less in hot shifts because toilets are far, locked, paid, dirty or unsafe. How: Free, maintained, well-lit, separate and wheelchair-accessible toilets with running water, soap, locks and menstrual-waste bins, treated as part of the city's heat plan, inside or beside markets. Where: Open street markets, weekly haats, bus-stand vending zones and wholesale mandis. Works if: No fee for vendors, at least during heat alerts; A named, paid caretaker cleans and stocks water every day; Open from early-morning to evening trading. Take care: A locked or dry block can be counted as delivered while vendors still drink less; Safe access for transgender and disabled vendors needs planning, not assumption. Upfront: Depends on whether an existing block is repaired or a new one built; local costing needed. Running: Caretaker wages, cleaning supplies, water and lighting. Who runs it: City and local governments, water and sanitation authorities, and market committees with women vendors' oversight. Equity and access: Removes the reason many women vendors drink less, which matters most in the hottest hours. Evidence: Study of the harm, not of this measure. A study links poor toilets at work to genitourinary problems among women workers; no evaluation of a market toilet upgrade on heat illness was found in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Days and hours the block is open, clean and watered during trading; how much vendors drink; reported genitourinary and heat symptoms.
- Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row [rec-water-point]. Addresses: Vendors leaving their stalls, or spending their earnings, to drink. How: A tap stand, refill point or cooler topped up through the day, close to where people trade, in shade so the water stays cool. Where: Every market row, loading bay and waiting edge. Works if: Someone paid to keep it supplied, clean and tested; Fixed quickly when it breaks, with a way to report it; Free or very cheap, and reachable by people using wheelchairs. Take care: Water left in the sun warms up and is drunk less; A point at one end of a long market helps only the stalls near it. Upfront: Low to moderate, depending on supply; local costing needed. Running: Water, cleaning and testing. Who runs it: Water utilities, city governments and market committees. Equity and access: Helps solo vendors and porters most, who cannot leave to find water. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation. No evaluation of market water points on vendors' heat illness was found in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Minutes walk from the furthest stall; days the point was dry; how much vendors drink on hot days.
#### C. Stall-minding, rest and porter-queue arrangements
Make it possible to drink, use a toilet and rest without losing goods or a paid turn.
- Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns [rec-stall-buddy]. Addresses: Vendors who cannot leave goods unguarded to drink, cool down or use a toilet, and porters who lose a paid load if they step out of the queue. How: Neighbouring stallholders agree a short-break rotation, of 10 to 15 minutes, to watch each other's stock in the hottest hours; porters' and loaders' associations hold a worker's place in the queue during agreed water and shade breaks. Where: Dense street rows, solo women-run vegetable and snack stalls, and wholesale loading bays. Works if: Organised through vendor or porter associations people trust; Water and a safe toilet close enough to reach and return within the break; Newcomers and migrant hawkers included, not only people with ties on the row. Take care: Informal arrangements can leave out people without friends on the row; Minding stalls is work: if it falls on the same people every day, it becomes an unpaid load; It adds to water, toilets and shade; it does not replace them. Upfront: no equipment to buy; time and coordination, local costing needed. Running: not assessed; local costing needed. Who runs it: Vendor associations, women's collectives, porters' unions and market committees. Equity and access: Removes the daily choice between guarding stock or income and drinking or using a toilet, especially for women trading alone. Evidence: Occupational guidance, written for workplaces. Workplace guidance describes workers watching one another in heat; stall-minding rosters and protected queue turns have not been evaluated in markets in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Breaks taken per shift by solo vendors; missed porter turns; self-reported heat symptoms.
- A shaded place to sit and recover [rec-shaded-rest]. Addresses: Nowhere cool to pause in the hottest hours. How: A shaded bench or rest point with water nearby, serving vendors, porters and shoppers, including older people and people with children. Where: Beside loading bays, at the market's edge or in a nearby public room. Works if: Close enough to the stalls and queue to use in a short break; Paired with stall-minding and protected queue turns, so resting costs nothing. Take care: A rest place helps only if people can afford to stop: porters paid by the load lose money when they rest. Upfront: Low: shade and seating; local costing needed. Running: Cleaning and upkeep. Who runs it: Market committees and city governments. Equity and access: Older, pregnant and disabled vendors and porters gain most from a place to sit. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation. No evaluation of market rest points was found in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Use of the rest point on hot afternoons; breaks taken by porters.
#### D. Produce cooling, ice and livelihood protection
Slow spoilage and cushion earnings when heat empties the aisles.
- Shared produce cooling, fair-price ice and heat-triggered cash for vendors [rec-spoilage-ice]. Addresses: Midday spoilage of vegetables, flowers and fish, rising ice costs, and falling footfall that pushes vendors into debt. How: Shaded evaporative produce chambers in dry heat, or a negotiated fair price for ice in fish and humid markets, together with cash that arrives when heat stops trading, paid by mobile money without needing a formal shop lease. Where: Produce, flower and fish markets where unsold stock at the end of the day is a direct loss. Works if: The cooling method suits the humidity: evaporative chambers work in dry heat, not in monsoon humidity; Cash arrives within days, not weeks, and reaches vendors without formal papers. Take care: Shared cold storage can price out the smallest sellers through daily fees; Who controls communal storage decides who benefits. Upfront: Depends on the measure; a negotiated ice price needs coordination rather than money. Running: Upkeep of chambers, ice supply, or the cost of a cash or insurance scheme. Who runs it: Market committees, fisheries and agriculture agencies, cooperatives, insurers and city governments. Equity and access: Protects the smallest traders, who borrow each morning to buy stock, from heat turning into debt. Evidence: Field report from markets. The survey shows the loss, not a remedy; no evaluation of combined cooling and cash packages on vendors' incomes was found in the sources checked. An ice-price agreement for fish traders in Sri Lanka (2023) is described elsewhere on the site but is not cited here, because its original notice is no longer online to check. Measure before and after: Share of stock spoiled before closing; ice cost as a share of daily sales; missed loan repayments in hot months.
#### E. Women's safety, childcare and inclusive access
Make cooling spaces, child care and warnings reach women, disabled, migrant and transgender vendors.
- A cool, supervised corner for children near the market [rec-shaded-creche]. Addresses: Children brought to hot stalls, or a day's trade lost, when heat closes schools. How: A cooled, safe, supervised corner for young children in a market cooling room, community hall or anganwadi nearby, open during trading hours and on school heat-closure days. Where: Neighbourhood markets and vending clusters where parents, mostly women, trade with young children. Works if: Paid, trusted local caregivers, not unpaid volunteers; Open during real market hours; Free, with no employer or address papers needed. Take care: Drinking water, oral rehydration salts, clean mats and backup power for fans keep the room from overheating in afternoon power cuts; Child care with no paid staff becomes one more unpaid job for women. Upfront: Cooling, mats and fans in an existing public room; local costing needed. Running: Caregivers' pay, water and electricity in alert weeks. Who runs it: City and local governments, women's collectives, NGOs and market associations. Equity and access: Keeps young children out of direct heat while parents keep earning, and older siblings in school. Evidence: Study of the harm, not of this measure. School heat closures are documented at scale; market-linked crèches have not been evaluated in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Children attending on alert days; parents' trading hours kept; children's heat-symptom visits.
#### F. Market governance, tenure protection and two-way alerts
A seat for vendors in design, protection for pitches, and alerts with real services behind them.
- Two-way market heat boards and trusted vendor messengers [rec-market-messengers]. Addresses: Alerts that are app-only or text-heavy, missing vendors who cannot read them, are deaf, speak another language or have no smartphone, and advice with no service behind it. How: Colour-coded heat boards at market entrances and on carts, with voice-note alerts in local languages sent to elected vendor leaders, who pass them along the row and report back missing water, broken fans or emergencies. Where: Any open market, labour chowk or multilingual mandi. Works if: Every alert names a water point, toilet or cool space that is open; A city or clinic contact acts on what vendors report. Take care: 'Stay indoors' advice does not fit people who have to trade to eat; Boards that rely on reading or hearing miss deaf and non-literate vendors unless they use colour and pictures. Upfront: Low: weatherproof boards and a messaging group. Running: Phone credit or small stipends for messengers on alert days, and the city's follow-through. Who runs it: Weather services, vendor unions, community groups and municipal heat cells. Equity and access: Reaches vendors without smartphones, reading or the local language, and gives them a way to be heard. Evidence: Field report from markets. Described as set up in Delhi; its effect on health or behaviour has not been evaluated in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Share of vendors on the row who know the day's alert level; time to fix a reported broken water point or toilet.
- Pitch protection and vendors on the committee before any upgrade [rec-pitch-protection]. Addresses: Shade, greening or street works that push informal, migrant, women and transgender vendors off their pitches, and decisions made without them. How: Before works begin, licensed and unlicensed vendors are listed, their places guaranteed in writing, and women vendors given seats on the committee that designs the upgrade. Where: Any market or vending street facing an upgrade, cooling project or beautification scheme. Works if: The list includes unlicensed and migrant vendors; Women vendors have a vote, not only a consultation. Take care: A consultation after the design is fixed changes little. Upfront: Coordination time. Running: Committee time. Who runs it: City governments, street-vending committees and vendor associations. Equity and access: Keeps the people a cooling project was meant for in the place it cools. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation. Common Shade's reading of the displacement risk; no evaluation of pitch protection in heat projects was found in the sources checked. Measure before and after: Vendors on the same pitches a year after the works; women vendors on the committee.

### Finder: what you observe, and where to look
Tick what you see. The finder lists measures that address those conditions, with the reason and what to find out next. It does not score a market or declare it safe: only measurement, vendors' and porters' own reports and qualified assessment can do that.
- No overhead shade on stalls: Direct sun and hot paving add the most heat to people standing still for hours. Look at: Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection; Trees for long-term shade at the market's edges; Pitch protection and vendors on the committee before any upgrade. Find out next: Note which stalls and queues sit in full sun at 13:00, and what is allowed overhead.
- Toilets locked, paid, far or unsafe: People drink less to avoid them. Look at: Free, clean, women-safe market toilets with water and menstrual hygiene; Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row; Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns. Find out next: Check opening hours, fees, water, locks and lighting against trading hours; ask women vendors privately.
- Vendors cannot leave stalls unguarded: A break costs goods or sales. Look at: Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns; Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row; A shaded place to sit and recover. Find out next: Ask who minds stalls now, and who has no one.
- Produce or fish spoiling by midday: Spoiled stock and fewer customers turn heat into debt. Look at: Shared produce cooling, fair-price ice and heat-triggered cash for vendors; Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection. Find out next: Record what spoils first, the ice price, and daily loan or rent payments.
- Porters lose turns if they rest: Rest has a price for people paid by the load. Look at: Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns; A shaded place to sit and recover; Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row. Find out next: Ask porters' associations how the queue works and whether a place can be held.
- Vendors fear eviction during upgrades: Cooling projects can displace the people they were meant for. Look at: Pitch protection and vendors on the committee before any upgrade; Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection; Trees for long-term shade at the market's edges. Find out next: List every vendor, licensed or not, before any design is agreed.
- Children at stalls when schools close: Children sit in the heat, or a parent loses a day's trade. Look at: A cool, supervised corner for children near the market; A shaded place to sit and recover. Find out next: Ask parents where children are on closure days and what a cool, supervised space would need.

### Worked examples (illustrative)
#### A women-majority vegetable market with no safe toilets and a sharp afternoon drop-off
- Observed problem: Most sellers are women trading alone. The nearest toilet is paid and closes at 18:00; several sellers say they drink little until they get home. Many leave by early afternoon.
- Missing information: Whether sellers leave early because of heat, the toilet, low footfall or care at home; how much they drink; whether the block has water.
- Candidate measures: Free, clean, women-safe market toilets with water and menstrual hygiene; Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row; Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns; Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection
- Arrangements: The city waives the fee for vendors and pays a caretaker; women vendors set hours with the market committee; neighbours agree a stall-minding rota for the hottest hours.
- Verification plan: Hours the block is open and watered; how much sellers drink on hot days; how late they stay; reported symptoms over a hot month.
#### A wholesale loading yard where porters skip water and shade to keep their turn
- Observed problem: Porters paid by the load queue in the open from 05:00. Anyone who steps away loses their place.
- Missing information: How the queue is run and by whom; loads per hour through the day; where water and shade could go.
- Candidate measures: Stall-minding buddy rosters and protected porter queue turns; A shaded place to sit and recover; Free drinking-water point within a short walk of every row
- Arrangements: The porters' association agrees that a place is held during a water break; the market committee puts shade and water beside the queue.
- Verification plan: Breaks taken without losing a turn; loads per day before and after; reported heat symptoms.
#### A coastal fish and produce market where midday spoilage and ice prices wipe out margins
- Observed problem: Fish sellers buy ice each morning; in the hottest weeks prices rise and footfall falls. Some miss loan repayments.
- Missing information: Ice cost as a share of sales; how much stock is thrown away; who controls cold storage; whether a cash scheme could reach sellers without papers.
- Candidate measures: Shared produce cooling, fair-price ice and heat-triggered cash for vendors; Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection
- Arrangements: The fisheries agency and the market committee bring traders and ice suppliers together on price; a heat-triggered cash scheme is explored with sellers.
- Verification plan: Ice cost and spoilage before and after; missed repayments in hot months.
#### A 'cool street' upgrade where unlicensed vendors risk displacement
- Observed problem: The city plans trees, shade and new paving on a busy vending street. Licensed vendors were consulted; unlicensed vendors were not counted.
- Missing information: Who trades there and when, including unlicensed and migrant vendors; whether the paving is reflective; where vendors go during works.
- Candidate measures: Pitch protection and vendors on the committee before any upgrade; Vendor-co-designed, storm-proof shared shade with pitch protection; Trees for long-term shade at the market's edges
- Arrangements: Every vendor is listed and their place guaranteed before works; women vendors sit on the design committee; reflective paving is paired with shade.
- Verification plan: Vendors on the same pitches a year later; radiant temperature at stalls before and after.

### What is not known
- Few independent evaluations of market shade on vendors' health or earnings: the measurements found are of temperature.
- Little measured evidence that sanitation upgrades in Asian markets reduce heat-linked dehydration or urinary problems.
- Stall-minding rosters, protected queue turns and market crèches are described or proposed, not evaluated.
- Heat alerts for vendors are documented as set up; their effect on what vendors do, or on illness, is not yet measured.
- Little is known about heat among deaf, disabled, migrant and transgender vendors in particular.

Worksheet to print: https://beattheheat.asia/market-heat/worksheet/


## Ahmedabad: who is doing what about heat?

Who is working on heat in the city, what exactly they are doing, what anyone can use, and what is still only planned. Built from public sources, each line checked against its source. Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/ahmedabad/who-is-doing-what/

Organisations and activities identified in public sources, read on 28 November 2026. It is not a complete list of everyone working on heat in Ahmedabad, and no organisation was contacted.

Ahmedabad wrote South Asia's first city heat action plan in 2013, after the 2010 heat wave, and an evaluation cited by the WHO Foundation credits it with lives saved. Since then the work has spread from warnings to homes, streets and income: cool roofs, a misted bus stop and a heat insurance for women in informal work, much of it carried by one women's housing organisation working with the city.

### Who is doing what

Each card is one piece of work. The lead is named only where a source names one; collaborators carry the role a source gives them. A joint project appears once, under all its partners.

Distinctions kept on every card: based in the city is not working in it; developing a tool that could serve the city is not using it there; announced money is not money spent; planned is not delivered.

- [ahm-hap] Heat Action Plan with early warnings (Underway). The city's plan, first launched in 2013: an early warning system, awareness campaigns, and since 2017 cool roofs. Scroll reported that parks stay open for shade, signboards explain heatstroke and all departments meet weekly on the plan. Lead: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. Where: Ahmedabad (City-wide). People: Residents. Evaluation: An evaluation by researchers credits the plan with 1,190 lives saved a year in its first five years; the evaluation itself was not read for this profile. Evidence: Independent reporting. Sources: https://www.who.foundation/post/in-india-a-plan-to-beat-the-heat-is-saving-lives https://scroll.in/article/1080066/hit-by-heatwave-mumbai-is-ignoring-a-quick-fix-to-cool-off-keeping-parks-open-in-the-afternoon

- [ahm-roof-pilot] Cool roof pilot on 3,000 low-income homes (2017) (Completed). Roofs of over 3,000 low-income homes painted with white lime paint under the Heat Action Plan, by city staff, student volunteers and civil society groups. In 2018 real estate developers were asked to apply cool roofs to private buildings voluntarily. Lead: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. With: Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), India programme (partner); Indian Institute of Public Health Gandhinagar (partner); Mahila Housing Trust (partner). Where: Low-income neighbourhoods (not named) (Neighbourhoods). People: Low-income households. Evaluation: Not evaluated in the sources read. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.nrdc.org/bio/anjali-jaiswal/new-cool-roof-programs-india-ahmedabad-part-2

- [ahm-cool-roofs] Cool Roofs Initiative in low-income homes (Underway). Heat-reflective paint on the roofs of low-income homes, run by Mahila Housing Trust within the city's Heat Action Plan. In 2019 the city was preparing a city-wide programme; by 2025 the city had included cool roofs in its plan. Lead: Mahila Housing Trust. With: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (included cool roofs in the Heat Action Plan). Where: Low-income neighbourhoods (not named) (Neighbourhoods). People: Low-income households, Women. Evaluation: Not evaluated in the sources read. Evidence: Own account and independent reporting. Sources: https://www.who.foundation/post/in-india-a-plan-to-beat-the-heat-is-saving-lives https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/beyond-the-thermometer-ahmedabad-uses-cool-roofs-misting-bus-stops-heat-insurance-for-climate-resilience https://www.nrdc.org/bio/anjali-jaiswal/new-cool-roof-programs-india-ahmedabad-part-2

- [ahm-bus-stop] Misted cool bus stop at Lal Darwaza (Completed). A high-pressure misting system at one bus stop, installed by Mahila Housing Trust with the city. Lead: Mahila Housing Trust. With: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (partner). Where: Lal Darwaza bus stop (Named sites). People: Bus passengers. Evaluation: Mahila Housing Trust reports at least 4 to 7°C of relief; no independent measurement was found. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/beyond-the-thermometer-ahmedabad-uses-cool-roofs-misting-bus-stops-heat-insurance-for-climate-resilience

- [ahm-insurance] Heat insurance for women in informal work (Underway). A parametric insurance that pays women a fixed sum when temperatures cross set thresholds, so a lost day's earnings is partly covered without a claim. Launched in April 2024; a payout was triggered in May 2024. Lead: Mahila Housing Trust. Where: Ahmedabad (City-wide). People: Women in informal work. Evaluation: Not evaluated in the sources read. Evidence: Independent reporting. Sources: https://www.who.foundation/post/in-india-a-plan-to-beat-the-heat-is-saving-lives https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/beyond-the-thermometer-ahmedabad-uses-cool-roofs-misting-bus-stops-heat-insurance-for-climate-resilience

### Money that has been announced

Each figure is attributed to whoever stated it and kept at the stage the source describes. A component is shown inside its parent, never added to it, and climate budgets are not counted as heat budgets. The figures are not summed.

- ₹700,000: Total cost of the 2017 cool roof pilot. Spent: Given by NRDC as the programme's total cost for 2017. Heat-specific: yes.

### What happened, and when

- 2010 (event): A heat wave; experts later estimated heat contributed to more than 1,000 deaths.

- 2013 (plan): The Heat Action Plan is launched, the first by a city in South Asia.

- 2017 (delivery): Cool roof pilot on over 3,000 low-income homes.

- April 2019 (plan): A city-wide cool roof programme in draft.

- April 2024 (delivery): Heat insurance for women in informal work launched.

- May 2024 (delivery): A temperature threshold is crossed and insurance payouts follow.

### Organisations

One card per organisation, with its verified names. Membership of the Collective does not on its own establish a role in any piece of work.

- Mahila Housing Trust (also MHT, Mahila Housing SEWA Trust): A women's housing organisation that runs the Cool Roofs Initiative in the city's heat plan, a misted bus stop with the city, and a heat insurance for women in informal work. Outside Ahmedabad: It works on heat plans in other cities (Churu and Varanasi, among others); that work is not counted here. Not known: How many roofs the initiative has coated since 2019, when NRDC gave a figure of over 100. How many women hold the heat insurance, and the total paid out.

- Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), India programme (also NRDC): A partner of the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation on the 2017 cool roof pilot and the city-wide programme that followed. Outside Ahmedabad: Its cool roof work in Telangana and elsewhere is counted on those cities' profiles. Not known: Its current role in the city's plan.

- Indian Institute of Public Health Gandhinagar (also IIPH-G, IIPH Gandhinagar): A partner of the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation on the 2017 cool roof pilot. Not known: Its current role in the plan and in evaluating it was not read for this profile.

### Who has public authority to act

- Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC): Leads the Heat Action Plan, first launched in 2013, and the city's cool roof programme.

### What is not known

- How many roofs have been coated city-wide since the 2017 pilot, and how many were maintained.

- The current edition of the Heat Action Plan was not read for this profile; its partners and budget are not described here.

- Whether the cool roofs, the misted bus stop or the insurance have been independently evaluated.

- Gujarati-language sources were not searched systematically for this first version.

### Where sources disagree

- Heat insurance terms: Down To Earth (June 2025) describes two thresholds of 43.7°C and 44.1°C, paying Rs 750 and a further Rs 1,250; the WHO Foundation (September 2024) describes one trigger of 44.2 ºC and Rs 2,000 a season. They may describe different seasons of the scheme.

## Bengaluru: who is doing what about heat?

Who is working on heat in the city, what exactly they are doing, what anyone can use, and what is still only planned. Built from public sources, each line checked against its source. Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/bengaluru/who-is-doing-what/

Organisations and activities identified in public sources, read between 24 and 28 November 2026. It is not a complete list of everyone working on heat in Bengaluru, and no organisation was contacted. Common Shade is not a member, partner or representative of the Bengaluru Heat Collective.

Common Shade is not a member, partner or representative of the Bengaluru Heat Collective, and this page does not speak for it or its members.

In July 2026 the city recorded its hottest July day on record. The response so far is a mix: a new coalition of research, worker and civic groups, ward climate plans with first budgets, a national heat pilot run through one city corporation, and seasonal cooling centres and kits for outdoor workers. Most of it is planned or in its first season; little has been evaluated.

### Bengaluru Heat Collective

Launched 15 July 2026; announcements published 17 July 2026 by WRI India and 17 July 2026 by KHPT.

The 11 founding members named at launch: ARTPARK, Bengaluru Sustainability Forum, C40 Cities, CSTEP, Hasiru Dala, HeatWatch, Jan Sahas, KHPT, NIMHANS, Socratus and WRI India.

Priority areas named for the initial phase (priorities, not delivered work): Understanding heat and its spatial dimensions to inform policy and investment; Enabling infrastructure interventions; Strengthening relief and resilience measures for vulnerable communities; Advancing ward-level microplanning.

A WRI India partner update after the launch reports that the members agreed a Charter document for the group to function as a collective body, and that a Strategy Note on heat resilience in Bengaluru was developed as a living document. Neither document was found published.

A later partner update reports that the Collective convened in August 2026 to begin developing a theory of change and a strategic workplan.

No secretariat, lead organisation, workstream leads, legal status or public contact address for the Collective was found in the sources reviewed. Its charter and strategy note were not found published.

### Who is doing what

Each card is one piece of work. The lead is named only where a source names one; collaborators carry the role a source gives them. A joint project appears once, under all its partners.

Distinctions kept on every card: based in the city is not working in it; developing a tool that could serve the city is not using it there; announced money is not money spent; planned is not delivered.

- [blr-ward-plans] Ward climate action plans in five pilot wards (Underway). Plans that list climate projects ward by ward, built with public consultations in Shantinagar, Jakkur, Begur, Vijinapura and Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar. Heat is not one of their sectors, but heat maps informed them and Begur's plan includes heat proofing of buildings. Lead: Greater Bengaluru Authority. With: WRI India (anchored the drafting (Shantinagar) and steered the enabling work (Begur)); Jan Sahas (working group: community engagement); Socratus (working group: community engagement); Hasiru Dala (working group); Sensing Local (working group); CSTEP (working group: anchors the energy sector); WELL Labs (working group: water); Bengaluru Central City Corporation (received the Shantinagar plan). Where: Five pilot wards, one in each zone (Wards). People: Residents, Informal workers, Waste workers. Evaluation: Not evaluated. Evidence: Own account and independent reporting. Sources: https://india.mongabay.com/2026/03/ward-level-plans-bring-climate-action-closer-to-communities/ https://citizenmatters.in/bengaluru-is-building-ward-level-climate-action-plans-here-is-how/ https://grove.rainmatter.org/t/4976/9 https://grove.rainmatter.org/t/4976/18

- [blr-begur-budget] First budget for a ward climate plan: Begur (Announced). Bengaluru South City Corporation announced money for phased implementation of the Begur ward plan, covering heat proofing of buildings, blue-green schools and groundwater recharge. Lead: Bengaluru South City Corporation. With: WRI India (steered the plan's enabling work). Where: Begur ward (One ward). People: Residents, Schools. Evaluation: Not evaluated; no spending reported. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://wri-india.org/media/eleven-organisations-launch-bengaluru-heat-collective-city-records-its-highest-july https://grove.rainmatter.org/t/4976/12

- [blr-niua-pilot] National heat resilience pilot through North City Corporation (Planned). Bengaluru takes part in the Building Heat Resilient Cities Programme under AMRUT 2.0, with a proposal submitted by Bengaluru North City Corporation. Planned measures include roof coating demonstrations on corporation buildings and protective gear for outdoor informal workers. Lead: Bengaluru North City Corporation. With: National Institute of Urban Affairs (Climate Centre for Cities) (runs the national pilot). Where: Bengaluru North City Corporation (One city corporation). People: Outdoor informal workers. Evaluation: Not evaluated; no installation or distribution under the pilot found reported. Evidence: Own account and independent reporting. Sources: https://wri-india.org/media/eleven-organisations-launch-bengaluru-heat-collective-city-records-its-highest-july https://thechenabtimes.com/2026/07/15/bengaluru-launches-heat-collective-to-combat-rising-urban-temperatures/

- [blr-cooling-centres] Cooling centres for outdoor workers (Completed). Three seasonal centres with drinking water, ORS, coolers, cots and first aid: at a construction site in Whitefield, in Greater Bengaluru Authority facilities in Vidyaranyapura and above an Anganwadi in Allalasandra. Staff also helped workers apply for welfare cards and benefits. Lead: Jan Sahas (Run by the Migrants Resilience Collaborative, which Jan Sahas initiated.). With: Greater Bengaluru Authority (hosts the Vidyaranyapura centre in its facilities). Where: Whitefield, Vidyaranyapura and Allalasandra (Named sites). People: Construction workers, Migrant workers, Pourakarmikas. Evaluation: Not evaluated; accounts come from workers, staff and the organisers. Evidence: Own account and independent reporting. Sources: https://themigrationstory.com/?p=19496 https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/centering-workers-in-heat-resilience-from-lived-experience-to-systemic-action

- [blr-cooling-kits] Cooling kits for outdoor public workers (Completed). Kits with a sun hat, cooling sleeves and an insulated bottle, plus shared neck fans, given to ASHAs, pourakarmikas, dry waste collection centre workers and traffic police, mostly in North City Corporation. The team proposed turning 63 Indira canteens into cooling centres during heat alerts. Lead: not named in the sources. With: Hasiru Dala (piloted the kits); C40 Cities (piloted the kits); Sensing Local (piloted the kits); Bengaluru North City Corporation (where most kits went; named for scale-up). Where: Mostly Bengaluru North City Corporation (One city corporation). People: ASHA workers, Pourakarmikas, Waste workers, Traffic police. Evaluation: An impact report was being prepared; not published when checked. Evidence: Independent reporting. Sources: https://citizenmatters.in/cooling-kits-help-bengaluru-workers-combat-heat-stress/

- [blr-waste-report] How heat hits waste workers' health and income (Completed). A survey of 154 waste workers on access to water and toilets, symptoms, lost income and medical costs in the heat. Lead: not named in the sources. With: HeatWatch (co-author); Hasiru Dala (co-author). Where: Bengaluru (City-wide). People: Waste workers, Women workers, Scheduled Caste workers. Evaluation: A survey of the harm, not an evaluation of any measure. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.heatwatch.in/report/rising-heat-and-waste-workers-impact-of-heat-stress-on-the-livelihood-and-health-of-waste-workers-in-bengaluru/

- [blr-apartment-charter] A heat safety charter for apartment workers (Completed). Measures apartment communities can adopt in extreme heat for the people who work there, from domestic and housekeeping staff to security guards, gardeners, delivery workers and drivers, in English, Kannada and Hindi. Lead: not named in the sources. With: Bangalore Apartment Federation (developed it); HeatWatch (developed it); Bengaluru Sustainability Forum (supported it). Where: Apartment complexes in Bengaluru (City-wide). People: Domestic workers, Security guards, Housekeeping staff, Delivery workers. Evaluation: No adoption figures or evaluation found. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.heatwatch.in/blogs/heat-safety-charter-for-workers-in-apartments

- [blr-domestic-workers] Domestic workers and heat (Underway). Participatory research, workshops and a replication playbook with domestic workers, unions and resident associations, alongside HeatWatch's ongoing work with the Domestic Workers Union. Lead: HeatWatch. With: Bengaluru Sustainability Forum (lists it among supported projects). Where: Bengaluru (City-wide). People: Domestic workers. Evaluation: Not evaluated. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.bengalurusustainabilityforum.org/addressing-heat-stress-among-domestic-workers-in-bangalore/ https://www.heatwatch.in/project/domestic-workers/

- [blr-open-parks] #OpenOurParks: parks as cool places in the day (Proposed). Volunteers audited parks closed between 11 AM and 4 PM and asked for longer hours and for parks to count as cooling and resting spaces. Lead: HeatWatch. Where: Parks in south Bengaluru (Neighbourhoods). People: Residents, Outdoor workers. Evaluation: No decision found reported. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.heatwatch.in/blogs/openourparks-keeping-bengalurus-parks-open-when-it-matters-most/

- [blr-climate-charche] Climate Charche: workers' conversations on climate (Completed). Focus groups with domestic, gig and migrant workers, pourakarmikas and ASHA workers, through art and conversation; water was the main theme, heat a secondary one. Lead: Socratus. With: Bengaluru Sustainability Forum (runs the Climate Charche initiative). Where: Bengaluru (City-wide). People: Domestic workers, Gig workers, Migrant workers, Pourakarmikas, ASHA workers. Evaluation: Not evaluated. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.globalresiliencepartnership.org/art-for-resilience-in-bengaluru/

- [blr-c40-hia] Two high impact heat actions for Bengaluru wards (Planned). Technical assistance commissioned to choose two high impact actions for urban heat in identified wards and write detailed project reports, with the Greater Bengaluru Authority. Lead: C40 Cities. With: Greater Bengaluru Authority (city counterpart). Where: Identified wards (not named) (Wards). Evaluation: Delivery not found reported. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.c40.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/RfP-_-Heat-Resilience-in-Bengaluru-Hubballi-Dharwad.pdf (archived copy: https://web.archive.org/web/20251001194846/https://www.c40.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/RfP-_-Heat-Resilience-in-Bengaluru-Hubballi-Dharwad.pdf)

- [blr-artpark-forecast] Sub-district heat-risk forecasts (Stage not stated). Heat-risk predictions for areas smaller than a district, up to seven days ahead, built with the state's disaster monitoring centre, disaster management authority and health department. Lead: ARTPARK. With: Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (government partner); Karnataka State Disaster Management Authority (government partner); Department of Health, Government of Karnataka (government partner). Where: Karnataka (coverage not stated) (State). Evaluation: No accuracy or use figures published on the page. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.artpark.in/about/programs/social-impact

- [blr-deft] An ecosystem-based adaptation tool for Bengaluru (Underway). A GIS-based tool to judge where blue-green measures could reduce heatwave and flood risk, with hyper-local risk maps and a household survey. Lead: CSTEP. With: IUCN (funder, through the Global EbA Fund). Where: Bengaluru, extending to Bangalore Urban District; a workshop used Hebbal as a case (District). People: Households (survey). Evaluation: Not evaluated. Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://cstep.in/projects/developing-an-ecosystem-based-adaptation-feasibility-tool-deft/

### Tools and resources

Things someone can open, read or ask for. A report can inform a decision without being a live tool, so each item says what kind of thing it is and whether the public can use it today.

- ARTPARK heat-risk forecasting (Forecast or warning service; Public access not verified). Owner: ARTPARK. Supports: Where heat risk may be highest in the coming week. Coverage: Karnataka, at sub-district level (extent not stated). Resolution: Sub-district; up to seven days ahead. Limits: A forecast horizon is not proof of accuracy; no validation is published on the page. No public view of the forecasts was found. Use in Bengaluru: Not independently documented. https://www.artpark.in/about/programs/social-impact

- DEFT: Ecosystem-based Adaptation Feasibility Tool (Planning or assessment method; In development). Owner: CSTEP. Supports: Where blue-green measures are feasible and could reduce heatwave and flood risk. Coverage: Bengaluru, extending to Bangalore Urban District. Resolution: Described as hyper-local; not quantified. Limits: Intended outputs are not yet published as a tool. Hyper-local is the project's word; the resolution is not stated. Use in Bengaluru: Built for Bengaluru; use by any authority not documented. https://cstep.in/projects/developing-an-ecosystem-based-adaptation-feasibility-tool-deft/

- Heat Safety Charter for Apartment Workers (Checklist or charter; Publicly usable). Owner: HeatWatch. Supports: What an apartment community can do for the people who work there in extreme heat. Coverage: Written for Bengaluru apartments. Resolution: Not applicable. Limits: No adoption figures found. No licence for reuse stated. Use in Bengaluru: Adoption by apartments not documented. https://www.heatwatch.in/blogs/heat-safety-charter-for-workers-in-apartments

- Rising Heat and Waste Workers (report) (Research report; Publicly usable). Owner: HeatWatch. Supports: What waste workers need to keep working safely in the heat. Coverage: Bengaluru. Resolution: City-wide survey of 154 workers. Limits: A survey of harm, not an evaluation of any measure. Self-reported symptoms and costs. Use in Bengaluru: Not documented. https://www.heatwatch.in/report/rising-heat-and-waste-workers-impact-of-heat-stress-on-the-livelihood-and-health-of-waste-workers-in-bengaluru/

- BHRIGU National Heat Insights Explorer (Interactive dashboard; Announced, not yet public). Owner: CSTEP. Supports: Where heat and other hazards combine across India. Coverage: India (planned); Bengaluru not named. Resolution: Not stated. Limits: Described as an envisioned outcome; no live address found. Not specific to Bengaluru. Use in Bengaluru: Not documented. https://cstep.in/projects/building-heat-resilience-in-indias-growing-urbanscapes-bhrigu/

- HeatWatch garment worker dashboard (Interactive dashboard; Public access not verified). Owner: HeatWatch. Supports: Where garment workers' heat exposure meets brand supply chains. Coverage: India's textile and garment sector; Bengaluru factories not evidenced. Resolution: Factory level (described). Limits: Not a Bengaluru deployment. ### Money that has been announced

Each figure is attributed to whoever stated it and kept at the stage the source describes. A component is shown inside its parent, never added to it, and climate budgets are not counted as heat budgets. The figures are not summed.

- ₹5 crore: Heat resilience, under the NIUA pilot (Building Heat Resilient Cities, AMRUT 2.0). Announced: Described as allocated, in a statement at the launch; no sanction order found. Heat-specific: yes.

- ₹1 crore: Protecting vulnerable populations, such as safety gear for outdoor informal workers. Announced: Described as dedicated, within the ₹5 crore. Part of ₹5 crore, not in addition to it. Heat-specific: yes.

- ₹2 crore: Phased implementation of the Begur Ward Climate Action Plan: heat proofing of buildings, blue-green schools, groundwater recharge and more. Announced: Announced as allocated; called a starting point, not a final budget. Heat-specific: partly.

- about ₹52 crore: Climate action in four of the five corporations' 2026-27 budgets. Allocated: Reported by WRI India as allocated; the budget documents were not checked. Heat-specific: not stated.

- ₹28 crore: Climate action, including proposed ward-level plans, in the former BBMP's 2025-26 budget. Allocated: Described as allocated by one report and as earmarked by another. Heat-specific: not stated.

### What happened, and when

- 2025 (event): HeatWatch and Hasiru Dala publish their waste-worker heat survey. The report page shows no date; the PDF on Hasiru Dala's site sits in a folder dated August 2025.

- September 2025 (authority): The Greater Bengaluru Authority's five city corporations come into being, after the BBMP.

- September 2025 (plan): A domestic-worker heat project starts, supported through Bengaluru Sustainability Forum.

- 19 October 2025 (plan): Deadline for C40's request for technical assistance on two high impact heat actions; work planned for November 2025 to March 2026.

- March 2026 (plan): Ward climate plan consultations completed in five pilot wards; zone-wise budgets not yet released.

- April 2026 (delivery): Cooling kits go to 202 outdoor public workers, mostly in North City Corporation.

- 10 April 2026 (delivery): Three cooling centres for outdoor workers open; they close in the first week of July.

- 27 June 2026 (money): Four of five corporations reported to have put about ₹52 crore towards climate action in 2026-27 budgets (not heat-specific).

- July 2026 (plan): After the launch, members reported to have agreed a charter and a strategy note (neither found published).

- 14 July 2026 (event): The city records 33.6°C, its hottest July day on record.

- 15 July 2026 (event): The Bengaluru Heat Collective is launched by 11 organisations. North City Corporation describes ₹5 crore under the NIUA pilot and plans roof coating demonstrations; South City Corporation announces ₹2 crore for the Begur ward plan.

- August 2026 (plan): The Collective reported to have begun a theory of change and strategic workplan.

- October 2026 (plan): Shantinagar's ward climate plan is completed and submitted to the Climate Action Cell and Bengaluru Central City Corporation.

- Bangalore Apartment Federation (also BAF): Not a member of the Collective. Developed the Heat Safety Charter for apartment workers with HeatWatch Foundation. Not known: How the federation is promoting the charter among member apartments.

### Who has public authority to act

- Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA): City-wide authority over five city corporations (Bengaluru Central, North, South, East and West) since September 2025; its Climate Action Cell leads the ward climate plans.

- Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP): The city's former municipal corporation, before the Greater Bengaluru Authority and its five corporations (September 2025). Its name is kept for older records, such as the 2025-26 climate earmark.

- Bengaluru North City Corporation (BNCC, North City Corporation): Submitted the city's proposal under the national heat resilience pilot; plans roof coating demonstrations; most cooling kits went to its workers.

- Bengaluru South City Corporation (BSCC, South City Corporation): Announced ₹2 crore for phased implementation of the Begur ward climate plan.

- Bengaluru Central City Corporation (BCCC): Received the completed Shantinagar ward climate plan.

- National Institute of Urban Affairs (Climate Centre for Cities) (NIUA): Runs the Building Heat Resilient Cities pilot under AMRUT 2.0 of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, in which Bengaluru takes part.

- Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC): Named by ARTPARK as a partner in its heat-risk forecasts.

- Karnataka State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA): Named by ARTPARK as a partner in its heat-risk forecasts.

- Department of Health, Government of Karnataka: Named by ARTPARK as a partner in its heat-risk forecasts.

- India Meteorological Department (IMD): Runs the city observatory whose records the July 2026 temperature figures come from.

### What is not known

- No published evaluation of any heat measure in Bengaluru was found: cooling centres, kits and plans are described by organisers or reporters.

- Whether the ₹5 crore and ₹2 crore have been sanctioned, released or spent. Only statements at the launch were found.

- Whether the planned roof coating demonstrations have been installed.

- The Collective's charter, strategy note, workstreams and any lead or coordinator.

- How many workers used Bengaluru's cooling centres; published figures are national.

- Whether the ARTPARK forecasts are used by any authority, and their accuracy.

- Where women, older and disabled people, and migrant workers shape decisions, as distinct from being consulted or receiving support.

- The Karnataka Heat Action Plan 2026 could not be read for this profile (its server returned an error), so its arrangements for Greater Bengaluru are not described here.

- Kannada-language sources were not searched systematically for this first version.

### Where sources disagree

- Pilot wards: Mongabay India names five (one per zone); Citizen Matters, three months earlier, reported plans for ten wards across five corporations.

- The ₹28 crore for climate action: described as allocated by the former body in one report and as earmarked for proposed plans in another.

- Member names vary across sources: Socratus appears as Socratus, Socratus Corporation, Socratus Collective Wisdom Corporation and Socratus Foundation; Jan Sahas also as Jan Sahas Foundation and Jansahas.

## Delhi: who is doing what about heat?

Who is working on heat in the city, what exactly they are doing, what anyone can use, and what is still only planned. Built from public sources, each line checked against its source. Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/delhi/who-is-doing-what/

Organisations and activities identified in public sources, read on 28 November 2026. It is not a complete list of everyone working on heat in Delhi, and no organisation was contacted.

Delhi's 2025 Heat Action Plan promised graded alerts, thousands of water coolers, hospital heatstroke units and cool roof pilots. Reporters and researchers found much of it hard to see on the ground, and found that heat cannot draw on the disaster fund. Worker organisations and researchers have filled in what the plan does not measure: lost hours, lost income and markets with no water.

## Hyderabad: who is doing what about heat?

Who is working on heat in the city, what exactly they are doing, what anyone can use, and what is still only planned. Built from public sources, each line checked against its source. Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/hyderabad/who-is-doing-what/

Organisations and activities identified in public sources, read on 28 November 2026. It is not a complete list of everyone working on heat in Hyderabad, and no organisation was contacted.

Hyderabad tested cool roofs on 25 homes in 2017, and Telangana turned that into India's first state cool roof policy in 2023, with targets and a building permit rule. Each summer the state heatwave plan and the city corporation add water kiosks, health camps and warnings on junction screens, though the plan is advisory.

### Who is doing what

Each card is one piece of work. The lead is named only where a source names one; collaborators carry the role a source gives them. A joint project appears once, under all its partners.

Distinctions kept on every card: based in the city is not working in it; developing a tool that could serve the city is not using it there; announced money is not money spent; planned is not delivered.

- [hyd-pilot] Cool roof pilot on 25 homes (2017) (Evaluated). Cool roofs on 25 homes in one low-income neighbourhood, measured against homes without them. Lead: Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation. With: Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI) (partner); IIIT Hyderabad (partner); Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), India programme (partner). Where: One low-income neighbourhood (not named) (Neighbourhoods). People: Low-income households. Evaluation: Indoor air on average 2°C cooler; 76% of residents in the trial group satisfied (NRDC's account). Evidence: The organisation's own account. Sources: https://www.nrdc.org/bio/anjali-jaiswal/keeping-it-cool-models-city-cool-roof-programs

- [hyd-policy] Telangana Cool Roofs Policy 2023-2028 (Underway). State targets for cool roofs, a rule in building permits, mandatory coatings in government low-cost housing, and delivery to low-income homes through city heat plans.
