## Heat from field to factory
https://beattheheat.asia/cotton-and-heat/
Cotton, informal work and the conditions that make protection possible.
Where heat meets the people who grow, pick, move and process cotton in Asia, how it affects workers, crops and livelihoods by different routes, why some workers have fewer ways to protect themselves, and which arrangements make protection usable: an interactive cotton journey, an intervention library with who acts and who pays, an explorer, and the evidence with its limits.

What would have to change for the person doing this work to stay safe without losing the income, security or support they depend on?
Before cotton becomes fabric, people prepare fields, tend plants, pick cotton, carry loads, move bales and operate machinery. Heat meets them in different places and under different working arrangements.
A worker's exposure depends on the weather and the task. Their ability to protect themselves also depends on pay, water, rest, transport, care responsibilities and who controls the working day.
The cotton journey below is an illustrative value-chain map, not a traceability record for any garment, brand or company. Real chains branch, skip stages and cross borders.

### The cotton journey (illustrative)
- Ginning separates cotton lint from seed; the seed is a coproduct with its own markets.
- Spinning turns fibre into yarn. Yarn becomes fabric through weaving or knitting.
- Dyeing and finishing can happen at several points: to fibre, yarn, fabric or finished garments.
- Production can cross borders: fibre, yarn and fabric are traded, so no single country need host every stage.
- Actual chains branch and vary. This map shows typical stages, not a route any particular product took.
#### A. Field preparation, planting and crop care
- Work: Preparing land, sowing, thinning, weeding, irrigating, applying fertiliser and pesticides, and carrying water, inputs and equipment.
- Who: Smallholder families including unpaid family members, tenant farmers and sharecroppers, and daily-wage workers hired for weeding and spraying. In a 2025 assessment of women cotton farmers in Sindh, nearly all sowed by hand and most weeded, while few operated irrigation or sprayed.
- Exposure: Hours in open fields with little shade, bending and lifting, and protective clothing for spraying that holds in heat. In Indian Punjab, sowing falls in April and May; in Sindh, planting can begin in March, so early field work can meet hot weather.
- What makes protection difficult: No shade or water point at the field; long walks home; household water collection on top of farm work; no labour-law or social-protection coverage for many small farmers.
- What could change: A shared water point and shade near the field; work moved to cooler hours by agreement; spraying planned for cooler, calm periods with suitable protection; help with water collection at home in the hottest weeks.
- Who controls it: The farmer or landholder sets the day for family and hired workers; landlords shape tenants' choices; extension services, farmer groups and programmes can supply water points and training; local government shapes water supply.
- Uncertain: No checked study measures heat strain or illness among cotton field workers in Asia on this page, or the effect of shade or water points in cotton fields.
#### B. Harvesting and collection
- Work: Hand-picking open bolls, often over several rounds; carrying picked cotton in cloth bundles; collecting and weighing it at the edge of the field.
- Who: Mostly women in hand-picked cotton in Pakistan, according to reports; family members; daily-wage and piece-rate pickers; seasonal and migrant pickers recruited through contractors.
- Exposure: Long days bent among plants in sun; carrying growing bundles; pesticide residues on plants. When picking falls depends on the place and the year: where sowing starts early, as in Sindh from March, picking can start while the weather is still hot.
- What makes protection difficult: Pay by weight means a break costs money; weighing points set the rhythm of the day; clinics may be far away; few pickers wear protective gear, and many report health effects during the picking season.
- What could change: A paid or protected cooling break that does not cut earnings; water and shade at weighing points; shorter carrying distances to collection points; first aid and transport to a clinic.
- Who controls it: The grower or contractor who sets the rate and the weighing schedule; buyers and programmes whose prices and standards shape what growers can afford; health services for referral.
- Uncertain: Checked studies here measure pesticide-related health costs, not heat strain; the share of pickers paid by weight and its effect on rest are not measured on this page.
#### C. Aggregation, weighing, storage and transport
- Work: Bringing seed cotton to traders, market yards, procurement centres and gins; loading and unloading trucks and trolleys; waiting to be weighed and paid; storing heaps and modules.
- Who: Farmers waiting with their crop; casual loaders and unloaders; truck and tractor drivers; traders' and yard workers.
- Exposure: Waiting in exposed yards and queues, sometimes for long periods, and heavy loading in the sun. In 2018 Pakistan was reported to have 1,200 ginneries, each fed with seed cotton brought from farms by road.
- What makes protection difficult: Losing a place in the queue to seek shade; payment that depends on being present; loaders paid per load; no toilets or water in the yard.
- What could change: Shaded waiting and loading areas; appointment or token systems that shorten exposed queues; water and toilets in yards; handling aids for loading.
- Who controls it: Yard and market operators, procurement agencies and gin owners; transport contractors; local authorities that run market yards.
- Uncertain: No checked source on this page describes heat in cotton market yards or tests appointment systems; this stage is described from how the work is organised and needs local assessment.
#### D. Ginning and baling
- Work: Separating cotton fibre (lint) from seed, cleaning out foreign material, and pressing lint into bales. Cottonseed is a coproduct, sold for crushing into oil and other uses, not simply waste.
- Who: Gin operators, feeders, press and bale workers, maintenance staff, and seasonal workers hired for the ginning season, many on short or informal terms.
- Exposure: Heat from machinery, motors and the building, cotton dust, noise and moving machinery, and heavy bale handling. Loose cotton fibre can smoulder if ignited, which shapes what cooling is safe.
- What makes protection difficult: Seasonal workers may fear losing the next shift if they report symptoms; dust and fire risks limit simple fixes such as fans or water sprays around lint.
- What could change: Engineered ventilation and dust control designed together; heat-source controls on motors and dryers; roof and building measures; water, toilets and a cool recovery area; machine guarding for handling aids; non-punitive symptom reporting.
- Who controls it: Gin owners and managers; equipment suppliers and engineers; fire and factory inspectorates where they apply; buyers who set delivery schedules.
- Uncertain: No checked study here measures heat in Asian cotton gins; the respiratory study and the fire testing describe other hazards that cooling choices have to respect.
#### E. Spinning
- Work: Turning cotton fibre into yarn in large machine halls.
- Who: Machine operators, often working continuous shifts.
- Exposure: Heat from running machines and the building; air conditions in some mills are controlled for the yarn as well as for people.
- What makes protection difficult: Shift patterns and production targets; see the indoor controls on the factory page.
- What could change: Indoor heat controls: ventilation, heat-source reduction, water, rest and fair targets.
- Who controls it: Mill owners and managers, with worker representatives.
- Uncertain: Covered in more depth on Heat inside factories.
- More: https://beattheheat.asia/factory-heat/#other-factories
#### F. Weaving or knitting, and wet processing
- Work: Making fabric from yarn by weaving or knitting; dyeing, printing and finishing, which can happen to fibre, yarn, fabric or finished garments.
- Who: Loom and knitting operators; dye-house and finishing workers.
- Exposure: Hot water, steam and wet floors in dyeing and finishing; heat from looms and knitting machines.
- What makes protection difficult: Chemical hazards that need protective equipment, which adds heat.
- What could change: Steam and moisture control at source, protective equipment chosen for heat as well as chemicals.
- Who controls it: Mill and dye-house owners and managers, with worker representatives.
- Uncertain: Covered in more depth on Heat inside factories.
- More: https://beattheheat.asia/factory-heat/#other-factories
#### G. Garment manufacturing
- Work: Cutting, sewing, pressing, finishing and packing garments.
- Who: Sewing operators, most of them women in many producing countries, pressers, finishers and packers.
- Exposure: Roof heat, pressing steam, crowded lines and heavy packing.
- What makes protection difficult: Line targets, piece rates and attendance bonuses that make breaks costly.
- What could change: See the garment-factory walkthrough and intervention library.
- Who controls it: Factory managers, worker representatives and buyers.
- Uncertain: Covered in depth on Heat inside factories.
- More: https://beattheheat.asia/factory-heat/#explore

### Three pathways
#### Heat affecting people
The same seven parts set a cotton worker's heat load as a factory worker's: air temperature, sun and radiant heat, humidity, air movement, the heat bodies make at work, clothing and protective equipment, and how long exposure lasts and whether people recover overnight.
- Documented: Women cotton pickers in Pakistani Punjab report health effects during the picking season that researchers relate mainly to pesticide exposure, alongside dust and sun.
- Plausible, to investigate: Long picking days in hot weather, paid by weight, with little shade or water, add up to heat strain; this page found no checked study measuring it in cotton fields in Asia.
#### Heat affecting cotton
Heat acts on the plant through its own routes: establishment, flowering, boll development, water demand, yield and fibre quality. Drought, rain and pests act alongside it, and the effects differ by cultivar, growth stage, irrigation and place.
- Documented: In a controlled-environment study, heat during flowering cut pollen germination by 71% and lint yield by 26% on average, and cultivars differed. Indian agronomists describe 27 to 32 °C as favourable for reproductive development, and rain at harvest damages fibre.
- Plausible, to investigate: Field effects depend on how heat combines with water stress and timing; a growth-chamber result does not give a field yield loss for any district.
#### Disruption affecting livelihoods and working conditions
Lost working time, medical costs, interrupted production, payment delays and contractual pressure can pass through households and firms, and the routes are not the same for everyone.
- Documented: Health costs of cotton picking fall on women pickers' households, and distance from hospital adds to them; in Sindh, women's days are split between cotton work and unpaid care.
- Plausible, to investigate: A bad season can mean less paid picking work, more debt for tenant farmers and pressure to work through symptoms; the size and direction of these effects need local evidence.
This page does not claim:
- That every crop loss causes the same effect on wages or prices.
- That every hotter season brings more pests.
- That higher cotton prices necessarily reach workers.
- That protecting crop yields protects workers.
- That a farm weather forecast measures any individual's exposure at work.

### Working arrangements
Informal does not mean unskilled, unimportant or outside formal supply chains. Pickers, loaders and gin workers carry skills and knowledge of the work and the weather, and informal work happens inside chains that end in registered firms and export contracts. The farmers trained in Madhya Pradesh were described as lacking coverage under labour legislation and social protection.
- Smallholder owner-operators: Farm their own land with family labour; carry crop risk and their own heat exposure; often outside labour law as self-employed.
- Tenant farmers and sharecroppers: Farm land they do not own, paying rent or sharing the crop; carry crop risk and often debt; decisions depend partly on the landholder.
- Unpaid contributing family workers: Work on the family farm without a wage of their own; often women and young people; their hours rarely appear in records.
- Daily-wage agricultural workers: Hired by the day for weeding, spraying or picking; paid only for days worked.
- Piece-rate harvest workers: Paid by the weight or amount picked; a break or a slower pace costs money directly.
- Seasonal and migrant workers: Move for the season; may lack local documents, housing, health access and benefits where they work.
- Contractor-recruited workers: Recruited and often paid through a labour contractor; responsibility is split between the contractor and the farm or gin.
- Casual loaders, drivers and warehouse workers: Paid per load, trip or day in yards, transport and storage.
- Informally employed workers inside registered enterprises: Work in a registered gin, mill or factory without a written contract, benefits or job security.
#### Who can actually stop? (Illustrative situations, not cases)
- A picker paid by weight takes a cooling break. Exposure: Hours bent in the sun, carrying a growing bundle. Constraint: Every minute resting is cotton not picked and money not earned. Arrangement: A paid break or a rate that does not penalise necessary rest; water and shade at the weighing point. Responsible: The grower or contractor who sets the rate and the schedule; buyers whose prices make it affordable.
- A casual loader waits in an exposed procurement yard. Exposure: Waiting and loading in an open yard in the afternoon. Constraint: Leaving the queue for shade risks losing the next load. Arrangement: Shaded waiting areas and a token or appointment system that keeps people's place. Responsible: The yard operator or procurement agency.
- A tenant farmer faces both crop risk and repayment obligations. Exposure: Field work in the heat at sowing and picking. Constraint: A poor crop still leaves rent or loan payments due, so cutting work hours feels impossible. Arrangement: Repayment terms that flex in a bad season, crop insurance that pays reliably, and work-hour changes that do not risk the crop. Responsible: Landholders, lenders and insurers; agricultural agencies.
- A seasonal gin worker fears losing the next shift after reporting symptoms. Exposure: Heat, dust and heavy lifting inside a gin. Constraint: Reporting dizziness may mean not being called back. Arrangement: Non-punitive reporting, paid recovery time and a written commitment that reporting does not affect rehiring. Responsible: The gin owner and manager; buyers and inspectors who check whether reporting is safe.

### Women and intersecting inequalities
Gender runs through every stage above, along with age, disability, migration, language, caste and ethnicity. These shape tasks, pay, access to toilets and clinics, and whose voice counts. They are not reasons to treat any group as uniformly vulnerable.
Design question: Does this protection expand someone's choices, or transfer more unpaid work, cost or risk to someone else?
- Tasks and control over earnings: In the Sindh assessment, women did most of the hand sowing, weeding and picking, and few operated irrigation, sprayed or sold cotton, which shapes who controls the income.
- Unpaid care and water collection: Women's waking hours were split almost evenly between cotton work and unpaid domestic and care work, and in Madhya Pradesh a participant described fetching water becoming harder in summer as supplies fell.
- Water, toilets and menstrual hygiene: Drinking water helps only if a safe, private toilet is within reach; the Madhya Pradesh workshops reported inadequate drinking water, sanitation and washing areas. This page found no checked study of menstrual hygiene in cotton fields.
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Precautionary occupational guidance and accommodation, not exclusion from work, apply in fields as in factories; India's health ministry has published guidance on heat and pregnancy for health workers.
- Transport and shift timing: Moving work to cooler hours can mean travel in the dark; safe transport is part of the arrangement, not an afterthought.
- Documents, benefits and grievance routes: Seasonal and migrant workers may lack local identity documents, benefits and health access; a grievance route is only useful if it is reachable and safe.
- Expertise and organisation: Workers and farmers know where heat collects and how the season runs. In Madhya Pradesh, the absence of farmers' associations limited collective dialogue on safety and welfare.

### Asian context
Examples start in India and Pakistan, where the evidence on this page is strongest. Other places appear only where a checked source supports them.
- Seasonal calendars differ: In Indian Punjab, sowing falls in April to mid-May; in Sindh, planting can begin in March. Picking times vary by place and year and are not given here from a checked source. Exposure at planting, crop care and harvest has to be read against the local calendar, not assumed.
- Rainfed and irrigated: Most of India's cotton is rainfed, which ties yields closely to the monsoon; irrigated systems face other limits, including groundwater.
- Manual and mechanised harvest: Cotton is picked by hand in the settings described here; in the United States it is machine-harvested. Where machines replace hand-picking, heat exposure shifts to fewer workers and to machine operation and maintenance, and work is lost.
- Smallholders and larger operations: Small and marginal farmers often lack the shade, water and money that larger operations can provide, and are often outside labour-law coverage themselves.
- Recruitment, payment and protection: Payment by weight, contractor recruitment and limited social protection change who can stop work; they differ by place and need local checking.
Countries important in garment manufacturing are not treated here as cotton-growing settings. Where this page has no checked source for a place, it says nothing about it.

### Intervention library
Evidence kinds: Occupational guidance; Research finding; Programme description; Worker testimony, as reported; News report; Proposal requiring validation.
#### Field and task controls
Shade, water, lighter loads, rest and adjustment, where the work happens.
- Shade and cooler recovery spaces near the work. Stages: field, harvest. Mechanism: Portable or fixed shade close to where people work lets them cool during breaks without a long walk. Beneficiaries: Pickers, weeders and family workers. Implements: Grower or landholder; farmer groups; programmes. Pays: Grower, often with programme or buyer support. Recurring: Moving, repairing and replacing shade through the season. Prerequisites: Shade within a short walk; time to use it. Possible harms or exclusions: A shade far away goes unused; shade without paid time protects only those who can afford to stop. Evidence: Occupational guidance; Research finding (A cooling station lowered heat strain in a pilot field trial in an indoor sawmill, not a cotton field.).
- Safe drinking water, replenishment and sanitation. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Water close by, kept cool and refilled, with a safe private toilet nearby, replaces sweat losses; people drink less when toilets are far or unsafe. Beneficiaries: Everyone working in heat, especially women. Implements: Grower, yard operator or gin owner; local government for supply. Pays: The employer or site operator; buyers and programmes can share costs. Recurring: Refilling, cleaning, testing and supplies, every day of the season. Prerequisites: A water source; someone responsible for refilling. Possible harms or exclusions: Water without toilets shifts the burden to women; one intake schedule does not fit everyone. Evidence: Programme description; Occupational guidance.
- Shorter carrying distances, handling aids and task redesign. Stages: field, harvest, yard. Mechanism: Collection points closer to pickers, carts and changed loads reduce the heat the body makes from carrying. Beneficiaries: Pickers, carriers and loaders. Implements: Grower, contractor, yard operator. Pays: Grower or operator. Recurring: Maintenance of carts; staffing of collection points. Prerequisites: Paths and equipment suited to the field. Possible harms or exclusions: Mechanisation can remove jobs or bring machine hazards. Evidence: Programme description (The programme trained safe postures for carrying loads.); Occupational guidance.
- Staffing and work-rest arrangements. Stages: field, harvest, gin. Mechanism: Enough people to share the work and rest planned around the heat and the workload, with strenuous work moved to cooler times. Beneficiaries: All workers, especially in the heaviest tasks. Implements: Grower, contractor or gin manager. Pays: Employer, reflected in prices. Recurring: Wages for extra staff. Prerequisites: Agreement on how rest is triggered. Possible harms or exclusions: Rest that is unpaid is rarely taken by those paid by weight. Evidence: Occupational guidance; Programme description (The programme trained farmers on adapting working hours during extreme heat.).
- Gradual acclimatisation for new and returning workers. Stages: field, harvest, gin. Mechanism: Building up time in heat over several days lets the body adapt; newcomers and returners are at higher risk. Beneficiaries: Seasonal and migrant workers, new recruits, people back from illness. Implements: Grower, contractor or gin manager. Pays: Employer. Recurring: Lower output in the first days. Prerequisites: Knowing who is new. Possible harms or exclusions: Production pressure on new arrivals. Evidence: Occupational guidance.
- Safe transport and worker-informed scheduling. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Changing hours with workers' input, and arranging safe transport for early or late shifts, makes cooler-hour working possible. Beneficiaries: Women, workers with care duties, migrants. Implements: Grower, contractor, local transport services. Pays: Employer or programme. Recurring: Transport costs. Prerequisites: Consultation before hours change. Possible harms or exclusions: Earlier starts can mean travel in the dark and conflict with childcare. Evidence: Programme description (Safe transport was among the gaps the workshops raised.).
#### Pay and working arrangements
So that people can use protection without losing income or standing.
- Paid cooling breaks and protection against retaliation. Stages: harvest, yard, gin, field. Mechanism: Breaks that are paid, and a promise that resting or reporting symptoms will not cost work, make protection usable. Beneficiaries: Daily-wage, piece-rate and seasonal workers. Implements: Grower, contractor, gin owner; buyers through prices. Pays: Employer, with buyer pricing. Recurring: Paid time. Prerequisites: Written terms, communicated and kept. Possible harms or exclusions: Informal pressure can undo written rules. Evidence: Research finding (In garment factories, quota pressure restricted drinking water: the same logic applies to pay by output in fields.); Proposal requiring validation (A right to stop work without loss of income is proposed in apparel research, not evaluated.).
- Piece rates that do not penalise necessary rest. Stages: harvest. Mechanism: A guaranteed minimum, a rate adjusted for hot days, or paid rest time stops pay by weight from punishing breaks. Beneficiaries: Piece-rate pickers. Implements: Grower or contractor; buyers and standards that shape rates. Pays: Grower, supported by buyer prices. Recurring: Higher labour cost on hot days. Prerequisites: Records of weights and hours. Possible harms or exclusions: If growers cannot afford it, work may shift to fewer or less protected workers. Evidence: News report (Shows payment by weight; the alternative arrangements are untested here.).
- Realistic workloads and revised targets in heat. Stages: harvest, gin, yard. Mechanism: Lower targets or quotas on hot days, agreed in advance, leave time to drink and rest. Beneficiaries: Workers on targets or quotas. Implements: Employer and buyer. Pays: Shared through prices and schedules. Recurring: Lower output on hot days. Prerequisites: Agreed triggers. Possible harms or exclusions: Targets cut without pay protection reduce earnings. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Clear responsibilities across farmers, contractors and buyers. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Writing down who provides water, shade, breaks and first aid where a contractor, a farmer and a buyer all play a part closes gaps where everyone assumes someone else is responsible. Beneficiaries: Contractor-recruited and seasonal workers. Implements: Buyers, contractors, growers. Pays: Agreed among them. Recurring: Monitoring. Prerequisites: Contracts that reach beyond the first supplier. Possible harms or exclusions: Costs pushed to the smallest party. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Sick leave or income support where it exists. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Income support when heat illness or extreme heat stops work removes the reason to work through symptoms. Beneficiaries: Workers without paid sick leave. Implements: Government social-protection agencies; employers where schemes exist. Pays: Public schemes, employers, insurers. Recurring: Benefit payments. Prerequisites: Coverage that reaches informal and migrant workers. Possible harms or exclusions: Schemes that require documents many workers lack. Evidence: Programme description (Small cotton farmers were described as lacking social-protection coverage.).
- Worker representation, reporting and grievance routes. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Associations and safe reporting routes let workers raise heat problems and negotiate fixes. Beneficiaries: All workers, especially informal ones. Implements: Workers' and farmers' organisations; employers; buyers. Pays: Time and facilitation from employers and programmes. Recurring: Meetings in paid time. Prerequisites: Freedom to organise without retaliation. Possible harms or exclusions: Token committees. Evidence: Programme description.
#### Crop and water management
Measures that protect the crop. Their benefits to workers are not assumed.
- Locally appropriate varieties and sowing dates. Stages: field. Mechanism: Choosing varieties and sowing windows suited to local heat and rainfall can reduce crop losses. Beneficiaries: The crop, and the farmers whose income depends on it. Implements: Farmers, seed agencies, extension services. Pays: Farmers and public research. Recurring: Seed costs; advice. Prerequisites: Local trials and advice. Possible harms or exclusions: A crop benefit; it does not by itself change working conditions, and earlier sowing can move field work into hotter weeks. Evidence: Research finding (Shows cultivars differ under heat and that sowing windows matter; not a field trial of a package.).
- Soil-moisture management and efficient irrigation where suitable. Stages: field. Mechanism: Keeping water in the soil and irrigating efficiently can help the crop through heat and dry spells. Beneficiaries: The crop and farmers. Implements: Farmers, irrigation agencies. Pays: Farmers and public schemes. Recurring: Energy, maintenance, water. Prerequisites: Water rights and energy. Possible harms or exclusions: Groundwater depletion and energy costs; more irrigation work can add field hours in heat. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Weather and agricultural advisories. Stages: field, harvest. Mechanism: Forecasts and advice help plan sowing, spraying and picking around heat and rain. Beneficiaries: Farmers and, if shared, workers. Implements: Meteorological and agricultural agencies; extension services. Pays: Public services. Recurring: Running the service. Prerequisites: Advice that reaches workers as well as farm owners. Possible harms or exclusions: A farm forecast does not measure a worker's exposure. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Integrated pest management. Stages: field, harvest. Mechanism: Reducing reliance on pesticides lowers residues pickers meet and the time spent spraying in protective gear. Beneficiaries: Sprayers and pickers. Implements: Farmers, extension services, programmes. Pays: Farmers, programmes. Recurring: Monitoring and advice. Prerequisites: Training and support. Possible harms or exclusions: Not a heat measure in itself; it does not assume hotter seasons bring more pests. Evidence: Research finding (These studies measure pesticide-related health effects among pickers; they did not test IPM.).
- Diversification where economically and agronomically feasible. Stages: field. Mechanism: Other crops or incomes can spread risk when cotton fails. Beneficiaries: Farm households. Implements: Farmers, agencies, markets. Pays: Farmers, public support. Recurring: Market access. Prerequisites: Markets and advice. Possible harms or exclusions: Can reduce paid picking work for labourers. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
#### Yards, transport and ginning
Waiting, loading and processing, designed with dust, machinery and fire in mind.
- Shaded waiting and loading areas. Stages: yard, gin. Mechanism: Shade where people queue and load cuts sun exposure during waits and heavy work. Beneficiaries: Farmers, loaders, drivers. Implements: Yard operators, procurement agencies, gin owners. Pays: Operators, possibly with public support. Recurring: Maintenance. Prerequisites: Space and structures. Possible harms or exclusions: Shade without a kept place in the queue goes unused. Evidence: Occupational guidance.
- Appointment or token systems that shorten exposed queues. Stages: yard, gin. Mechanism: Booked slots or tokens let people wait elsewhere without losing their place. Beneficiaries: Farmers, drivers, loaders. Implements: Yard operators, procurement agencies. Pays: Operators. Recurring: Running the system. Prerequisites: A way to communicate slots, including to people without smartphones. Possible harms or exclusions: Digital-only systems exclude some farmers. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Mechanical handling with machine-safety safeguards. Stages: yard, gin. Mechanism: Conveyors, lifts and carts reduce lifting, if guarded and maintained. Beneficiaries: Loaders and gin workers. Implements: Gin owners, yard operators. Pays: Owners. Recurring: Maintenance. Prerequisites: Guarding and training. Possible harms or exclusions: Machine injuries; fewer jobs. Evidence: Occupational guidance.
- Roof and building measures appropriate to the facility. Stages: gin, yard. Mechanism: Reflective or insulated roofs and shading reduce the heat entering gins and warehouses. Beneficiaries: Gin and warehouse workers. Implements: Building owners. Pays: Owners. Recurring: Upkeep. Prerequisites: Sound roofs and permission. Possible harms or exclusions: Roof changes need to respect fire and ventilation design. Evidence: Research finding (A building simulation for a garment factory; not tested on a gin.).
- Engineered ventilation, dust control and heat-source controls. Stages: gin. Mechanism: Ventilation designed with dust extraction, and controls on hot motors and dryers, remove heat without spreading lint or dust. Beneficiaries: Gin workers. Implements: Gin owners, engineers. Pays: Owners. Recurring: Energy, filters, maintenance. Prerequisites: Engineering design for dust, fire and electrical safety. Possible harms or exclusions: Fans, misting or water sprays placed without design can spread lint, wet electrical equipment or stored cotton, and raise fire and machinery risks. Evidence: Research finding (These describe dust and fire hazards that cooling has to respect; they do not test cooling.).
- Water, sanitation and recovery areas at yards and gins. Stages: yard, gin. Mechanism: Drinking water, toilets and a cool place to rest near the work. Beneficiaries: Everyone at the site. Implements: Operators and owners. Pays: Operators. Recurring: Cleaning and supplies. Prerequisites: Space and water supply. Possible harms or exclusions: Facilities that are locked or far away. Evidence: Occupational guidance.
#### Health and public systems
Warnings linked to action, first aid, clinics and social protection.
- Heat alerts linked to funded action. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Warnings that trigger agreed, funded changes (hours, water, breaks) rather than advice alone. Beneficiaries: Workers and farmers. Implements: Meteorological agencies, local government, employers. Pays: Public budgets and employers. Recurring: Running the warning and the response. Prerequisites: A plan that says who does what when a warning comes. Possible harms or exclusions: Advice without means to act. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Trained first aid and emergency referral. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Someone who knows the warning signs, and a way to reach a clinic quickly. Beneficiaries: Everyone at work in heat. Implements: Employers, programmes, health services. Pays: Employers and public health. Recurring: Training refreshers; transport. Prerequisites: A clinic within reach. Possible harms or exclusions: Training without transport to care. Evidence: Programme description (Training covered warning signs needing medical attention; it is not evidence that illness fell.).
- Rural health-service readiness and accessible transport. Stages: field, harvest. Mechanism: Clinics ready for heat illness, and transport to reach them. Beneficiaries: Rural workers and families. Implements: Health departments. Pays: Public budgets. Recurring: Staff, supplies, transport. Prerequisites: Funding and staff. Possible harms or exclusions: Costs fall on households when clinics are far. Evidence: Research finding (Distance from hospital affected pickers' health costs.).
- Social-protection access for seasonal and migrant workers. Stages: harvest, gin. Mechanism: Benefits and health coverage that move with workers, or that destination areas extend to them. Beneficiaries: Seasonal and migrant workers. Implements: Social-protection agencies at origin and destination. Pays: Public schemes. Recurring: Benefits and administration. Prerequisites: Portable entitlements and documents. Possible harms or exclusions: Schemes tied to a home address. Evidence: Programme description.
- Safe housing and overnight recovery. Stages: harvest, gin. Mechanism: Cooler, safer housing for seasonal workers lets the body recover overnight. Beneficiaries: Seasonal and migrant workers. Implements: Employers providing housing; local authorities. Pays: Employers, public programmes. Recurring: Upkeep. Prerequisites: Standards for worker housing. Possible harms or exclusions: Crowded hot housing undoes daytime protection. Evidence: Research finding (From factory case studies: heat at home disrupts sleep and recovery.).
#### Buyers, finance and governance
Institutional measures: who schedules, who pays and who checks.
- Purchasing terms that allow realistic schedules. Stages: gin, spin, fabric, garment, harvest. Mechanism: Delivery dates and prices that allow for hot-season slowdowns stop pressure being passed down the chain. Beneficiaries: Workers at every stage. Implements: Brands, retailers and traders. Pays: Buyers, through pricing. Recurring: Flexibility in schedules. Prerequisites: Buyers who see beyond their first supplier. Possible harms or exclusions: Institutional: effects are rarely evaluated. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation (Apparel research proposes allowances in production schedules for climate events; not evaluated.).
- Shared funding for shade, water, sanitation and running costs. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Buyers, industry bodies and programmes share the cost of facilities and, crucially, of keeping them running. Beneficiaries: Workers at farms, yards and gins. Implements: Buyers, industry associations, programmes. Pays: Shared. Recurring: Running costs, not only installation. Prerequisites: Agreed responsibility for upkeep. Possible harms or exclusions: One-off installations that stop when funding ends. Evidence: Programme description (An industry body supported a drinking water point.); Research finding (From garment factories: larger investments need buyer support.).
- Worker participation in checking whether protection is usable. Stages: field, harvest, yard, gin. Mechanism: Workers help check whether water, shade and breaks are actually reachable and used. Beneficiaries: All workers. Implements: Buyers, programmes, worker organisations. Pays: Buyers and programmes. Recurring: Paid time for monitors. Prerequisites: Safety from retaliation. Possible harms or exclusions: Audits on cool days or without workers find little. Evidence: Research finding (From garment factories: workers know where heat collects.).
- Insurance or emergency finance, with its limits explained. Stages: field. Mechanism: Crop insurance or emergency credit can cushion a bad season, if it pays reliably. Beneficiaries: Farmers, tenant farmers. Implements: Insurers, lenders, governments. Pays: Premiums, subsidies. Recurring: Premiums. Prerequisites: Clear terms. Possible harms or exclusions: Exclusions and basis risk: a payout triggered by an index can miss a farmer's actual loss; workers are rarely covered. Evidence: Proposal requiring validation.
- Support for small producers, not transferred compliance costs. Stages: field, harvest. Mechanism: Programmes that pay for water points, training and shade for small farmers, rather than demanding standards they cannot afford. Beneficiaries: Small and marginal farmers and their workers. Implements: Buyers, industry bodies, governments. Pays: Buyers and public programmes. Recurring: Ongoing support. Prerequisites: Reach to small farmers. Possible harms or exclusions: Standards that exclude small producers from markets. Evidence: Programme description.

### What makes protection usable?
Choose a stage, a working arrangement and the main barrier. The explorer returns arrangements that could make protection usable, who needs to take part, the evidence behind each, and what to assess locally. It is a learning and planning aid: not a medical diagnosis, a compliance certificate or a safe-work calculator, and it never says work is safe.
Temperature or a heat index alone does not describe a worker's heat stress. Occupational guidance uses a heat stress index such as WBGT, which combines humidity, radiant heat and air movement, and interprets it with workload, clothing and acclimatisation. Thresholds come from qualified assessment and the rules that apply where the work happens.
- The heat exposure itself: assess locally Where and when exposure peaks at this stage; a measured heat stress index at the work position, interpreted with workload, clothing and acclimatisation.
- Losing income by stopping: assess locally How pay is calculated, and what a break costs in practice.
- Water and toilets: assess locally Walking distance to water and toilets, who refills, and whether women can use them safely.
- Transport: assess locally Travel times, safety in the dark, and transport to a clinic.
- Care responsibilities: assess locally Who collects water and cares for children and older people, and how changed hours affect them.
- Authority to stop: assess locally Who decides when work pauses, and whether workers can raise heat without retaliation.
- Access to services: assess locally Distance to clinics, documents needed for benefits, and whether warnings reach workers.

### How risk can pass along the chain
Three mechanisms to investigate. Each is plausible from how work is organised; the full causal path is not established by the evidence on this page.
- Lost earnings → pressure to keep working → more exposure. When pay depends on output and a hot spell cuts what people can pick, the pressure to work longer or through symptoms rises. Interruption point: Pay that does not penalise rest, and income support in heatwaves. Actor: Growers and contractors; buyers through prices; social-protection agencies.
- Production disruption → compressed schedules → pressure downstream. A late or heat-damaged harvest can squeeze the time for ginning, spinning and garment production when delivery dates stay fixed. Interruption point: Delivery schedules with room for climate disruption. Actor: Brands, retailers and traders who set delivery dates.
- Household water and care demands → less recovery → harder to work safely. In hot weeks, collecting water and caring for others take more time, leaving less rest before the next working day. Interruption point: Water supply closer to homes, and hours that allow recovery. Actor: Local government for water; employers for hours.
People across a chain are connected through production, places and institutions, a community of fate in the sense used on Who shares the heat. But exposure, bargaining power and responsibility are unequal along it: a picker and a brand share a chain, not a burden.

### The fibre moves indoors. The heat problem changes.
Follow cotton into spinning, fabric production and garment manufacturing.
https://beattheheat.asia/factory-heat/

### Evidence gaps
- No checked study on this page measures heat strain or heat illness among cotton field workers, pickers, yard workers or gin workers in Asia. Studies of rice, sugarcane and salt work are summarised below as nearby evidence.
- No checked evaluation tests shade, water points, paid breaks or appointment systems in cotton production.
- The pickers' studies measure pesticide-related health effects and costs, not heat.
- The crop study is a controlled-environment experiment; field yield losses from heat for any district are not given here.
- No checked source describes heat in cotton market yards or gins in Asia.
- No checked study on menstrual hygiene or pregnancy in cotton field work was found.
- No checked source supports contrasts with other Asian cotton regions, such as mechanised harvesting in China, so none is made.

### Nearby evidence: heat strain measured in other Asian field work
No checked study measures heat strain among cotton workers in Asia. Researchers have measured it in neighbouring work: rice and sugarcane fields, farming villages and salt pans in India, Thailand, Viet Nam, Malaysia and Sri Lanka. These studies are not about cotton, and crops differ in season, posture, pace and pay; they show what has been found where people looked, and what a cotton study could measure.
#### Strain in the body
- In rice fields in West Bengal, India, hourly heat (WBGT) was 26-32°C. Among 124 harvesters, most reported exhaustion and pain on hot days; in 48 whose heart rate was recorded, it recovered more slowly at high heat, and bundles collected fell by about 5% for each degree of WBGT above 26°C.
- Among 200 men harvesting paddy in West Bengal from April to June 2024, heat (WBGT) predicted physiological strain hour by hour; older age added to the strain and work experience was protective.
- In a small study of 14 people transplanting paddy by hand in Northeast India, oral temperature rose by 0.5°C after 65 minutes of work at the lower heat levels studied. The authors propose work-rest cycles that shorten as heat rises, down to 35 minutes of work and 22 of rest at a WBGT of 31-32°C.
- In the hottest month of a Thai sugarcane harvest, cane cutters faced high heat stress and strain, with dehydration and rises in heart rate and body temperature across the shift; workers in the sugar factory were at low risk.
- In Nakhon Sawan, Thailand, sugarcane harvesters' heat stress exceeded the occupational limit (ACGIH) for 72.7% of working time in the cooler months and 90.9% in the hotter month; harvesting burnt cane added to the heat.
#### Symptoms people report
- Among 379 rice farmers in Ha Tinh province, Viet Nam, 83.4% reported at least one heat-related symptom during the 2021 summer-autumn harvest. More than 4 hours outdoors in the heat and heavy tasks were associated with more illness, and drinking more water with less.
- Among 295 Thai sugarcane workers (165 men, 130 women), 98% reported at least one heat-related symptom and 74% at least one severe symptom. Symptoms rose with each degree of full-shift heat, and the study found no significant difference in risk between women and men.
- Among 200 sugarcane farmers in Kamphaeng Phet, Thailand, 48% reported heat-related illness symptoms in summer. Being a woman and wearing two-layer shirts were associated with higher risk, and drinking 3.1-5.0 litres a day with lower risk.
#### Water, salt and kidneys
- In seven Indian salt pans, where there is no pesticide exposure, 87% of 352 workers exceeded the heat-stress limit and median water intake over the workday was one litre. Workers above the limit had 2.9 times the odds of reduced kidney function.
- Among 50 sea salt workers in Thailand, more than half were dehydrated after work.
- Among agricultural and brick-field workers in eastern India, sweat gland activity was higher in summer. Blood electrolytes stayed in the normal range at the monitoring sessions, but full-shift heat above a WBGT of about 23-25°C was associated with a higher probability of low blood sodium.
- Thai sugarcane cutters and farmers, most of them women, both had higher urinary markers of kidney injury after the shift than before, more so among cutters. Cutters exceeded recommended heat exposure; farmers did not.
- In chronic kidney disease hotspot villages of Bargarh district, Odisha, screening of 1,136 people identified 157 potential cases of heat stress nephropathy, 63.3% of them farmers. The study is cross-sectional and does not show cause.
- Among 261 agricultural workers in four villages of Sri Lanka's North Central Province, a heat stress and dehydration symptom index was not associated with urine albumin or urine concentration; the authors note that urine albumin is not a reliable marker of early disease.
Kidney findings are cross-sectional: they show patterns at one time, not cause. The Sri Lanka study found no association, and is listed for that reason.
#### Heat with pesticides
- Over six months in Malaysia, conventional farmworkers adapted less well to heat than agroecological farmers; the authors link this to earlier metabolic effects of pesticide exposure.
Cotton work often combines both exposures; no checked study measures the two together in cotton.
#### Output and pay
- Among 287 Thai sugarcane workers, each degree of full-shift heat was associated with about 9 fewer stalks harvested per hour.
- Across 11 districts of Tamil Nadu, WBGT measured at outdoor workplaces exceeded 30°C, and among 1,560 informal outdoor workers higher heat was associated with 1.4 times the risk of reported productivity loss.
Where pay follows output, fewer stalks or bundles an hour can mean less income, which is one reason rest can feel unaffordable.
#### What the research itself leaves out
- A 2026 mapping review of 210 field reports from low- and middle-income countries found 40% from the South-East Asia Region and 30% from India; agriculture made up 33%. 39% of reports included no women, and only 9% included any intervention to protect workers.
On women and men, the studies differ: one Thai sugarcane study found no significant difference in symptom risk, another found women at higher risk, and many reports include no women at all. This is one reason the page does not assume a single pattern.
What a cotton study could borrow: hourly heat measured where people work (WBGT), heart rate and body temperature across a shift, urine concentration before and after work, output per hour alongside pay, and women counted and reported, all agreed with workers and their organisations before any measurement starts.
Searched in Europe PMC (November 2026): heat strain, body temperature, heart rate, WBGT, urine specific gravity, heat-related illness and kidney markers among farmers and agricultural, rice, sugarcane, tea, salt and brick workers in South and Southeast Asia, 2008 to 2026, with intervention terms. No measured field study from Pakistan or Bangladesh was found, and no field trial of shade, water or rest in Asian agriculture; one Indian study proposes work-rest cycles from measurements but did not test them over a season.

### Withheld
- Better Cotton's account of an individual cotton worker in Pakistan and its Pakistan programme page could not be read from the build session and are not used; the page names no individuals in any case.
- Named testimony in the sources (in the ILO release and the 2017 news report) is described without names.
- Figures on heat-related cotton yield losses by country, and on the share of pickers paid by weight, were not found in a checked source.


## Who shares the heat: one market through one hot season

https://beattheheat.asia/shared-heat/

A worked example of how a hot day ties lives together through shared places, work and services, why people sharing the heat do not share the same power over it, and what makes protection last beyond one season.

### Connected by the heat

On a hot afternoon at a market, whether a porter can rest depends on whether leaving the queue costs a paid load. Whether a vendor has water depends on who orders the refill. Whether a child can learn depends on the classroom, and whether a parent keeps a shift depends on the school's hours. And whether any of them recovers overnight depends on water, electricity and the home they go back to.

Heat ties these lives together through the places, work, institutions and services they share. Common Shade calls such groups communities of fate: people whose wellbeing becomes connected through shared conditions, even when their exposure, money, rights and say in decisions are far from equal. The connection can run beyond one street, along a commuting route, a labour contract, a supply chain or a public service.

Building resilience, in this sense, means giving people a greater say in those shared conditions and making protection dependable: something a household can count on, not a project that ends with its funding.

A way of looking, not a measured finding. Common Shade uses the phrase as a lens and does not trace it to a single thinker or theory.

### What resilience means here

The ability of people and institutions to see heat coming and reduce the risk, to respond when it arrives, to recover without falling further behind, and to change the arrangements that cause the same harm every year. It rests on a household's own means and skills as well as on shared services, institutions that take responsibility, and public investment.

- Before heat arrives: Preparing and preventing: resources agreed, people named, sites ready and tested.

- During heat: Protection people can actually use, and essential services such as water, power and clinics that keep running.

- After heat: Recovery of health, income and services, without new debt, lost work or a lost place in the queue.

- Between seasons: Learning what failed, maintaining what works, and changing what causes the same harm each year.

When something is said to build resilience, it helps to ask:

- Whose ability improves?

- To withstand or respond to which disruption?

- Through what service, resource, right or institutional change?

- Who is responsible for keeping it going?

- Who could still be left out, or end up paying more?

### Shared heat, unequal ground

People in the same street, market or workplace share the same hot afternoon, but not the same exposure, money, rights or say over what changes. Shared consequences do not make responsibility equal, and they do not create agreement on their own. Protection tends to hold better when the people most exposed take a real part in decisions: organising, negotiating, and bringing what they know about their own day.

### The worked example (fictional)

The town, the people and every event here are made up, and continue the market town of The Heat Assembly. The relationships they illustrate are drawn from the sources behind that game and the pages linked below; no figure here is a measurement.

#### Shared exposure

A hot season is forecast for the market town. The public hall beside the market is shaded and open, and almost empty. The loading lane, the stalls, the tea stall at the bay and the homes around the square will all take the same heat.

#### Different constraints

The same heat, five different reasons the hall does not help. The municipal officer controls the hall and a small budget; the market association controls the loading order; the porters have no seat at first.

- Tara, a porter paid per load loses about two loads by leaving the queue to rest.

- Jeevan, a porter on a day rate loses nothing by resting, so is the person others ask to cover the loads.

- Noor, a stitcher paid per piece, caring for a child of three can work only while the childcare centre is open; nothing on offer cools Noor's home.

- Kiran, a stall holder can leave the stall in the afternoon lull, not at the midday peak.

- Hira, an older tea seller cannot walk to the hall in the heat; a rickshaw costs a day's money.

#### A collective decision

Before the season, the market association calls a meeting with the municipal officer, the neighbourhood services coordinator and a workers' representative, invited after porters raised the queue. Traders object to paying for cover; the association agrees to keep places in the queue only with a day's notice. After two meetings they agree four things: places are kept for anyone who rests, with a paid relief porter on alert days; the hall opens at midday and in the afternoon; a water point and shade go to the loading bay; and childcare keeps its hours on alert days.

They do not agree on everything. The traders accept the cost of relief cover for one season only, and the workers' representative wanted it every hot day, not only on alert days.

#### Resources and responsibilities

- Arrangement: Queue places kept, with relief cover; Who authorises it: Market association; Who pays first: Municipal operating budget, this season; Who pays each season: Not yet agreed; Who runs it: Workers' representative names the relief porter; How a failure is raised and fixed: Porters tell the association; it replies the same day

- Arrangement: Hall open midday and afternoon; Who authorises it: Municipal officer; Who pays first: Already paid for (building); Who pays each season: Municipal operating budget (staff hours); Who runs it: Services coordinator sets the caretaker's timetable; How a failure is raised and fixed: A number posted on the door; the coordinator logs each closure

- Arrangement: Water and shade at the loading bay; Who authorises it: Market association, with the municipal officer; Who pays first: A one-off grant; Who pays each season: Market association (refills); Who runs it: A named trader orders refills; How a failure is raised and fixed: Hira and the tea sellers report a dry tap

- Arrangement: Childcare keeps its hours on alert days; Who authorises it: Services coordinator; Who pays first: No new cost; Who pays each season: Relief staff from the operating budget; Who runs it: Childcare centre; How a failure is raised and fixed: Parents raise it with the coordinator

#### Who gains access

- Tara can rest at midday on alert days without losing a place.

- Kiran rests in the hall in the afternoon.

- Hira gets water and shade at the bay, where the work is, rather than at the hall.

- Noor keeps the childcare hours, and the paid work that depends on them.

- Jeevan is no longer the unpaid cover, because the relief porter is paid.

#### What remains

- Noor's home is still hot at night. Housing sits with another department, which was not at the meeting.

- Relief cover is funded for one season. Who pays next year is not agreed.

- On hot days without an official alert, Tara still pays for a break in lost loads.

- Nobody yet records who used the hall, at what hour, so the next meeting cannot see who it missed.

#### Learning for the next season

- Record use of the hall and the water point by hour, and ask who could not come and why.

- Move relief cover from a one-season allocation into the municipal budget, or into the market's own fees.

- Invite the housing department, and ask what would cool the homes around the square at night.

- Agree in advance what changes on a hot day without an alert, so protection does not wait for the warning.

#### Through the season

- Before heat arrives: The meeting, the agreements and the budget line

- During heat: The hall, the kept places, the water at the bay and the childcare hours

- After heat: Checking earnings lost and failures fixed

- Between seasons: The four lessons above, before the next forecast

The question: What would need to change here so that protection remains available when the project team leaves?

### The same lens, three other places

- A school. Who shares it: Pupils, teachers, support staff and families. Classroom heat affects all of them at once. If a school shortens its hours on hot days, care moves home and a parent can lose a shift. Opening a school to the neighbourhood in the holidays needs its own permission, staffing and safeguarding. Children, meal staff and teachers know where the heat is worst; the School Management Committee can help choose what changes.

- A rented neighbourhood. Who shares it: Tenants, landlords, the power utility and the municipality. Whether a room cools at night depends on a roof the tenant does not own, power the utility supplies and trees the municipality plants. A landlord can pass the cost of a cooler roof into the rent. Tenants' groups can say which rooms stay hottest and when the power goes; that knowledge can set priorities for repairs.

- A workplace and its supply chain. Who shares it: Workers, contractors, employers and the buyers they supply. A buyer's deadline sets the pace of work in the heat; a contractor decides whether a break costs pay. When protection is not paid for up the chain, the worker pays for it. Workers' organisations can negotiate rest, shade and timing, and report what actually happens on site.

### What keeps protection working

A shade, a water point or a rest break protects people only while it keeps working. Five things usually decide whether it does:

- Ownership and authority: Someone holds the site and can say yes, and everyone knows who.

- Operating money and maintenance: Money for water, cleaning and repairs through the season, not only to build.

- Staffing and access: Someone opens it at the hours people need it, and people can reach it: step-free, close to their work, without losing pay or a place.

- A say for workers and residents: The people who use it help decide where it goes and when it opens, and can raise a problem without risk to their work.

- Monitoring, and a way to fix failures: A way to report a failure, someone who fixes it, and a record of how long it took.

### Who pays first, and who keeps paying

Setting protection up is often paid once, from a budget or a grant. Running it comes back every season, and that cost lands somewhere. Three common ways it moves, as illustrations:

- Onto households: A cooling space open only by day leaves the cost of a hot night (fans, power, water) to each household.

- Onto informal workers: A rest break with no pay protection is paid for by the worker, in lost loads or lost sales.

- Onto unpaid carers: Shorter school or childcare hours on hot days move care to whoever is at home, and can cost that person paid work.

For any measure, ask who paid to set it up, who pays to run it each season, and who pays if it stops. Proposed, funded and operating are different states; the cases on this page say which each one is.

### Questions to bring to a commitment

An announcement is a start, not protection. These questions help read one; the record shows only what its evidence shows.

- Which people and services does it cover?

- Who can authorise action when heat arrives?

- Are money and staff there when they are needed?

- Can the people affected shape how it is delivered?

- What evidence would show that protection reached people?

### Before the plan is finished: four questions

A plan holds up when it names the shared arrangement it depends on. Check that yours answers:

- The shared service or arrangement: Which one needs to improve: a water point's refill, a school timetable, a queue rule, a night supply of power?

- Who controls it, and who depends on it: The body that can change it, and the people whose day depends on it, including those with no seat at the table yet.

- The next agreement: The one decision or agreement needed next, and who has to say yes.

- How to check it works for different people: One observable check, read for people in different circumstances: a porter paid per load, a carer, an older person who cannot walk far.

## Who could help a household through a hot season

https://beattheheat.asia/social-protection/

Public schemes that could cushion a household through a hot season, in 6 countries: 55 schemes, the steps of access and what is measured, delivery routes and organisations, and where no public system responds. This is not an eligibility check. Scheme rules change often; each status has the date it applies to. Households appear only in aggregate.

#### Open questions for Bangladesh (study designs and sizes are our suggestions; sizes are illustrative)

- Does an allowance top-up before a heatwave reduce lost work and medical spending? What is known: A Rajshahi delivery simulation was reported. [B5] A study that could answer it: Randomised phased invitation or top-up timing across comparable neighbourhood clusters, with aggregate income, medical-spending and timing outcomes. (Illustrative design: 40-60 clusters; final size from power calculations.)

- At which access step do heat-exposed urban households stop receiving support? What is known: HIES measures past receipt but not a linked eligibility-to-receipt ladder. [B3] A study that could answer it: A repeated representative household survey linked only to consented, de-identified process totals; publish aggregate transitions and reasons. (Illustrative design: 1,500-2,000 households across several cities.)

- How often does public support meet the costs of medically diagnosed heat illness? What is known: A historical SSK financial-risk evaluation exists; heat-specific claims were not reported. [B7] A study that could answer it: Prospective facility-cost study comparing public benefits, out-of-pocket costs, referral and foregone care across one hot season. (Illustrative design: 10-15 facilities; power and case-volume check first.)

- Does assisted application improve timely receipt among migrants and women outdoor workers? What is known: Delivery organisations describe support, but no comparable independent local effect was read. [B6, B12, B13] A study that could answer it: Randomise outreach timing among consenting community clusters and track aggregate application, receipt, cost and delay. (Illustrative design: 30-50 clusters over one application cycle.)

- [Unmeasured: Adequate, On time] When heat arrives, how much of a household's lost earnings and care costs does an allowance or top-up cover, and does it arrive before the hottest days? What is known: Implementer reports count households that received cash in Rajshahi and Dhaka. None of the sources checked measures how far the money went, or when it arrived compared with the heat. A study that could answer it: Follow recipient households through one hot season, recording lost work days, care costs and payment dates against heat-alert dates. (Illustrative: about 300 households in two cities over one hot season)

- [Unmeasured: Aware, Eligible, Documented, Applied, Enrolled] How many heat-exposed urban households know of an allowance, qualify for it, hold the documents, apply and are enrolled? What is known: None of the sources checked measures these steps for the schemes on this page in Bangladesh. A study that could answer it: A household survey in hot wards that asks the same people about each step, for the same schemes. (Illustrative: about 1,000 households in four wards)

### India (research as of 5 November 2026; sources checked 7 November 2026)

- Official announcements describe rural-employment changes from July 2026 and pension changes approved in October. Pension implementation and current disaster-relief details remain partly unverified.
