## Signals

https://beattheheat.asia/signals/

Which way heat policy, finance, research and practice are moving in South and Southeast Asia: what was announced, found or agreed, what the evidence confirms for each promise, and what would show the next step.

A count shows what this site has checked, not what has happened. Each deliverable is counted once, at the furthest step it has any evidence for; evidence at one step does not show the steps before it. Missing evidence means not verified, never failed. The ladder records how far a promise has got, never how well an institution performs, and it says nothing about places or institutions not shown.

Of 32 deliverables in 21 commitments tracked here, among 33 records in all (21 commitments, 2 gatherings, 9 findings, 1 guidance). This is a selection of developments the site has checked, not a census of the region.

Overview, by the furthest step each deliverable has evidence for: Announced 9 (1 on secondary reports only); Adopted 13 (3 on secondary reports only); Funded 7 (4 on secondary reports only); Delivered 3 (1 on secondary reports only); Evaluated 0.

Evidence states: Checked against an original source; Reported by secondary sources; original not checked; Not verified: no source passed a content check.

How records are kept: One canonical record per initiative, with stable identifiers for each record, deliverable and milestone; later developments are added to the same record, and nothing inconvenient is deleted. A commitment is tracked deliverable by deliverable. Funding announced, committed, paid out and spent are separate steps, as are a rule's adoption, the date it takes effect, and evidence that it is applied. Each milestone names its sources and what each one establishes. Whether it is confirmed comes from the site's source check (data/inbox/*/link-check.json): a page that merely opens is not evidence, and a secondary report is shown as reported until the original is checked. An evaluation is recorded with its findings, positive, mixed or negative, and is not treated as proof of cause. Interpretation is labelled as Common Shade's reading and kept apart from what sources say. Broad climate or health funding is never shown as money for heat unless the source says so. Maintenance: node tools/signals-review.js lists records due for review and what each source's check found, and turns a proposed milestone into a record only with its evidence. Nothing is published without review.

### El Niño watch: implications for Asia's next hot season

El Niño watch (bulletin: NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, issued 12 November 2026; next scheduled 10 December 2026)
- Official status: El Niño Advisory. NOAA's alert status when El Niño conditions are observed and expected to continue.
- What changed: No substantive change since NOAA's discussion of 12 November 2026: no newer monthly discussion has been issued (the next is due 10 December 2026). NOAA's weekly update of 23 November, the Bureau of Meteorology's weekly values to 22 November and ASMC's status page are consistent with it. WMO's update of 20 November 2026 is a project update on preparedness, not a new forecast.
- Observed: El Niño strengthened compared with the previous month: sea surface temperature anomalies exceeded 4.0 °C and extended farther west across the eastern equatorial Pacific. The weekly Niño-3.4 index reached +2.5 °C, and rainfall stayed suppressed over Indonesia. NOAA's monthly review of conditions in the tropical Pacific. The +2.5 °C Niño-3.4 figure is the latest weekly value it reports, not the three-month RONI used to classify events.
- Forecast (January to March 2027): A strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027 (a greater than 79% chance), before it begins to weaken in early 2027.
- For March to May 2027, NOAA Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of El Niño at 80%, most likely weak (53%) or moderate (25%); for April to June 2027, ENSO-neutral becomes more likely (61%) than El Niño (38%).
- ENSO phase probabilities (NOAA Climate Prediction Center, issued November 2026; Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), Niño-3.4 region, 1991–2020 base, ±0.5 °C thresholds): January to March 2027: El Niño 100%, neutral 0%, La Niña 0%; February to April 2027: El Niño 98%, neutral 2%, La Niña 0%; March to May 2027: El Niño 80%, neutral 20%, La Niña 0%; April to June 2027: El Niño 38%, neutral 61%, La Niña 1%.
- Strength, March to May 2027: weak 53%, moderate 25%, strong 2%, very strong 0% (these share out the 80% chance of El Niño; they are not added to it).
- NOAA Climate Prediction Center calls an event historic if its three-month RONI reaches +2.5 °C or more, and gave that about a 60% chance for October to December 2026 and for November 2026 to January 2027.
- Observed, NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO: Recent Evolution, Current Status and Predictions (weekly update), issued 23 November 2026, covers recent weeks to 23 November 2026, Tropical Pacific (Weekly Niño indices and RONI (weekly values are not three-month indices)): A weekly monitoring summary between monthly discussions, not a new outlook. Suppressed convection and rainfall has persisted over Indonesia since June 2026. https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/lanina/enso_evolution-status-fcsts-web.pdf
- Observed and forecast, Australian Bureau of Meteorology, Climate driver update: ENSO and the Indian Ocean, issued November 2026, covers week ending 22 November 2026; outlook to March to May 2027 (southern autumn), Tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean (Weekly relative Niño3.4 (not RONI); weekly Indian Ocean Dipole index): Weekly relative Niño3.4 of +2.67 °C for the week ending 22 November 2026, below the event's peak so far of +2.88 °C. Most models expect warming to peak in December or January and to stay above El Niño thresholds into the southern autumn of 2027 (March to May 2027). The Bureau notes that a strong Niño3.4 signal does not necessarily mean strong impacts. https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/enso/
- Observed and forecast, ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, Regional Climate: El Niño / La Niña (status with October 2026 values), issued November 2026, covers October 2026, and August to October 2026; outlook to April 2027, Niño3.4 region, read for Southeast Asia (Relative Niño3.4; RONI (three-month); events classified at ±0.65 °C): Relative Niño3.4 of 2.3 °C for October 2026 and 2.0 °C for August to October 2026. The index is predicted to peak during November to December 2026; strong El Niño conditions are predicted to persist until February to March 2027, with El Niño continuing until at least March to April 2027; most models (more than 70%) predict El Niño will still be present in April 2027. https://asmc.asean.org/asmc-el-nino/
- Observed and forecast, India Meteorological Department, ENSO and IOD Bulletin, October 2026, issued October 2026, covers September 2026; outlook through January to March 2027, Tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean, read for India (Niño 3.4 SST anomaly, ±0.5 °C (Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecast System, September 2026 start); Dipole Mode Index, ±0.4 °C): A high likelihood of strong-to-very strong El Niño conditions persisting through January to March 2027. Neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions prevail and are most likely to continue; IMD notes some international centres expect the positive phase to continue in the near term. This was IMD's latest bulletin online on 26 November 2026. https://mausam.imd.gov.in/ClimateInformation/imdweb/CLIMATE_FCST/Bulletin/ENSO_IOD_Update_Bulletin.pdf
- Forecast, World Meteorological Organization, Global Seasonal Climate Update for November 2026 to January 2027, issued 21 October 2026, covers November 2026 to January 2027, Niño 3.4 region and the Indian Ocean (Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly, multi-model ensemble mean (not RONI)): The seasonal average anomaly is forecast at about +3.8 °C, peaking around December 2026; a positive Indian Ocean Dipole is forecast to decline to +0.3 °C. https://wmo.int/resources/publication-series/global-seasonal-climate-updates/gscu-ndj2026
- Forecast, World Meteorological Organization, El Niño/La Niña Update (WMO's latest quarterly update; no newer one was found by 26 November 2026), issued 3 September 2026, covers through February 2027, Tropical Pacific (Consensus of WMO Global Producing Centres): An exceptionally high likelihood, nearly 100%, that El Niño persists through February 2027. https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027
- Forecast, ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, Seasonal forecast for November 2026 to January 2027, issued 5 November 2026, covers November 2026 to January 2027, ASEAN region (Multi-model rainfall and temperature terciles): Below-normal rainfall over parts of the southeastern and northeastern Maritime Continent and southeastern mainland Southeast Asia, and above-normal temperature over the ASEAN region. National services hold the national-scale outlook. https://asmc.asean.org/asmc-seasonal-outlook/
- The Indian Ocean: Agencies read the Indian Ocean Dipole differently, because each uses its own index and threshold. The Bureau of Meteorology reports a weekly index of +0.53 °C for the week ending 22 November 2026 and expects the positive event to weaken and return to neutral in early southern summer; ASMC expects positive conditions to return to neutral in January 2027; IMD's October bulletin reports neutral conditions on its ±0.4 °C threshold. Read each with its own date; they are not averaged.
- Our reading (Common Shade's interpretation): The odds favour El Niño persisting into the start of the hot season in much of South and Southeast Asia, then easing. That is a reason to get ordinary heat protection working early, in the places where people already spend the hottest hours. It is not a forecast of a heatwave anywhere.
- Uncertain locally: A Pacific probability is not any town's chance of a heatwave, a water shortage or a flood. NOAA's strength odds describe the Pacific index, not the strength of local impacts. Local outcomes depend on the season, geography, other drivers such as the Indian Ocean Dipole, long-term warming and local conditions; national seasonal outlooks and official local warnings carry that detail.
- Earlier bulletins, kept as history: Meteorological Service Singapore, El Niño/La Niña status, issued 16 October 2026 (The relative Niño3.4 index was 2.1 °C for September and 1.7 °C for July to September, and was predicted to peak during October to December 2026.).

An outlook is a finding, not a commitment; it stays outside the commitment counts. Explainer: https://beattheheat.asia/el-nino/

A hot, dry season can strain water, power, work, schools and care at once, in the same households; the explainer shows how these pathways connect.

### Questions to bring to a commitment

An announcement is a start, not protection. These questions help read one; the record shows only what its evidence shows.

- Which people and services does it cover?

- Who can authorise action when heat arrives?

- Are money and staff there when they are needed?

- Can the people affected shape how it is delivered?

- What evidence would show that protection reached people?

- El Niño set to bring more heat into 2027 [sig-el-nino-2026-2027] (Finding; Global; latest development 9 November 2026). By mid-August 2026 El Niño had become firmly established. WMO's State of the Climate release says it has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December. That is a forecast, not an observed record: NOAA's discussion of 12 November 2026 put the chance of a historic event (a three-month RONI of +2.5 °C or more) at about 60% for October to December 2026 and for November 2026 to January 2027. WMO calls El Niño a risk multiplier for health and writes that WHO has, for the first time, classified the anticipated health impacts as a health emergency. WHO's own plan describes a Grade 3 response, its internal grading of its operational response; no declaration of a public health emergency under the International Health Regulations was found.
  What to watch: Early warnings and heat plans ready for the 2027 hot season, above all in Southeast Asia, where El Niño and warming broke records in April 2016.

- The Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings opens for endorsement [sig-cop31-antalya-compact-2026] (Commitment; Global (UN climate process); latest development 29 October 2026). Ahead of the conference, the COP31 Presidency launched the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, which aims for a 25% cut in the operational energy intensity of buildings worldwide by 2035, compared with 2020. Its actions include stronger energy codes, faster renovation and the electrification of heating and cooling. It covers buildings and energy as a whole, not heat alone; it bears on heat because cooler, more efficient buildings ease the indoor heat people live and work in, and the cost of cooling them.

- Only 35% of countries report health early warning systems for heat-related illness [sig-ifrc-heat-warnings-2026] (Finding; Global; latest development October 2026). - 98% of surveyed maternity and newborn clinicians say they have cared for a pregnant woman they believe heat harmed [sig-clinicians-heat-pregnancy-2026] (Finding; Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe; latest development September 2026). A survey commissioned by Wellcome asked 1,000 practising clinicians in pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal and newborn care, 250 of them midwives, in Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe (fieldwork by Censuswide, September 2026). Across the five countries, 98% said they had cared for a pregnant woman, and 99% for a baby, whose health they believed extreme heat had harmed; 73% reported more heat-related complications in pregnant women over the past five years and 76% in foetal or newborn health, and 92% want more training and resources. As reported by Down To Earth, among the 200 respondents in India, 62% reported more complications in pregnant women and 66% in foetal or newborn health, and 26% had seen pregnancy complications that needed extra monitoring or treatment. The findings were presented on 13 November on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, where a UN Climate Change official said that about 1% of formal climate finance goes to health. These are clinicians' reports of what they believe they have seen, not measured outcomes. What clinicians in India can already use: on 6 May 2026 the health ministry and UNFPA India published guidance on heat and pregnancy for healthcare providers and community health workers, with a heat-risk checklist, preparedness for health facilities including functional referral systems, and counselling that covers breastfeeding.
  What to watch: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether the guidance clinicians already have reaches antenatal clinics and community health workers before the hot season, and whether national heat plans and health budgets fund it.
  Review: record last reviewed 19 November 2026; next review due 27 November 2026.

- Warming will overshoot 1.5 °C: the Emissions Gap Report 2026 [sig-emissions-gap-2026] (Finding; Global; latest development 2026). UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2026, The Point of Return, finds that with global temperature rise set to exceed 1.5 °C, urgent and stringent cuts are needed to minimise the size and length of the overshoot and return to 1.5 °C by the end of the century. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8 °C this century; if all national pledges are delivered, 2.6 °C.
  Heat link (Common Shade's reading): A projection of warming; what it means for heat exposure is Common Shade's reading.
  What to watch: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether adaptation plans for heat assume the warming these projections describe.
  Review: record last reviewed 16 November 2026; next review due 27 November 2026.

- Adaptation finance covers a fraction of what is needed [sig-adaptation-gap-2026] (Finding; Developing countries; latest development 2026). UNEP's Adaptation Gap Report 2026 estimates that developing countries need about US$305 billion a year for adaptation by 2035. International public adaptation finance to developing countries was about US$28 to 32 billion in 2024. Even if the COP30 aim of tripling it is met, it would cover only about 20 to 29% of needs. The report covers adaptation as a whole, not heat alone; it bears on heat because heat plans draw on the same adaptation money.
  Heat link (Common Shade's reading): The figures are for adaptation finance as a whole; no share for heat is given, and none is implied here.
  What to watch: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether COP31's finance outcomes reach heat plans, and whether heat is named in them.
  Review: record last reviewed 16 November 2026; next review due 27 November 2026.

## Funding, open calls and careers

Who funds work relevant to extreme heat in South and Southeast Asia, through which programmes, and how each can be reached. A funder is not an open call: most of these programmes are not accepting applications today, and several are reached only through an accredited entity, a government nomination, a consortium or an invitation.

Open calls and tenders: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-economy/money/opportunities/ · Careers: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-economy/money/careers/ · Programmes: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-economy/money/#landscape

Status rules: application status (upcoming, open, deadline day, rolling, closed, withdrawn, unknown) and verification (verified, review due, source unavailable, conflicting information) are separate; 'verified open' needs both. A future deadline does not prove a call is open; no deadline does not mean rolling.

### Open calls and tenders (as of the build; check each official page)
- Nexa Lighthouse: Transition to Scale funding for climate and health innovation in Asia and the Pacific (Grand Challenges Canada; Grant call; Grant, debt or equity). Funds proven innovations that help local health actors turn climate-risk signals into timely action, for hazards including extreme heat. Status: Open; Verified. Deadline: 8 December 2026, 14:00 ET. Funding: USD 250,000 to USD 2,000,000 per award. Who can apply: Applicants incorporated and implementing in countries across Asia and the Pacific; the full list of eligible countries is in Appendix B of the funding opportunity.. https://www.grandchallenges.ca/funding-opportunity-nexa-lighthouse/
- IKI Small Grants: eighth call (GIZ; Grant call; Grant). Local climate and biodiversity projects by non-profit organisations in ODA-eligible countries. Status: Open; Verified. Deadline: No deadline published. Funding: EUR 60,000 to EUR 200,000 per award. Who can apply: Sub-national, national and regional non-profit organisations in ODA-eligible countries.. https://iki-small-grants.de/
- Horizon Europe: integrating climate-related exposures into the human exposome (HORIZON-HLTH-2027-01-ENVHLTH-02) (European Commission; Grant call; Grant). Research on climate-related exposures and how the human exposome changes with climate change. Status: Upcoming; Conflicting information. Deadline: No deadline published. Funding: Not published. Who can apply: Consortia; international cooperation is encouraged. ## The Heat Assembly

https://beattheheat.asia/heat-assembly/

The Heat Assembly: A shaded hall is open beside the market, and almost nobody who needs it can use it. Take a seat at the table, make agreements over four rounds of heat, and see who could take a break, whose earnings changed and why.

Fictional: The market town, the people and the events here are made up. The direction of each relationship comes from the sources listed below; every number in the game is a game mechanic, not a measurement.

By the end, you could explain from your own game how a decision about pay, care, staffing or authority changed who could use heat protection.
About 10 minutes on your own, or 15 to 20 minutes around a table.

The opening, 11:40 a.m.: The public hall beside the market is open, shaded and paid for. It is nearly empty. Out in the loading lane, porters wait in a queue for the next truck. Leaving the queue means going to the back of it, and maybe losing the next paid load. Across the square, a caretaker is due at the childcare centre this afternoon. The same caretaker is the only person who can keep the hall open. A forecast has just come in: a hot day tomorrow, a hot night after it, and a second heat alert to follow.

People:
- Tara, Queue porter, paid per load. Paid for each load carried. A place in the queue is the only security in the job. No one at home depends on Tara during the day. Needs: A midday break in the hall, without losing a place in the queue.
- Jeevan, Porter on a day rate. Hired by one trader for the whole day at a fixed rate, so a break costs Jeevan no earnings. Free to rest whenever the hall is open. Needs: Any open hour in the hall.
- Noor, Home-based stitcher, cares for a child of three. Paid for each piece finished at home. The hours the childcare centre is open are the hours Noor can work. Looks after a child of three. Needs: Childcare at midday and in the afternoon; nothing on the table cools Noor's home in the day.
- Kiran, Stall holder with a fixed pitch. Sells from a pitch Kiran holds. A neighbour can mind the stall in the afternoon lull, not at the midday peak. Lives in a solid house that cools at night. Needs: An afternoon break in the hall.
- Hira, Older tea seller at the loading bay. Earns from daily sales at the bay. Cannot walk to the hall in the heat; a rickshaw costs a day's money. Needs: Water and shade at the bay itself.

Seats at the table:
- Workers' representative. Resource: Two rota days for the whole game: a day when a porter on a fixed rate covers the queue so others can rest. Constraint: On a rota day, Jeevan covers the loads at midday, so Jeevan can rest only in the afternoon. What the others need to hear: Leaving the queue costs a porter paid per load about two loads. A porter on a day rate loses nothing.
- Market association. Resource: The loading order. Constraint: Changing the queue rule takes one round's notice, and the loads still have to move: every round the rule runs, someone has to cover them. What the others need to hear: Trucks run late on hot days, so midday is the heaviest unloading.
- Municipal officer. Resource: An operating budget of three units for the whole game, and authority over the public hall. Constraint: Staff money approved now buys cover next round. Hiring on the day costs twice as much and gives less. What the others need to hear: The hall's funding covers the building, not extra staff hours.
- Neighbourhood services coordinator. Resource: A caretaker who can work two blocks a day (one at night) and an attendant who can work one. Constraint: One person, one service, one block at a time. Whoever works the evening is not there next morning. What the others need to hear: Noor's paid hours are the childcare hours. Hira cannot walk to the hall.

Rounds:
1. The forecast (11:40 a.m., the day before the heat)
2. The first hot market day (Midday and afternoon)
3. The hot night and the morning after (Evening and next morning)
4. The second heat alert (Midday and afternoon)

Assumptions:
- Budget, rota days and staff blocks are counted in simple game units, not money or hours from any real place.
- Simplifying assumption: each household has a reserve of 0 to 3 days of money. Losing a day's earnings lowers it by one. Someone pays their own way to a break only if at least one day remains afterwards, so a loss now makes the next break harder, which can mean a further loss. A loss when the reserve is already empty is counted as a day the household could not cover.
- A cool evening adds one day to the reserve of someone who spends it in the hall, standing in for recovering ground before the next day; a solid house does the same for Kiran.
- Money approved ahead buys staff one round later; hiring on the day costs twice as much and gives less. A queue rule agreed now runs from the next round.
- The game counts breaks, earnings and reserves. It does not predict illness or death, and a break in the hall is not a measured health benefit.

The direction of each relationship comes from evidence already on Common Shade. The sizes are the game's own.
- Why a break costs a porter paid per load more than one on a day rate. Piece-rate pay and fixed deadlines that make stopping cost money, and no inspection. Source: NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024 (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)
- Why an open hall can stay unusable for someone who cannot leave work. A cooled building nobody can reach, open at the wrong hours, or a worker who cannot leave work to use it. Source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the GHHIN resource library (https://heathealth.info/wp-content/uploads/cdc_47657_DS1-compressed-1.pdf)
- The same limit for worker cooling stations. A station nobody can leave work to use, or one that closes when the day is hottest. Source: People’s Courage International, 2025: emergency response to the heatwave crisis in South and Southeast Asia (https://www.peoplescourageinternational.org/pdfs/Emergency%20response%20to%20heat%20wave%20crisis%20in%20South%20and%20Southeast%20Asia.pdf)
- Why a hot day without protection lowers earnings. In Singapore, a study of 355 workers found each hot day cost a median S$21, about 24% of a day’s pay. Source: NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024 (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)
- Why traders lose income in a heatwave. Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income. Source: Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024 (https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/press/16737/new-report-by-greenpeace-india-and-national-hawkers-federation-reveals-harsh-heatwave-toll-on-street-vendors/)
- Why informal workers cut hours in the heat. In Bangkok, nearly 80% of informal workers surveyed had cut their hours because of heat. Source: WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand, 2025 (https://www.wiego.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/WIEGO-Policy-Brief-33-Climate-Change-and-Heat-Stress.pdf)
- Why spending that starts when the heat does arrives late. Procurement that starts when the heat does. Source: The Hitavada, 11 May 2026 (https://www.thehitavada.com//Encyc/2026/5/11/green-nets-at-city-squares-relief-measure-or-another-half-planned-half-planned-civic-experiment.html)
- Why money helps most when it arrives in time. Social protection can cushion the income workers lose to extreme heat, if it is designed to arrive in time. Source: ILO: addressing the impacts of extreme heat through social protection (https://www.ilo.org/resource/article/addressing-impacts-extreme-heat-through-social-protection)
- Why the game makes no claim about health outcomes. A 2025 review found no study that measured health outcomes for people using cooling centres; in simulated heatwaves, the benefits were short-lived. That is not evidence of no benefit. Source: Dearman et al., UKHSA, 2025: public health effectiveness of cooling centres, a systematic review (https://researchportal.ukhsa.gov.uk/en/publications/public-health-effectiveness-of-cooling-centres-during-periods-of-/)

Workshop question: In your own market, workplace or neighbourhood, who could change the equivalent of the queue rule?

## State of the field

A monthly briefing on heat resilience in South and Southeast Asia: one argument about what changed, what the evidence establishes, what it could mean for decisions, and what to watch next.

State of the field brings a few selected developments together into one argument, with its limits stated. Signals (https://beattheheat.asia/signals/) follows each outside development on its own, with what the evidence confirms. Watch Common Shade grow (https://beattheheat.asia/growing/) records every change to Common Shade. The evidence map (https://beattheheat.asia/evidence-map/) examines the knowledge base: what is studied and what is not.

Editions: November 2026 (https://beattheheat.asia/whats-new/2026-11/, published 16 November 2026); October 2026 (https://beattheheat.asia/whats-new/2026-10/, published 31 October 2026, revised 16 November 2026).

Questions so far: October 2026: How do heat-health pilots in Southeast Asia keep their institutional footing once their first funding ends? (Revisited in November 2026. New evidence: None was added to the knowledge base by the cut-off. Did the reading change? No: the reading in October stands. Still unresolved: Which parts of a pilot continue after the first grant, and who pays for them.) November 2026: When a heat rule for outdoor work takes effect, what public record would show whether it reaches subcontracted and migrant workers? (Asked in the latest edition; the next edition can revisit it.)

### State of the field: November 2026

**A heat rule for outdoor work is scheduled to take effect; whether rules reach workers is not yet visible**

- Reporting period: 1 to 15 November 2026
- Evidence cut-off: 15 November 2026
- Published: 16 November 2026
- Stable link: https://beattheheat.asia/whats-new/2026-11/

#### The argument

Singapore's heat stress measures for outdoor work, announced on 28 August 2026, are scheduled to become mandatory on 1 December 2026. Two further developments on heat at work were reviewed this month, but rest on secondary reports. None of this yet shows whether rules are applied on worksites, or whom they reach.

What this rests on: One rule checked against its original source, one set of guidelines known only from news reports, and one survey reported by a ministry. Three items do not make a regional trend; they show where evidence of implementation would need to come from.

This month's most consequential date falls just after the cut-off: on 1 December 2026, heat stress measures for outdoor work in Singapore move from advice to requirement. The Philippines issued workplace heat guidelines and compensation rules in October, though their text was not located among the sources checked. A survey in Viet Nam's two largest cities shows why the question matters. What none of these sources can yet show is whether the rules are applied, and whether they reach subcontracted and migrant workers.

#### In brief

Singapore's heat stress measures for outdoor work, announced on 28 August 2026, are scheduled to become mandatory on 1 December 2026. Two further developments on heat at work were reviewed this month, but rest on secondary reports. None of this yet shows whether rules are applied on worksites, or whom they reach.
- Singapore's heat stress measures for outdoor work become mandatory on 1 December: Announced on 28 August 2026 and scheduled to take effect on 1 December 2026; the date alone will not show compliance.
- The Philippines issues heat stress guidelines and compensation rules, as reported: Reported on 24 and 27 October 2026; the advisory texts were not located among the sources checked.
- A survey of outdoor workers in Viet Nam shows why the question matters: A 2026 survey in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, reported by a ministry, found most outdoor workers report a heat-related health problem during heatwaves; it is a finding, not a rule.
Opportunity: Making a workplace heat rule checkable. A rule's value shows in how it is applied; published inspection findings on heat would let workers, employers and funders see that, and no source checked shows such findings yet.
Open question: When a heat rule for outdoor work takes effect, what public record would show whether it reaches subcontracted and migrant workers?

#### Developments worth understanding

##### Singapore's heat stress measures for outdoor work become mandatory on 1 December

- Happened: 28 August 2026 (Announced; scheduled to take effect on 1 December 2026)
- Reviewed by Common Shade: 15 November 2026
- Outside this edition's period. Why it is here: Announced in August, before this edition's period, and first reviewed by Common Shade on 15 November 2026. It is included because it takes effect two weeks after the cut-off, which makes it the month's most consequential date.

Common Shade's reading: A requirement, rather than advice, can give workers, worker organisations and inspectors a common standard to refer to. Its value will show in how it is applied, which no source can show before 1 December.

What the sources establish:

- The Ministry of Manpower announced on 28 August 2026 enhancements to its heat stress framework that take effect on 1 December 2026. [1] Establishes: The announcement and the effective date. It does not establish how compliance will be inspected or reported.
- A legal update describes the measures, including drinking water, as mandatory for outdoor work from 1 December 2026. [2] Establishes: What the measures include, as read by a law firm. It is a secondary account, not the legal text.

Limits:

- An effective date is not compliance.
- How the measures reach subcontracted and migrant workers is not assessed in the sources checked.

What would strengthen or change this reading: Inspection or enforcement reports after 1 December 2026, and the legal text that sets the duties.

##### The Philippines issues heat stress guidelines and compensation rules, as reported

- Happened: 27 October 2026 (Guidelines reported issued (compensation rules on 24 October, workplace guidelines on 27 October))
- Reviewed by Common Shade: 15 November 2026
- Outside this edition's period. Why it is here: Issued in late October and first reviewed by Common Shade in November. Included because it adds compensation for heat illness to workplace rules, a step beyond prevention.

Common Shade's reading: Compensation rules would mean heat illness at work is recognised as a work injury, which matters for workers' income when heat stops work. That reading depends on the text, which has not been seen.

What the sources establish:

- The Department of Labor and Employment issued guidelines requiring employers to protect workers from heat stress during El Niño. [3] Establishes: That a news report describes the guidelines. The advisory text itself, its coverage and its effective date are not verified.
- The Department set out how heat stress and heat-related illness at work are compensated. [4] Establishes: That a news report describes the rules. Claims filed or paid are not verified.

Limits:

- Both items rest on news reports; the original advisories were not located among the sources checked.
- Guidelines are not implementation, and compensation rules are not compensation paid.

What would strengthen or change this reading: The advisory texts, and compensation claims for heat illness being filed and paid.

##### A survey of outdoor workers in Viet Nam shows why the question matters

- Happened: June 2026 (Survey reported)
- Reviewed by Common Shade: 15 November 2026
- Outside this edition's period. Why it is here: Reported in June 2026 and first reviewed by Common Shade in November. Included as context for the rules above: it describes the exposure the rules address, in two of the region's largest cities.

Common Shade's reading: Self-reported problems at this scale suggest the exposure that workplace rules address is common in large cities, not confined to a few trades.

What the sources establish:

- A 2026 study with UNDP surveyed 734 outdoor workers in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City; 94% reported at least one heat-related health problem while working during heatwaves. [5] Establishes: What workers reported, as summarised by a ministry. The answers are self-reported, and how workers were sampled is not known until the original study is read.

Limits:

- A secondary summary of the study, not the study itself.
- Self-reported health problems are not diagnoses, and the sample may not represent all outdoor workers.

What would strengthen or change this reading: The original study, with its sampling and questions, and whether Viet Nam's labour or social protection rules add heat.

#### An opportunity the evidence supports

##### Making a workplace heat rule checkable

A rule's value shows in how it is applied; published inspection findings on heat would let workers, employers and funders see that, and no source checked shows such findings yet.

- The problem: Outdoor workers covered by new heat rules, including subcontracted and migrant workers who may be hardest to reach.
- What to examine: Published inspection or enforcement findings on heat measures, by sector and by type of employment, so a rule's reach can be seen.
- The evidence:
  - How compliance with Singapore's measures will be inspected and reported is not set out in the sources checked. [1] Establishes: That the announcement sets the duties and the date. It does not describe reporting.
  - For the Philippines guidelines, the advisory texts, coverage and effective dates were not located among the sources checked. [3] Establishes: Only that a news report describes the guidelines.
- Its limits: Inspection records show what inspectors find, not every workplace. Publishing findings depends on the inspectorate's own rules and capacity.
- Who could take part (a proposal): A possible arrangement, for discussion. No organisation has agreed to it. Authorise: The authorities that set workplace rules. Deliver: Labour inspectorates, with employers' and workers' organisations. Finance: Public budgets, with philanthropy or research funding for an independent review. Maintain: Labour inspectorates and worker organisations.
- The main unresolved dependency: Whether inspection findings are recorded by sector and type of employment, and can be published.
- A next question to check locally: Ask the labour inspectorate where you work whether heat measures are part of its inspections, and whether its findings are published.

#### A question that matters for action

##### What public record would show whether a heat rule at work reaches the workers it covers?

> When a heat rule for outdoor work takes effect, what public record would show whether it reaches subcontracted and migrant workers?

- Why it matters now: A rule takes effect in Singapore on 1 December, and guidelines were reported in the Philippines in October. The first months after a rule takes effect are when a record of its reach is cheapest to start.
- What is known: The rules and their dates are known from an official announcement and from news reports. Most outdoor workers surveyed in Viet Nam's two largest cities report heat-related health problems.
- What is not known: How compliance is inspected and recorded, and whether records distinguish subcontracted and migrant workers.
- Which decision depends on it: Whether worker organisations, inspectorates and funders invest in monitoring a rule's reach, and what that monitoring records.
- What could answer it: An account from an inspectorate of how heat is inspected, or an independent review of a rule's first season, recording who is covered (our suggestion).

Revisiting the October 2026 question (How do heat-health pilots in Southeast Asia keep their institutional footing once their first funding ends?): new evidence: None was added to the knowledge base by the cut-off. Did the reading change? No: the reading in October stands. Still unresolved: Which parts of a pilot continue after the first grant, and who pays for them.

#### What to watch

- Singapore's measures after 1 December 2026. Evidence that would matter: Inspection or enforcement reports, and the legal text.
- The Philippines advisories. Evidence that would matter: The advisory texts, with coverage and effective dates.
- COP31's outcome on health and heat. Evidence that would matter: The closing synthesis on Signals, written only after review.

#### For your work

- City and public-service teams: Which outdoor workers does your city employ or contract, and would they be covered by a national heat rule?
- Worker and community organisations: When a heat rule takes effect, who will workers tell if it is not applied, and is that recorded?
- Funders and philanthropic institutions: Would support for an independent review of a heat rule's first season show more than support for another pilot?
- Researchers and ecosystem builders: What would an inspection record need to hold to show a rule's reach by type of employment?

#### On Common Shade this month

Signals now tracks each commitment deliverable by deliverable, with what the evidence confirms. Every city page has heat today and heat over time, with a check that withdrew Bangkok's daytime trends after a change at the station. A policy brief sets out how social security could cushion lost work in the heat.

## The learning agenda: questions the evidence has not yet answered

https://beattheheat.asia/evidence-map/

What we have restates the limits the cited studies give themselves; what could answer it and the scale are our suggestions. Advanced means new evidence narrows a question; it is not an answer.

- How much of the load on clinics in South and Southeast Asia during a heatwave is heat illness, and which early actions lower it? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A global health assessment that does not give Asia’s share, and one before-and-after evaluation in Ahmedabad where other changes may explain part of the effect. Work under way (not yet an answer): Singapore's HEAT-MAP study is building a fuller picture of how common heat-related illness is now and could become, with findings used to help older people recognise its symptoms. (Ministry of Health, Singapore: Using findings of HEAT-MAP study to help elderly recognise common symptoms of heat-related illnesses, 2026, https://www.moh.gov.sg/newsroom/using-findings-of-heat-map-study-to-help-elderly-recognise-common-symptoms-of-heat-related-illnesses-and-seek-timely-medical-advice/) What could answer it: Compare clinic records across hot seasons in cities with and without early-warning plans. Scale: Two or three cities, two seasons

- How many heat deaths go uncounted, and which ways of counting close the gap? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Official counts that rise partly because reporting improves, and part-season counts that show the gap but not the true toll. What could answer it: Compare excess deaths with recorded heat deaths in a few districts, and test simple reporting changes. Scale: A few districts, one or two seasons

- Does money spent on prevention before summer reduce what is spent during heatwaves? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: One modelled estimate for Bangkok, multi-hazard estimates, and a review of heat plans as they stood in 2023. Work under way (not yet an answer): Bangkok’s 2026 financing strategy costs the city’s heat plan and proposes climate budgeting to identify and report adaptation spending. Spending tagged this way over several seasons could show what a city spends before heatwaves. (UNDP and Bangkok Metropolitan Administration: Bangkok's financing strategy for tackling urban heat, 2026, https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2026-10/en-undp-bma_financial_strategy_on_urban_heat.pdf) What could answer it: Track what a city spends before and during heatwaves over several seasons, with its health and work outcomes. Scale: One or two cities, three seasons

- How often does heat illness lead households to borrow, and how much? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Studies of household debt that do not measure heat’s part, and an older national survey of all medicine costs. What could answer it: Follow households through a hot season with a short monthly survey of illness, costs and loans. Scale: Two countries, one season

- How do small firms and their lenders in Asia respond when a heatwave empties streets and shops? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Evidence from rich economies and from Mexico, an industry statement naming heat among several causes, and one self-reported survey of vendors in Delhi. What could answer it: With willing lenders, compare microfinance repayments against daily heat records. Scale: Two or three lenders, two seasons

- Who cannot afford to keep cool, measured directly rather than estimated? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A global model that estimates the risk of lacking cooling from income, power and heat data. What could answer it: Add a few cooling questions to an existing national household survey. Scale: One country, one survey round

- How much learning do children lose in hot classrooms and heat closures in Asia? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Strong evidence from schools in the United States, and counts of closures in Asia that measure days lost rather than learning lost. What could answer it: Compare learning results with classroom temperatures over a school year. Scale: One country, one school year

- When heat cuts a harvest, how often does debt follow, and what helps farmers recover? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A debated national association, and studies from single sites or single crops. What could answer it: Follow farm households across seasons, linking heat to yields, loans and recovery. Scale: Two regions, three seasons

- When Asian cities add parks and trees, do rents rise and do residents move? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A multi-city study with no Asian cities, mostly US reviews, and one qualitative study in Bangkok. What could answer it: Track rents and who lives where around new green spaces, before and after. Scale: Two cities, three years

- Which street trees in humid Asian cities survive repeated heatwaves, and what care keeps them alive? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Tree-loss figures from Berlin, and a global comparison of species’ natural climate ranges. What could answer it: Survey street-tree survival after each hot season, with watering and care records. Scale: Two cities, three seasons

- Does heat, on its own, push people to move within Asian countries, and where do they land? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Worst-case scenarios to 2050 that cover every climate driver together, not heat alone. What could answer it: Link existing migration surveys with local heat records. Scale: One or two countries

- How large are uninsured losses from heat, and could money arranged in advance narrow the gap? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Figures for all natural catastrophes together, and a qualitative regional review. What could answer it: Estimate uninsured heat losses for one sector in one country, and test a pre-arranged payout design. Scale: One sector, one country

- Which protections lower heat risks in pregnancy in South and Southeast Asia: rest and lighter work, cooler homes, antenatal advice, or cash that lets women stop work? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A review of 70 studies in 27 countries, only seven of them low- or middle-income, and one cohort of 800 working women in Tamil Nadu; none tests what reduces the risk. What could answer it: Add heat exposure and simple protections to antenatal records in a few districts, and compare outcomes across hot seasons. Scale: Two or three districts, two to three years

- How hot do labour wards and newborn units get in a heatwave, and what keeps them safe when the power fails? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A WHO, UNICEF and UNFPA call to action that names heat among the risks to mothers and newborns, and no measurements from facilities in the region that we have found. What could answer it: Log indoor temperatures and power cuts in a sample of facilities through one hot season, alongside any cooling and back-up power they have. Scale: Twenty to thirty facilities, one season

- Beyond farm households in India, how does heat affect self-harm and suicide across South and Southeast Asia, and does income support in bad seasons reduce it? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: One national study of India over 47 years linking heat in the growing season to suicides through crop losses; little from cities or other countries. What could answer it: Link daily temperatures with suicide and self-harm records where they exist, and study districts where crop insurance or cash reached households in bad years. Scale: Two or three countries, existing records

- Why is heat linked to more intimate partner violence in South Asia, and do income support, cooler homes or women’s groups weaken the link? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A cross-sectional study of 194,871 women in India, Nepal and Pakistan, using yearly temperatures; it shows an association, not the reasons for it. What could answer it: Add heat and household strain questions to existing violence surveys, and compare places with and without seasonal income support. Scale: Existing surveys, with a qualitative study in a few districts

- How much does heat add to diarrhoea and undernutrition in young children in the region, and how much do safe water and oral rehydration offset it? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A review of 26 studies finding about 7% more diarrhoea per 1 °C, uneven across regions and with signs of publication bias. What could answer it: Combine clinic records of child diarrhoea with temperature and water-supply data in a few towns over several seasons. Scale: Three to five towns, three seasons

- Do heat warnings people can understand, with help to travel, get disabled and housebound older people to care sooner? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Interviews in Bangladesh and Thailand describe barriers and reliance on family; no evaluation of a support package in the region. What could answer it: Offer accessible warnings and assisted transport in some neighbourhoods and compare time to care with similar neighbourhoods. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over one hot season

- Does a practical cooling package for workers' dormitories improve sleep after hot shifts? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Migrant workers in Singapore link hot dormitories with poor sleep; no tested dormitory intervention in the region. What could answer it: Compare sleep, next-day tiredness and costs in dormitories with and without simple cooling changes. Scale: Illustrative: a few dormitories over six weeks

- Do reliable drinking water and planned breaks help school-age adolescents protect themselves from heat? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A study of young adults aged 19 to 24 in Yogyakarta; younger adolescents were not included. What could answer it: Compare protective habits and symptoms in schools with and without water points and break schedules. Scale: Illustrative: twenty schools over one hot season

- How does indoor heat affect health and care-seeking in the first weeks after birth? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Guidance in India covers breastfeeding and infant care in heat, but no study in the region measures postpartum heat outcomes. What could answer it: Follow mothers and babies after birth with indoor temperature sensors and records of symptoms and clinic visits. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred mothers over two hot seasons

- What stops people without secure housing from using a nearby cool place during hot spells? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Research on people without secure housing in Nagpur and Delhi exists, but outcome evidence is thin. What could answer it: Ask people without secure housing about the barriers, then test changes to opening hours, location and outreach. Scale: Illustrative: two cities over one hot season

- Which repeated heat exposures lead to kidney harm that lasts beyond the hot season? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Single tests in Tamil Nadu and self-reports in Thailand raise the concern; persistent harm and other causes are hard to separate, and heat alone does not explain Sri Lanka's kidney disease of unknown cause. What could answer it: Follow workers before, during and after the hot season, with personal exposure, drinking and repeat kidney tests at least three months apart. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred workers over two hot seasons

- When does borrowing for treatment and lost income in a heatwave leave debt outstanding after the season? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Worker accounts from Dhaka describe borrowing; repayment over time is rarely tracked. What could answer it: Keep monthly household accounts alongside illness records and local heat, with cooler months for comparison. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over two years

- Does a cooler night help people recover for the next day's work without adding costs they cannot afford? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Studies link heat with poorer sleep, and small roof comparisons measured daytime heat; the two have not been tested together in the region. What could answer it: Try night cooling in a crossover design, measuring bedroom heat, sleep, next-day function and spending. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred workers over six weeks

- How does heat shift unpaid care, housework and paid work done at home? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Surveys show heat getting in the way of housework and care competing with paid work, but little time accounting. What could answer it: Collect time diaries from several household members in hot and cooler weeks, with indoor heat. Scale: Illustrative: two hundred households

- Does repeated heat at home affect babies' growth, once diet and infections are taken into account? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A study in Bangladesh was found but its full text could not be checked, so no effect is shown on the map. What could answer it: Follow families from pregnancy into infancy with home heat, feeding, infections and measured growth. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred families over two years

- How much extra heat do people face when the power fails during a hot, low-water spell? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Utility accounts record supply limits, and cyclone research finds humid heat soon after storms; household heat during outages is rarely measured. What could answer it: Link outage logs with indoor sensors and daily symptoms, comparing areas with faster and slower restoration. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over one hot season

- Does one warning for heat and polluted air together protect people better than two separate warnings? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Thai research finds pollution more deadly on hot days, but heat and pollution do not always peak together. What could answer it: Compare warning formats across similar communities, measuring understanding, behaviour and personal exposure. Scale: Illustrative: two dozen communities over one hot season

- Do learning spaces built for storms and heat together keep more children learning through both? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Cox's Bazar has a rebuilt centre with fans and solar backup, without a comparison of heat or attendance. What could answer it: Compare indoor heat, closures and attendance in rebuilt and similar centres through a hot season and a storm season. Scale: Illustrative: twenty learning centres over a year

- Can cooling for staff reduce heat strain while keeping infection protection in place? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Health workers reported heat symptoms in protective clothing, and a small test found an iced drink improved comfort. What could answer it: Test staff cooling in a crossover trial under infection-control rules, measuring heat strain, symptoms and tasks. Scale: Illustrative: about eighty health workers in four facilities

- Do heat and later floods leave the same households less able to recover than either alone? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Pakistan's 2022 assessment records food pressures building from heat to floods, but not for the same households. What could answer it: Follow households hit by both and by one, recording harvests, food and recovery spending. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over two farming seasons

- Does keeping soils moist lower afternoon heat without raising the humid heat that farmworkers feel? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Research on India's 2015 heatwave links drying soils to the heat, and irrigation research shows cooler but more humid air. What could answer it: Compare matched fields with different soil-moisture practices, measuring air heat, humid heat and soil water. Scale: Illustrative: twenty to thirty paired fields over two hot seasons

- Do earnings lost or health costs paid in a heatwave make cooling harder to afford the next season? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Income shapes which cooling households own, but the steps from lost earnings to debt to less cooling are not tracked. What could answer it: Follow households monthly through heat, earnings, illness costs, debt, electricity spending and actual cooling use. Scale: Illustrative: several hundred households over two hot seasons

- Does moving air conditioner condensers lower street heat and later electricity use in real neighbourhoods? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A model of Rajkot city blocks suggests it could; it has not been tested in occupied buildings. What could answer it: Compare paired buildings before and after moving condensers, with outdoor and indoor sensors and electricity meters. Scale: Illustrative: a dozen to twenty buildings over one hot season

- Does a hot, short night raise the next day's heat strain during ordinary work? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Small laboratory studies found no overall rise after short sleep, but they did not test long humid workdays. What could answer it: Measure bedroom heat, sleep, next-day exposure and heat strain repeatedly in working people, without depriving anyone of sleep. Scale: Illustrative: a hundred or more workers over four to six weeks

- How well do national estimates of work lost to heat describe workers on the Maldives' outer islands? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A national model with stated limits on local data and on assumptions about workers. What could answer it: Compare personal heat, rest time and output across matched workplaces on several islands. Scale: Illustrative: about a hundred workers on six islands over one hot season

- Do heat symptoms and clinic visits differ between lowland, hill and highland settlements? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Nepal has workplace measurements in the Tarai and studies of warming by altitude, but no linked comparison. What could answer it: Use the same sensors and symptom definitions across altitudes, linked to clinic records. Scale: Illustrative: a dozen settlements across three altitudes over two hot seasons

- How many heat-related clinic visits can a linked reporting pilot find where national profiles leave the field empty? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Timor-Leste's profile leaves heat-related deaths and illness unspecified, alongside an approved health adaptation plan. What could answer it: Pilot agreed case definitions, daily weather links and record checks in a few facilities. Scale: Illustrative: four health facilities for six months

- Does cooling matched to local heat reduce strain in homes without adding bills people cannot afford? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Short laboratory trials show fans help in some conditions and not others; there is no household evidence in the region. What could answer it: Compare supported cooling packages in occupied homes, with consent, health oversight and cost tracking. Scale: Illustrative: about a hundred households in contrasting climates over one hot season

- Does pay-per-use cold storage cut food losses and leave producers better off after fees? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A pilot in Muzaffarpur, India, offered pay-per-use storage; its outcomes have not been independently checked. What could answer it: Phase access in with comparison producers, temperature logs and accounts of what producers earn after fees. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred producers at four markets over two harvests

- How long does protection last after people leave a cooling space? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A review found only short-lived benefits in simulations and no real-world health outcomes for users. What could answer it: Follow consenting users and similar non-users through the rest of hot days, measuring exposure and health. Scale: Illustrative: about 150 people over six hot weeks

- Can heat plans, budgets and cooling spaces keep running through a heatwave longer than any on record? [open; open 2026-11-16] What we have: A 2026 modelling study projects that some future heatwaves in India and Pakistan could outlast the 2019 heatwave, the region’s reference event, even with low emissions. A 2025 study projects that far more people in Southeast Asia could face a week or more of extreme humid heat stress. What could answer it: Test one city’s plan, budget and staffing against a heatwave twice as long as its worst on record, with each department that would run it. Scale: Illustrative: one city, a two-day exercise with each lead department

## Heat Tool Finder

https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/

Which heat tool fits the decision in front of you? Find tools for warnings, risk assessment, cooling and protection planning. Compare what they need, what they produce, and where their limits matter.

A navigation and comparison service. Inclusion is not endorsement or certification. Check local applicability, current source information and professional requirements before relying on a tool. Common Shade has not run any of these tools; reviewed never means validated or certified.

### Country services and assessments
Named coverage of one country. Coverage is not local validation.
- ARTPARK heat-risk forecasting (Karnataka) (ARTPARK (IISc), with KSNDMC, KSDMA and the Karnataka Department of Health; Tool: modelling; Source description found; further checks needed): Sub-district heat-risk predictions up to seven days ahead, built with Government of Karnataka bodies. No public view of the forecasts was found. Important limit: A forecast horizon is not evidence of accuracy; no validation is published on the page. Coverage: Country specific: India. ### Broader tools to assess locally
Global or multi-region coverage. Not validated for a particular place in Asia: check it against local conditions.
- Bureau of Meteorology climate driver update (Australian Bureau of Meteorology; Dataset: data portal; Source description found; further checks needed): ENSO and Indian Ocean Dipole monitoring with recent weekly index values and the Bureau's model outlook. Important limit: Weekly values move from week to week; they are not the three-month index used to declare an event. Coverage: Global. Access: Free to read; Reuse licence not verified. Public description reviewed, 2026-11-26. Source: https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/enso/ Profile: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/bom_enso/
- CHIRTS-ERA5 daily temperature and heat data (UC Santa Barbara Climate Hazards Center; Dataset; Public documentation reviewed): Analyse recent and past daily heat across a quasi-global high-resolution grid. Important limit: A gridded estimate built partly from reanalysis, not a local measurement; outdoor grid values do not describe indoor rooms or specific workloads. Coverage: Global. Access: Free to read; Reuse licence not verified. Public description reviewed, 2026-11-17. Source: https://chc.ucsb.edu/node/499 Profile: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/chirts_era5/
- ClimateCHIP WorkHeat (ClimateCHIP; Tool: modelling; Public documentation reviewed): Explore modelled heat challenges for work today and in future climates. Important limit: Modelled output losses are not measured wages. Grid estimates cannot clear an individual worker for work. Coverage: Global. Access: Access terms not verified; Reuse licence not verified. Public description reviewed, 2026-11-10. Source: https://www.climatechip.org/heat-effects-assessment-tool Profile: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/workheat/
- Copernicus ERA5-HEAT (Copernicus / ECMWF; Dataset; Public documentation reviewed): Analyse historical outdoor thermal conditions. Important limit: Reanalysis is not a local measurement; outdoor grid estimates do not describe indoor rooms or specific workloads. Coverage: Global (except Antarctica). Access: Registration needed for data; Reuse licence not verified. Public description reviewed, 2026-11-10. Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/derived-utci-historical?tab=overview Profile: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/era5/
- GHHIN Heat Tool Directory (GHHIN; Directory; Public documentation reviewed): Discover additional operational heat-health resources. Important limit: A listing is not an independent validation. Verify each underlying resource's coverage and current operation. Coverage: Several regions. Access: Free to read; Reuse licence not verified. Public description reviewed, 2026-11-10. Source: https://heathealth.info/tools-products-and-services/ Profile: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/ghhin/
- IFC EDGE (IFC; Tool: modelling; Public documentation reviewed): Explore building resource-efficiency options, including cooling-related design. Important limit: Energy savings do not demonstrate safe indoor conditions during extreme heat. Software access and certification costs are separate. Coverage: Coverage set by the provider; check your country. Access: Free to use, as the provider describes it; Reuse licence not verified. Public description reviewed, 2026-11-10. Source: https://www.ifc.org/en/pressroom/2023/ifc-recognizes-20-global-edge-champions-for-sustainable-building-commitment Profile: https://beattheheat.asia/heat-tools/edge/
